subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define anatomical position.
answer_html:
Definition Anatomical position is the standard reference position of the body used all over the world to describe the location of body parts. Because everyone uses the same position, words like "above", "front" or "outer side" mean the same thing to every doctor and nurse.

Features of the anatomical position

  1. Body stands erect (upright)
  2. Head, face and eyes look straight forward
  3. Upper limbs hang by the sides of the trunk
  4. Palms face forward – thumbs point away from the body
  5. Feet are together with the toes pointing forward

Importance: anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, proximal and distal are always described in this position, even when the patient is lying in bed.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the planes of the body.
answer_html:
Introduction A plane is an imaginary flat surface that passes through the body. Planes help us describe sections (cuts) of the body seen in CT and MRI scans.

Planes of the body

  1. Median (mid-sagittal) plane – vertical plane through the midline; divides the body into equal right and left halves
  2. Sagittal (para-sagittal) plane – any vertical plane parallel to the median plane; gives unequal right and left parts
  3. Coronal (frontal) plane – vertical plane at right angles to the median plane; divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts
  4. Transverse (horizontal/axial) plane – divides the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts
  5. Oblique plane – any slanting plane between the above

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: List the cavities of the body.
answer_html:
Introduction Body cavities are closed spaces that hold and protect the internal organs.

1. Dorsal (posterior) cavity

  • Cranial cavity – contains the brain
  • Vertebral (spinal) canal – contains the spinal cord

2. Ventral (anterior) cavity

  • Thoracic cavity – two pleural cavities (lungs), pericardial cavity (heart), and the mediastinum (heart, great vessels, oesophagus, trachea)
  • Abdominopelvic cavity
    • Abdominal cavity – stomach, liver, spleen, intestines, kidneys
    • Pelvic cavity – urinary bladder, rectum, internal reproductive organs

The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define the terms flexion, extension, abduction and adduction.
answer_html:
Introduction These are the basic movements that take place at joints. Nurses use them while doing range-of-motion exercises and positioning patients.

Definitions

  1. Flexion – bending movement that decreases the angle between two parts (bending the elbow or knee)
  2. Extension – straightening movement that increases the angle (straightening the knee)
  3. Abduction – movement away from the midline of the body (raising the arm sideways)
  4. Adduction – movement towards the midline (bringing the arm back to the side)

Memory aid: abduction takes the limb away – like abducting (kidnapping) someone; adduction adds the limb back to the body.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Draw a labelled diagram of simple cuboidal epithelium.
answer_html:
Definition Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-shaped cells whose height and width are about equal. Each cell has a round, centrally placed nucleus, and all cells rest on a basement membrane.

Sites

  • Tubules of the kidney
  • Follicles of the thyroid gland
  • Small ducts of glands
  • Surface of the ovary (germinal epithelium)

Functions: secretion and absorption.

How to draw: a row of squares sitting on a thin line (basement membrane), with a dark round dot (nucleus) in the centre of each square; label the free surface, nucleus, cell and basement membrane.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the types of cartilage with one example of each.
answer_html:
Definition Cartilage is a firm but flexible connective tissue made of cells (chondrocytes) lying in spaces called lacunae inside a gel-like matrix. It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.

Types of cartilage

  1. Hyaline cartilage – the commonest; smooth and glassy
    • Example: articular cartilage of joints, costal cartilages, rings of the trachea
  2. Fibrocartilage – the strongest; contains thick bundles of collagen fibres
    • Example: intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci of the knee
  3. Elastic cartilage – most flexible; contains elastic fibres
    • Example: pinna (auricle) of the ear, epiglottis

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the phases of mitosis.
answer_html:
Definition Mitosis is the type of cell division in which one cell divides into two identical daughter cells, each with 46 chromosomes. It helps in growth and in repair of tissues.

Phases of mitosis

  1. Prophase – chromosomes become thick and visible; the nuclear membrane disappears; spindle fibres form
  2. Metaphase – chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell
  3. Anaphase – the two chromatids of each chromosome separate and move to opposite poles
  4. Telophase – a nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes
  5. Cytokinesis – the cytoplasm divides to give two cells

Note: interphase is the preparatory stage before mitosis, when DNA is copied.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Classify epithelial tissue with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Epithelial tissue (epithelium) is the tissue that covers body surfaces, lines cavities and tubes, and forms glands. It is the body's first line of contact with the outside world.

1. Characteristics of epithelium

  • Cells are closely packed with very little intercellular substance
  • Rests on a basement membrane
  • No blood vessels – nourished by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue
  • Has a free surface facing a lumen or the outside
  • Regenerates quickly – lost cells are rapidly replaced

2. Classification – based on the number of layers and the shape of the cells

A. Simple epithelium (one layer of cells)

Type Shape Sites Function
Simple squamous flat, like floor tiles alveoli of lungs, lining of heart and blood vessels (endothelium), Bowman's capsule diffusion, filtration
Simple cuboidal cube-shaped kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, gland ducts secretion, absorption
Simple columnar tall, pillar-like stomach, intestine (with microvilli and goblet cells) secretion, absorption
Ciliated columnar tall, with cilia fallopian tubes moves the ovum
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar looks layered but is a single layer trachea, bronchi traps and sweeps mucus

B. Stratified (compound) epithelium (many layers)

  • Stratified squamous keratinised – epidermis of skin; tough and waterproof
  • Stratified squamous non-keratinised – mouth, oesophagus, vagina, cornea; resists friction
  • Transitional epithelium – urinary bladder, ureters; cells change shape and stretch as the organ fills
  • Stratified cuboidal / columnar – ducts of sweat glands, part of the male urethra (rare)

C. Special forms

  • Glandular epithelium – forms glands (thyroid, salivary glands)
  • Neuroepithelium – sensory cells of taste buds, retina, olfactory area

3. Functions of epithelium

  • Protection, absorption, secretion, excretion, filtration, diffusion of gases and sensation

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • The Pap smear samples the cervix where columnar and squamous epithelium meet – the zone where cervical cancer starts
  • In smokers, ciliated epithelium of the airway changes to squamous type (metaplasia), so mucus is not cleared
  • Most cancers (carcinomas) arise from epithelium

Conclusion Epithelium is classified by layers and cell shape, and each type is suited to the work of the organ it lines.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the membranes of the body.
answer_html:
Introduction A membrane is a thin, pliable sheet of tissue that covers a surface, lines a cavity or divides a space. Most body membranes are made of epithelium resting on connective tissue.

1. Mucous membrane (mucosa)

  • Lines cavities and tubes that open to the outside – digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive tracts
  • Made of epithelium on a layer of loose connective tissue (lamina propria)
  • Goblet cells secrete mucus
  • Functions: keeps the surface moist, traps dust and microbes, protects against digestive enzymes, helps absorption (intestine)

2. Serous membrane (serosa)

  • Lines closed body cavities and covers the organs inside them
  • Has two layers:
    • Parietal layer – lines the wall of the cavity
    • Visceral layer – covers the organ
  • A thin film of serous fluid between the two layers prevents friction when organs move
  • Examples: pleura (lungs), pericardium (heart), peritoneum (abdominal organs)

3. Cutaneous membrane

  • The skin – stratified squamous keratinised epithelium on the dermis
  • Dry, waterproof, protective

4. Synovial membrane

  • Lines the cavities of freely movable joints, bursae and tendon sheaths
  • Made of connective tissue only (no epithelium)
  • Secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and nourishes the articular cartilage

5. Other membranes

  • Meninges – cover the brain and spinal cord
  • Periosteum – covers bones

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Inflammation gives pleurisy, pericarditis, peritonitis, synovitis and meningitis
  • Fluid collecting between serous layers causes pleural effusion, pericardial effusion and ascites
  • Mucous membranes are a route of entry for infection and of drugs (sublingual, rectal, vaginal)

Summary table

Membrane Location Secretion Function
Mucous lines openings to the exterior – GI, respiratory, urinary, reproductive tracts mucus protection, lubrication, absorption
Serous lines closed body cavities – pleura, pericardium, peritoneum serous fluid reduces friction between organs
Cutaneous skin sweat, sebum protection, temperature regulation
Synovial lines joint cavities synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes joints

Conclusion Membranes protect, lubricate and separate organs; their inflammation and fluid collections are common in clinical practice.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Classify glands.
answer_html:
Introduction A gland is a single cell or a group of epithelial cells specialised to make and release a secretion such as sweat, mucus, enzymes or hormones.

1. According to the presence of ducts

  • Exocrine glands – pour their secretion through ducts onto a surface or into a cavity (salivary, sweat, gastric glands)
  • Endocrine glands – ductless; release hormones directly into blood (thyroid, pituitary, adrenal)
  • Mixed (heterocrine) glands – have both parts, e.g. pancreas (enzymes through a duct and insulin into blood), ovaries, testes

2. According to the number of cells

  • Unicellular – a single cell, e.g. goblet cells of the intestine and airways
  • Multicellular – most glands of the body

3. According to the shape of the secretory part (exocrine glands)

  • Simple tubular – intestinal glands
  • Simple coiled tubular – sweat glands
  • Simple branched tubular – gastric glands
  • Simple branched alveolar (acinar) – sebaceous glands
  • Compound tubulo-alveolar – salivary glands, pancreas
  • Compound alveolar – mammary glands

4. According to the mode of secretion

  • Merocrine (eccrine) – secretion leaves by exocytosis; the cell stays intact (salivary glands, most sweat glands)
  • Apocrine – the tip of the cell breaks off with the secretion (mammary glands, axillary sweat glands)
  • Holocrine – the whole cell breaks down and becomes the secretion (sebaceous glands)

5. According to the nature of secretion

  • Serous – thin, watery, enzyme-rich (parotid gland)
  • Mucous – thick, slimy (sublingual gland)
  • Mixed – both (submandibular gland)

6. Applied importance

  • Blockage of sebaceous glands causes acne; blocked salivary ducts swell (mumps affects the parotid)
  • Endocrine gland disorders (diabetes, thyroid disease) are lifelong conditions needing nursing care

Exocrine vs endocrine glands

Exocrine glands Endocrine glands
have ducts ductless
secretion poured on a surface or into a cavity secretion (hormone) poured directly into the blood
act locally act on distant target organs
e.g. sweat, salivary, mammary, gastric glands e.g. pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands
Mixed glands (both): pancreas, testes, ovaries

Conclusion Glands are classified by ducts, number of cells, shape, mode and nature of secretion.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Differentiate between skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.

diagram.caption: Three types of muscle tissue
labels: skeletal fibre with striations and peripheral nuclei
smooth muscle spindle cell with central nucleus
cardiac fibres with branches and intercalated discs

answer_html:
Introduction Muscle tissue is specialised for contraction. There are three types, and they differ in structure, control and location.

Differences

Feature Skeletal muscle Smooth muscle Cardiac muscle
Other names striated, voluntary non-striated, involuntary, visceral heart muscle
Location attached to bones by tendons walls of hollow organs (stomach, intestine, uterus, bladder) and blood vessels wall of the heart only
Control voluntary (under our will) involuntary involuntary
Shape of fibre long, cylindrical, unbranched spindle-shaped (tapering ends) short, cylindrical, branched
Nuclei many, at the edge (peripheral) one, central one (sometimes two), central
Striations present absent present
Intercalated discs absent absent present
Nerve supply somatic motor nerves autonomic nerves autonomic nerves, but beats on its own
Speed of contraction fast slow and sustained rhythmic
Fatigue tires easily does not tire easily never tires (works lifelong)
Regeneration limited good very poor (scar after MI)
Example biceps, deltoid, diaphragm muscle of the stomach and uterus myocardium

Points to remember

  • Cardiac muscle is "striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary like smooth muscle"
  • Intercalated discs allow the impulse to spread quickly so the heart contracts as one unit

Applied / nursing importance

  • Skeletal muscle wastes in immobility – passive and active exercises prevent this
  • Smooth muscle spasm causes colic (renal, biliary, intestinal)
  • Damaged cardiac muscle cannot regenerate – an infarct heals by a scar

Properties of muscle tissue (common to all three)

  • Excitability – responds to stimuli
  • Contractility – shortens to produce movement
  • Extensibility – can be stretched
  • Elasticity – returns to its original length after stretching

Common disorders

  • Skeletal muscle – cramps, strains, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis, atrophy due to disuse
  • Smooth muscle – spasm causing colic (intestinal, renal, biliary), bronchospasm in asthma
  • Cardiac muscle – myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias

Conclusion The three types of muscle differ in structure and control, matching the job each one performs.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define cell. Draw a labelled diagram of a typical animal cell and explain the functions of its organelles. (2 + 3 + 5)

diagram.caption: Structure of a typical animal cell

answer_html:
(a) Definition of cell (2 marks)

  • The cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of the body that can carry out all the activities of life – taking in food, producing energy, growing, reproducing and responding to stimuli
  • The adult body has about trillions of cells of more than 200 types (nerve, muscle, blood, epithelial cells and so on)
  • Similar cells group together to form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form systems
  • Size ranges from a few micrometres (red cell about 7.5 µm) to over a metre long (some nerve cells)

Main parts of a cell

  1. Cell membrane
  2. Cytoplasm with organelles
  3. Nucleus

(b) Diagram (3 marks) Draw an oval cell with a large round nucleus near the centre and label:

  • Cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nucleolus, nuclear membrane with pores
  • Mitochondria, rough ER with ribosomes, smooth ER
  • Golgi apparatus, lysosome, centrioles, vacuole
  • Microvilli on one surface

(c) Organelles and their functions (5 marks)

1. Cell (plasma) membrane

  • Thin, flexible covering of the cell, about 7.5 nm thick
  • Made of a double layer of phospholipids with proteins floating in it (fluid mosaic model); cholesterol gives stability
  • Functions:
    • Selectively permeable – decides what enters and leaves
    • Carries receptors for hormones, drugs and neurotransmitters
    • Helps cells recognise and stick to each other

2. Cytoplasm

  • Jelly-like fluid (cytosol) between the membrane and the nucleus
  • Holds the organelles and is the site of many chemical reactions (glycolysis)

3. Nucleus – the control centre

  • Largest organelle; surrounded by a double nuclear membrane with pores
  • Contains chromatin (DNA) – 46 chromosomes in body cells – which carries the genetic code
  • Nucleolus makes ribosomes
  • Functions: controls all activities of the cell, protein synthesis, growth and cell division; passes hereditary characters to daughter cells
  • Mature red cells have no nucleus

4. Mitochondria – "powerhouse of the cell"

  • Rod-shaped organelles with a double membrane; the inner membrane is folded into cristae
  • Produce energy as ATP by aerobic respiration
  • Have their own DNA (inherited from the mother)
  • Plentiful in active cells – heart muscle, liver, kidney tubules

5. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) – a network of membranous channels

  • Rough ER – studded with ribosomes; makes and transports proteins
  • Smooth ER – no ribosomes; makes lipids and steroid hormones, stores calcium in muscle and detoxifies drugs in the liver

6. Ribosomes

  • Tiny granules of RNA and protein, free or attached to rough ER
  • Site of protein synthesis

7. Golgi apparatus (Golgi complex)

  • Stack of flattened sacs near the nucleus
  • Modifies, sorts and packs proteins into vesicles for secretion; forms lysosomes
  • Well developed in secretory cells (pancreas, salivary glands)

8. Lysosomes

  • Small sacs containing powerful digestive enzymes
  • Digest worn-out organelles, bacteria and debris (intracellular digestion)
  • Called "suicide bags" because their rupture can destroy the cell itself

9. Peroxisomes – break down fatty acids and destroy harmful hydrogen peroxide.

10. Centrosome with centrioles

  • A pair of centrioles near the nucleus
  • Form the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart during cell division

11. Cytoskeleton

  • Microtubules and microfilaments
  • Maintain the shape of the cell and help movement of organelles

12. Surface projections

  • Microvilli – increase the surface for absorption (intestine, kidney tubules)
  • Cilia – sweep mucus and particles (trachea, fallopian tube)
  • Flagellum – moves the sperm

Applied / nursing importance

  • Many drugs act on receptors on the cell membrane (insulin, beta-blockers)
  • Cancer is uncontrolled cell division; anticancer drugs and radiation attack rapidly dividing cells, so hair loss, mouth ulcers and low blood counts occur in patients on chemotherapy
  • Mitochondrial damage (cyanide poisoning) stops energy production
  • Lysosomal enzyme defects cause storage diseases

Cell division (in brief)

Point Mitosis Meiosis
Where body (somatic) cells germ cells in the testes and ovaries
Number of divisions one two
Daughter cells 2 4
Chromosomes 46 (diploid) – same as parent 23 (haploid) – half of parent
Genetic make-up identical to the parent cell different (crossing over)
Purpose growth, repair, replacement formation of sperm and ova
  • Phases of mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis; interphase is the resting (growing) stage between divisions
  • Applied: uncontrolled mitosis leads to cancer; errors in meiosis cause chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21)

Conclusion The cell is a complete living unit; each organelle has a definite job, and disease often begins with damage at the cell level.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define anatomy. Name its branches.
answer_html:
Definition Anatomy is the science that deals with the structure of the human body and the relationship of its parts. The word comes from the Greek ana (up) and tome (cutting) – "cutting up", because it was first studied by dissection.

Branches of anatomy

  1. Gross (macroscopic) anatomy – structures seen with the naked eye
  2. Microscopic anatomy (histology) – tissues and cells studied under the microscope
  3. Developmental anatomy (embryology) – development from fertilisation to birth
  4. Surface anatomy – projection of deeper organs on the body surface
  5. Radiological anatomy – study of structures by X-ray, CT and MRI
  6. Applied (clinical) anatomy – use of anatomy in diagnosis and treatment
  7. Systemic and regional anatomy – study system by system or region by region

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the levels of structural organisation of the human body.
answer_html:
Introduction The human body is organised from the simplest to the most complex level.

Levels of organisation

  1. Chemical level – atoms (carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen) and molecules (water, proteins, DNA)
  2. Cellular level – the cell, the basic structural and functional unit of life
  3. Tissue level – groups of similar cells doing a common function (epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous)
  4. Organ level – two or more tissues forming a structure with a definite function (stomach, heart)
  5. System level – organs working together (digestive system)
  6. Organism level – all systems working together as a living human being

Example: muscle cells → cardiac muscle tissue → heart → cardiovascular system → human body.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the four basic tissues of the body.
answer_html:
Definition A tissue is a group of similar cells and intercellular material that work together to perform a particular function. The study of tissues is histology.

Four basic tissues

  1. Epithelial tissue – covers body surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands (skin epidermis, lining of the gut)
  2. Connective tissue – supports, binds and protects other tissues (bone, cartilage, blood, fat, tendons)
  3. Muscular tissue – produces movement (skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle)
  4. Nervous tissue – receives and conducts impulses (brain, spinal cord, nerves); made of neurons and neuroglia

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Write a note on lysosomes.
answer_html:
Definition Lysosomes are small, membrane-bound vesicles in the cytoplasm that contain powerful digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes. They are formed by the Golgi apparatus.

Functions

  1. Intracellular digestion – digest food particles, bacteria and foreign material taken in by the cell (very active in white blood cells and macrophages)
  2. Autophagy – remove worn-out organelles
  3. Autolysis – after cell death, the enzymes are released and digest the cell; hence lysosomes are called "suicide bags"
  4. Bone resorption by osteoclasts
  5. Help in removal of the uterine lining and other tissue remodelling

Applied: absence of particular lysosomal enzymes causes lysosomal storage diseases (e.g. Tay–Sachs disease).

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell?
answer_html:
Introduction Mitochondria are rod-shaped or oval organelles with two membranes. The inner membrane is folded into cristae, and the inner space (matrix) contains enzymes and their own DNA.

Why "powerhouse"?

  1. They carry out aerobic cellular respiration – the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain
  2. They produce most of the cell's ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency of the cell
  3. Hence cells needing more energy – heart and skeletal muscle, liver, kidney tubules, nerve cells – have more mitochondria

Other points

  • Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother
  • They also help in heat production, calcium storage and programmed cell death (apoptosis)

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Name the nine regions of the abdomen.
answer_html:
Introduction The abdomen is divided into nine regions by two vertical lines (right and left mid-clavicular lines) and two horizontal planes (the transpyloric or subcostal plane above and the transtubercular plane below).

Nine regions

Right Middle Left
right hypochondriac epigastric left hypochondriac
right lumbar umbilical left lumbar
right iliac (inguinal) hypogastric (suprapubic) left iliac (inguinal)

Use: describing the site of pain and organs – e.g. liver in the right hypochondrium, appendix in the right iliac region, full bladder in the hypogastrium.

Four quadrants (a simpler method): right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower quadrants, divided by vertical and horizontal lines through the umbilicus.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define pronation, supination, inversion and eversion.
answer_html:
Introduction These are special movements described from the anatomical position.

Definitions

  1. Pronation – turning the forearm so that the palm faces backwards (or downwards); occurs at the radio-ulnar joints
  2. Supination – turning the forearm so that the palm faces forwards (or upwards), as in holding a bowl of soup; the biceps is a strong supinator
  3. Inversion – turning the sole of the foot inwards (towards the midline)
  4. Eversion – turning the sole of the foot outwards (away from the midline)

Applied: sprains of the ankle usually occur in forced inversion; supination of the forearm is used while giving injections in the forearm and in physiotherapy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Explain the anatomical terms of position and direction with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction To describe the body clearly and without confusion, anatomists use standard terms. All terms are used in relation to the anatomical position – the body standing erect, face forwards, eyes looking straight ahead, arms by the sides with palms facing forwards, and feet together. Nurses use these terms daily while describing wounds, pain, injection sites and findings.

1. Superior and inferior

  • Superior (cranial) – towards the head; the heart is superior to the diaphragm
  • Inferior (caudal) – towards the feet; the stomach is inferior to the diaphragm

2. Anterior and posterior

  • Anterior (ventral) – towards the front; the sternum is anterior to the heart
  • Posterior (dorsal) – towards the back; the kidneys are posterior to the intestines

3. Medial and lateral

  • Medial – nearer to the midline; the ulna is medial to the radius
  • Lateral – away from the midline; the thumb is on the lateral side of the hand
  • Intermediate – between the two; the ring finger is intermediate between the little and middle fingers

4. Proximal and distal (used for limbs)

  • Proximal – nearer to the trunk or point of origin; the elbow is proximal to the wrist
  • Distal – farther from the trunk; the fingers are distal to the wrist

5. Superficial and deep

  • Superficial – nearer to the surface; the skin is superficial to the muscles
  • Deep – farther from the surface; the bones are deep to the muscles

6. Internal and external

  • Used for hollow organs and cavities – the internal surface of the stomach is lined by mucosa; the external ear

7. Ipsilateral and contralateral

  • Ipsilateral – on the same side; the right arm and right leg
  • Contralateral – on the opposite side; a stroke in the left brain causes contralateral (right-sided) paralysis

8. Central and peripheral

  • Central – towards the centre (central nervous system)
  • Peripheral – towards the outer parts (peripheral nerves, peripheral IV line)

9. Palmar, plantar and dorsal

  • Palmar – front of the hand; plantar – sole of the foot; dorsum – back of the hand or top of the foot (dorsalis pedis pulse)

10. Prone and supine

  • Prone – lying face down; supine – lying on the back, face up

Nursing importance

  • Accurate documentation – "a 3 cm laceration on the lateral aspect of the left forearm, 5 cm proximal to the wrist"
  • Correct identification of injection sites, pulse points and positions
  • Clear communication with doctors and other nurses

Conclusion Terms such as superior–inferior, anterior–posterior, medial–lateral, proximal–distal, superficial–deep and ipsilateral–contralateral, used from the anatomical position, allow precise description of the body and accurate nursing records.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the body cavities and the organs they contain.
answer_html:
Introduction A body cavity is a space within the body that contains and protects internal organs. There are two main cavities – the dorsal (posterior) cavity and the ventral (anterior) cavity.

A. Dorsal cavity 1. Cranial cavity

  • Formed by the skull bones
  • Contains the brain, its meninges and the cerebrospinal fluid

2. Vertebral (spinal) canal

  • Formed by the vertebral foramina of the vertebral column
  • Contains the spinal cord, meninges and the roots of spinal nerves
  • Continuous with the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum

B. Ventral cavity Divided by the diaphragm into the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.

1. Thoracic cavity

  • Bounded by the ribs, sternum, thoracic vertebrae and the diaphragm
  • Two pleural cavities – each contains a lung
  • Mediastinum – the central partition between the lungs; contains the heart in the pericardial cavity, the great vessels, trachea, oesophagus, thymus, thoracic duct and nerves

2. Abdominal cavity

  • From the diaphragm above to the pelvic brim below
  • Contains the stomach, small intestine, most of the large intestine, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, ureters (upper parts) and adrenal glands
  • Lined by the peritoneum

3. Pelvic cavity

  • Surrounded by the pelvic bones
  • Contains the urinary bladder, the rectum, the lower parts of the ureters and the reproductive organs – uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries and vagina in females; prostate and seminal vesicles in males

Other small cavities

  • Oral, nasal, orbital, middle ear and synovial (joint) cavities

Membranes lining the cavities

  • Pleura (lungs), pericardium (heart) and peritoneum (abdomen) – serous membranes that reduce friction

Nursing importance

  • Knowledge of cavities helps in understanding referred pain, the spread of infection (peritonitis), collections of fluid (pleural effusion, ascites) and procedures such as thoracentesis, paracentesis and lumbar puncture

Conclusion The dorsal cavity (cranial cavity and vertebral canal) protects the brain and spinal cord, while the ventral cavity, divided by the diaphragm into thoracic and abdominopelvic parts, holds the heart, lungs and the abdominal and pelvic organs.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the types of cartilage.
answer_html:
Introduction Cartilage is a firm, flexible connective tissue. It consists of cells called chondrocytes, lying in small spaces (lacunae), surrounded by a firm, rubbery matrix containing fibres. Most cartilage is covered by a fibrous membrane, the perichondrium, which supplies nutrition. Cartilage has no blood vessels and no nerves, so it receives nutrients by diffusion and heals slowly.

1. Hyaline cartilage

  • The most common type; bluish-white, glassy appearance
  • Matrix contains fine collagen fibres that are not visible under the ordinary microscope
  • Sites:
    • articular surfaces of bones (no perichondrium here)
    • costal cartilages joining ribs to the sternum
    • cartilages of the nose, trachea and bronchi
    • thyroid and cricoid cartilages of the larynx
    • epiphyseal (growth) plates and most of the fetal skeleton
  • Functions: smooth surfaces for joint movement, support, flexibility, and growth of long bones

2. Elastic cartilage

  • Yellowish; matrix contains a network of elastic fibres
  • Very flexible – returns to shape after bending
  • Sites:
    • pinna (auricle) of the external ear
    • epiglottis
    • auditory (Eustachian) tube
    • small cartilages of the larynx (corniculate, cuneiform)
  • Functions: maintains shape while allowing flexibility

3. Fibrocartilage (white fibrocartilage)

  • Matrix contains thick bundles of collagen fibres; no perichondrium
  • The strongest and toughest type; resists pressure and tension
  • Sites:
    • intervertebral discs
    • pubic symphysis
    • menisci of the knee joint
    • articular discs of some joints and the labrum of the hip and shoulder joints
  • Functions: shock absorption and strong support

Comparison

Type Fibres Perichondrium Example
Hyaline fine collagen present (except articular) costal cartilage
Elastic elastic present ear pinna
Fibrocartilage thick collagen bundles absent intervertebral disc

Applied anatomy

  • Osteoarthritis – wear and tear of articular hyaline cartilage
  • Slipped (prolapsed) intervertebral disc – fibrocartilage tears; the nucleus presses on nerves, causing sciatica
  • Meniscal tears in sports injuries
  • Calcification of costal cartilages in the elderly makes the chest wall stiff

Conclusion Cartilage is an avascular connective tissue of three types – hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage – which give smooth joint surfaces, flexible support and shock absorption respectively.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the structure and functions of the cell membrane.

diagram.caption: Fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane

answer_html:
Introduction The cell (plasma) membrane is the thin, flexible outer boundary of the cell, about 7–10 nanometres thick. It separates the cell contents from the surrounding fluid and controls what enters and leaves. Its structure is explained by the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).

A. Structure (fluid mosaic model)

1. Phospholipid bilayer

  • Two layers of phospholipid molecules
  • Each molecule has a hydrophilic (water-loving) head facing outwards and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) tail facing inwards
  • The bilayer is fluid – molecules can move sideways

2. Cholesterol

  • Present between phospholipids; gives stability and controls fluidity

3. Proteins – scattered like a "mosaic"

  • Integral (transmembrane) proteins – pass through the whole membrane; form channels and carriers
  • Peripheral proteins – attached to the inner or outer surface; act as enzymes and support

4. Carbohydrates

  • Attached to proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids) on the outer surface, forming the glycocalyx
  • Act as identity markers – e.g. the ABO blood group antigens on red cells

B. Functions

  1. Protective boundary – encloses and protects the cell contents
  2. Selective permeability – allows some substances to pass and blocks others
  3. Transport of substances:
    • passive – diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion (no energy needed)
    • active – sodium–potassium pump (needs ATP)
    • bulk transport – endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis) and exocytosis
  4. Receptors for hormones, neurotransmitters and drugs (insulin receptors)
  5. Cell recognition and immunity – the immune system recognises "self" and "non-self"
  6. Cell adhesion – joins cells together to form tissues (cell junctions)
  7. Maintains the resting membrane potential – essential for nerve and muscle impulses

Applied importance

  • Many drugs act on membrane receptors and channels (calcium channel blockers, beta blockers)
  • Mismatched blood transfusion – antibodies react with red cell surface antigens
  • IV fluids – the membrane allows water to move by osmosis; wrong fluids can swell or shrink cells

Conclusion The cell membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with cholesterol, proteins and carbohydrates; it protects the cell, controls transport, carries receptors and identity markers, and maintains the membrane potential.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the important bony and surface landmarks used in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Bony landmarks are parts of bones that can be seen or felt under the skin. Surface landmarks are points on the surface that indicate the position of deeper organs. Nurses use them to locate injection sites, pulse points, organs and procedure sites safely.

A. Landmarks of the head, neck and trunk

  1. Mastoid process – bony prominence behind the ear
  2. Spine of C7 (vertebra prominens) – the most prominent spine at the back of the neck; used for counting vertebrae
  3. Suprasternal (jugular) notch – at the upper border of the sternum; trachea felt here
  4. Sternal angle (angle of Louis) – junction of manubrium and body of sternum; at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage; used to count ribs and intercostal spaces
  5. Xiphoid process – lower tip of the sternum; avoid pressing it during CPR
  6. Costal margin – lower border of the rib cage
  7. Umbilicus – at about the level of the L3–L4 disc

B. Landmarks of the limbs and pelvis

  1. Acromion process – tip of the shoulder; the deltoid injection site is about 2.5–5 cm (2–3 finger-breadths) below it
  2. Olecranon process – point of the elbow; medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus
  3. Styloid process of the radius – at the wrist; the radial pulse is felt just medial to it
  4. Iliac crest – a line joining the highest points of the two crests passes through the L4 spine – the landmark for lumbar puncture
  5. Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) – used for the ventrogluteal site and McBurney's point
  6. Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) – used to mark the dorsogluteal site
  7. Greater trochanter of the femur – landmark for the ventrogluteal and vastus lateralis sites
  8. Ischial tuberosity – the bone we sit on; pressure ulcer site in wheelchair users
  9. Patella, tibial tuberosity and the medial and lateral malleoli at the ankle

C. Surface landmarks of organs and procedures

  • Apex beat – left 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
  • McBurney's point – junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus – appendix
  • Chest drain site – 4th or 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line, just above the upper border of a rib
  • Fundal height of the uterus – symphysis pubis, umbilicus and xiphisternum as reference points

D. Landmarks for intramuscular injections

  • Deltoid – 2.5–5 cm below the acromion
  • Ventrogluteal – palm on the greater trochanter, index finger on the ASIS, middle finger along the iliac crest; inject in the "V"
  • Vastus lateralis – middle third of the anterolateral thigh

Conclusion Bony landmarks such as the sternal angle, acromion, iliac crest, ASIS and greater trochanter, and surface landmarks such as the apex beat and McBurney's point, guide nurses in safe injections, procedures and assessment.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe the organ systems of the body with their main organs and functions.
answer_html:
Introduction An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform a common function. The human body has eleven organ systems, and all of them work together to maintain homeostasis – a stable internal environment.

System Main organs Main functions
Integumentary skin, hair, nails, sweat and sebaceous glands protection, temperature regulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis
Skeletal bones, cartilages, joints, ligaments support, protection, movement, blood cell formation, mineral storage
Muscular skeletal muscles, tendons movement, posture, heat production
Nervous brain, spinal cord, nerves, sense organs control and coordination, sensation, thinking, memory
Endocrine pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, gonads control by hormones – growth, metabolism, reproduction
Cardiovascular heart, blood vessels, blood transport of oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes
Lymphatic and immune lymph vessels, lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils return of tissue fluid, immunity, fat absorption
Respiratory nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs gas exchange, voice, acid–base balance
Digestive mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas digestion, absorption, elimination of faeces
Urinary kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra excretion of wastes, water, electrolyte and acid–base balance, BP control
Reproductive testes, ovaries, uterus, ducts, breasts production of gametes and hormones, reproduction

How the systems work together – an example

  • During exercise, the muscular system works harder; the nervous system increases the heart and breathing rates; the respiratory system brings in more oxygen; the cardiovascular system carries it to muscles; the integumentary system sweats to remove extra heat; the urinary system adjusts water and salt balance

Nursing importance

  • Nurses assess patients system by system (head-to-toe or systems review)
  • A disease of one system affects others – e.g. kidney failure causes anaemia, high BP and fluid overload
  • Holistic care considers all systems

Conclusion The eleven organ systems – integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive – each have their own organs and functions, but together they maintain homeostasis and life.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Define tissue. Name the basic tissues. Describe connective tissue – its components, types and functions. (2 + 2 + 6)

diagram.caption: Loose (areolar) connective tissue under the microscope

answer_html:
(a) Definition of tissue (2 marks)

  • A tissue is a group of similar cells, along with the intercellular substance, that perform a particular function
  • The study of tissues is called histology
  • Tissues develop from the three germ layers of the embryo – ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm

(b) Basic tissues (2 marks)

  1. Epithelial tissue – covering, lining and glandular
  2. Connective tissue – supporting and binding
  3. Muscular tissue – skeletal, smooth and cardiac
  4. Nervous tissue – neurons and neuroglia

(c) Connective tissue (6 marks) Connective tissue is the most abundant and widely distributed tissue. It connects, supports, protects and binds other tissues and organs. It develops from the mesoderm (mesenchyme). Unlike epithelium, its cells are scattered in a large amount of intercellular matrix, and most connective tissues have a good blood supply (except cartilage).

1. Components of connective tissue

(i) Cells

  • Fibroblasts – the most common cells; produce fibres and ground substance; important in wound healing
  • Macrophages (histiocytes) – engulf bacteria and debris (defence)
  • Mast cells – release histamine and heparin (allergy, inflammation)
  • Plasma cells – produce antibodies
  • Adipocytes (fat cells) – store fat
  • White blood cells that move in from the blood

(ii) Fibres

  • Collagen (white) fibres – thick, very strong, resist pulling (tendons, ligaments)
  • Elastic (yellow) fibres – thin, branching, stretchable (skin, lungs, large arteries)
  • Reticular fibres – fine networks that support soft organs (liver, spleen, lymph nodes)

(iii) Ground substance

  • A gel-like material of water, proteins and glycosaminoglycans (e.g. hyaluronic acid) in which cells and fibres lie; allows diffusion of nutrients and wastes

2. Types of connective tissue

A. Connective tissue proper

  • Loose connective tissue
    • Areolar tissue – the most widespread; under the skin, around organs, vessels and nerves; binds and allows movement
    • Adipose tissue – fat; under the skin, around the kidneys and heart; stores energy, insulates, cushions
    • Reticular tissue – framework of the liver, spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow
  • Dense connective tissue
    • Dense regular – parallel collagen fibres; tendons and ligaments
    • Dense irregular – fibres in all directions; dermis of the skin, capsules of organs and joints, periosteum
    • Elastic – walls of large arteries, ligamenta flava of the vertebral column, vocal cords

B. Specialised (supporting) connective tissues

  • Cartilage – hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage
  • Bone (osseous tissue) – compact and spongy bone; matrix hardened by calcium salts

C. Fluid connective tissues

  • Blood – cells in liquid plasma
  • Lymph

D. Embryonic connective tissue

  • Mesenchyme, and mucoid tissue (Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord)

3. Functions of connective tissue

  1. Binding and support – holds organs in place; forms the framework of the body
  2. Protection – bones protect organs; fat cushions the kidneys and eyeballs
  3. Transport – blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes
  4. Defence – macrophages, plasma cells and white cells fight infection
  5. Storage – fat stores energy; bones store calcium and phosphate
  6. Insulation – fat reduces heat loss
  7. Repair – fibroblasts form scar tissue in wound healing
  8. Movement – tendons, ligaments and bones work with muscles

Applied importance

  • Wound healing depends on fibroblasts and collagen; vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) weakens collagen and delays healing
  • Keloids – excess collagen in scars
  • Obesity – excess adipose tissue
  • Oedema – fluid collects in the areolar tissue
  • Connective tissue diseases – rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Subcutaneous injections are given into the loose areolar and adipose tissue under the skin

Conclusion A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common function. Connective tissue, the most abundant tissue, is made of cells, fibres and ground substance; it includes loose, dense, cartilage, bone, blood and lymph, and it binds, supports, protects, transports, stores and repairs.

subject: Applied Anatomy
unit_title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms and Organization of the Human Body
question: Describe cell division – mitosis and meiosis – with diagrams. Add a note on its significance. (5 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction Cell division is the process by which one cell divides to form new cells. It is needed for growth, repair and reproduction. There are two types:

  • Mitosis – occurs in body (somatic) cells; produces two identical cells
  • Meiosis – occurs in germ cells of the testes and ovaries; produces four sex cells (gametes) with half the number of chromosomes

Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) – the diploid number. Gametes have 23 – the haploid number.

(a) Mitosis (5 marks)

Interphase (preparatory stage)

  • The cell is not dividing but is very active; DNA is replicated (each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at the centromere); centrioles duplicate; the cell grows
  • Sub-stages: G1 (growth), S (synthesis of DNA), G2 (preparation)

1. Prophase

  • Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each with two chromatids
  • Nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear
  • Centrioles move to opposite poles and the spindle fibres form

2. Metaphase

  • Chromosomes line up at the equator (metaphase plate) of the cell
  • Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres
  • Chromosomes are best seen and counted at this stage (used in karyotyping)

3. Anaphase

  • The centromeres split; sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles
  • Each pole now has a full set of 46 chromosomes

4. Telophase

  • Chromosomes uncoil; nuclear membranes reform around each set; nucleoli reappear

5. Cytokinesis

  • The cytoplasm divides by a cleavage furrow, forming two identical daughter cells

Result: one diploid cell → two diploid (46) cells, genetically identical to the parent.

(b) Meiosis (3 marks) Meiosis has two successive divisions but DNA is replicated only once.

Meiosis I (reduction division)

  • Prophase I – the longest stage; homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments (crossing over), producing new combinations of genes (stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis)
  • Metaphase I – homologous pairs line up at the equator
  • Anaphase I – homologous chromosomes separate (sister chromatids stay together)
  • Telophase I – two cells form, each with 23 chromosomes (haploid)

Meiosis II (equational division)

  • Similar to mitosis; sister chromatids separate
  • Result: four haploid cells (23 chromosomes each), genetically different from each other

In males – one primary spermatocyte forms four sperms; in females – one primary oocyte forms one ovum and three small polar bodies.

Differences between mitosis and meiosis

Point Mitosis Meiosis
Site somatic cells germ cells (testis, ovary)
Divisions one two
Daughter cells 2 4
Chromosome number 46 (diploid) 23 (haploid)
Crossing over absent present in prophase I
Daughter cells identical genetically different
Purpose growth and repair gamete formation

(c) Significance of cell division (2 marks)

  • Growth of the body from a single fertilised egg
  • Repair and replacement of worn-out cells – skin, blood cells, gut lining, wound healing
  • Maintains the chromosome number – meiosis halves it so that fertilisation restores 46
  • Genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment – no two children (except identical twins) are alike

Applied importance

  • Cancer is uncontrolled mitosis; many anticancer drugs and radiotherapy act on dividing cells, so they also affect hair follicles, bone marrow and the gut lining (hair loss, low blood counts, mouth ulcers)
  • Non-disjunction (failure of chromosomes to separate) in meiosis causes Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome; the risk rises with maternal age
  • Karyotyping at metaphase helps diagnose chromosomal disorders

Conclusion Mitosis divides a body cell into two identical diploid cells for growth and repair, while meiosis divides a germ cell twice to form four genetically different haploid gametes; both are essential for life, and their errors cause cancer and chromosomal disorders.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: List the muscles of respiration.
answer_html:
Introduction Muscles of respiration change the size of the chest cavity so that air can move in and out of the lungs.

1. Muscles of inspiration

  • Diaphragm – the main muscle (about 75% of quiet breathing); supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)
  • External intercostal muscles – lift the ribs

2. Accessory muscles of inspiration (used in deep or difficult breathing)

  • Sternocleidomastoid, scalene muscles, pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior

3. Muscles of expiration

  • Quiet expiration is passive (elastic recoil)
  • Forced expiration: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, transversus abdominis)

Ward tip: a patient using neck muscles to breathe is in respiratory distress.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the paranasal sinuses and state their functions.
answer_html:
Definition Paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the bones of the skull around the nose. They are lined with mucous membrane and open into the nasal cavity.

Paranasal sinuses

  1. Frontal sinuses – in the frontal bone, above the eyes
  2. Maxillary sinuses – in the maxilla, below the eyes; the largest
  3. Ethmoidal sinuses – small air cells between the eyes
  4. Sphenoidal sinuses – in the sphenoid bone, behind the nose

Functions

  • Make the skull lighter
  • Give resonance to the voice
  • Warm and humidify the inspired air
  • Act as a cushion against injury to the face

Applied: infection causes sinusitis with headache and facial pain.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right main bronchus?
answer_html:
Introduction The trachea divides at the carina into the right and left main bronchi. The two are not alike.

Features of the right main bronchus

  1. Shorter – about 2.5 cm (left is about 5 cm)
  2. Wider in diameter
  3. More vertical – almost in line with the trachea, while the left bronchus is pushed sideways by the heart

Result

  • Aspirated food, vomitus, a peanut or a coin, and an endotracheal tube pushed too far, usually enter the right lung
  • Aspiration pneumonia is therefore commoner on the right side, often in the right lower lobe

Nursing point: keep unconscious patients in the lateral position to prevent aspiration.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the nasal cavity and its applied anatomy.

diagram.caption: Lateral wall of the nasal cavity

answer_html:
Introduction The nasal cavity is the first part of the respiratory tract. It extends from the nostrils (anterior nares) in front to the posterior nares (choanae), which open into the nasopharynx. It is divided into right and left halves by the nasal septum.

1. Boundaries

  • Roof – narrow; mainly the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, through which the olfactory nerves pass
  • Floor – hard palate in front and soft palate behind (it separates the nose from the mouth)
  • Medial wall – nasal septum, formed by septal cartilage, vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
  • Lateral wall – three curved bony shelves: superior, middle and inferior conchae (turbinates); the space below each is called a meatus

2. Openings into the nasal cavity

  • Paranasal sinuses open into the meatuses
  • Nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus – that is why the nose runs when we cry
  • Posteriorly it opens into the nasopharynx

3. Lining (mucous membrane)

  • Vestibule – lined by skin with coarse hairs (vibrissae) that filter large dust particles
  • Respiratory region – pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and a very rich blood supply
  • Olfactory region – in the roof; contains olfactory receptor cells for smell

4. Blood and nerve supply

  • Arteries from the ophthalmic, maxillary and facial arteries; they meet on the front of the septum
  • Nerves: olfactory nerve (smell) and branches of the trigeminal nerve (general sensation)

5. Functions

  • Passage of air
  • Filters, warms and moistens the inspired air
  • Sense of smell
  • Resonance of voice

6. Applied anatomy

  • Epistaxis – most nosebleeds come from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the front of the septum. First aid: sit up, lean slightly forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes, cold compress
  • Deviated nasal septum and nasal polyps block breathing
  • Rhinitis and sinusitis – infection spreads easily from the nose into the sinuses
  • Nasogastric tube – passed along the floor of the nose, directed backwards, never upwards
  • Fracture of the cribriform plate can cause CSF rhinorrhoea and loss of smell

Conclusion The nasal cavity conditions the air we breathe; its rich blood supply explains frequent nosebleeds.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the respiratory system and list the common disorders of each part.
answer_html:
Introduction The respiratory system brings air close to the blood so that oxygen can enter and carbon dioxide can leave the body. It is divided into the upper and lower respiratory tracts.

1. Upper respiratory tract – nose to larynx 2. Lower respiratory tract – trachea to alveoli

3. Parts and common disorders

Part Key features Common disorders
Nose and nasal cavity septum, conchae, ciliated lining rhinitis, epistaxis, deviated septum, nasal polyps
Paranasal sinuses frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal, sphenoidal sinusitis
Pharynx naso-, oro- and laryngopharynx; tonsils and adenoids pharyngitis, tonsillitis, adenoid enlargement, peritonsillar abscess
Larynx cartilages, vocal cords laryngitis, laryngeal oedema, cancer of larynx, vocal cord palsy
Trachea C-shaped cartilage rings tracheitis, foreign body, stenosis after long intubation
Bronchi and bronchioles branching airways bronchitis, bronchial asthma, bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis (infants)
Lungs and alveoli lobes, about 300 million alveoli pneumonia, tuberculosis, COPD/emphysema, lung cancer, pulmonary oedema, ARDS
Pleura visceral and parietal layers pleurisy, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, empyema

4. Functions of the respiratory system

  • Exchange of gases
  • Maintenance of acid–base balance (removal of CO₂)
  • Voice production
  • Sense of smell
  • Protection – cough, sneeze, mucus and cilia

5. Nursing importance

  • Tuberculosis is a major public health problem in India – early detection and full treatment under the National TB Elimination Programme
  • Pneumonia is a leading cause of death in children under five
  • Smoking and indoor smoke (chulha) damage the airways – health education is important

Upper and lower respiratory tract

  • Upper tract – nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx and larynx; common problems: common cold, sinusitis, tonsillitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis
  • Lower tract – trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs; common problems: bronchitis, pneumonia, asthma, tuberculosis, COPD, lung cancer

Defence mechanisms of the respiratory tract

  • Nasal hairs and mucus trap dust; cilia sweep mucus upwards (mucociliary escalator); sneezing and coughing reflexes; alveolar macrophages engulf microbes; lymphoid tissue (tonsils, adenoids) fights infection

Conclusion Each part of the respiratory tract has its own common diseases; knowing the parts helps nurses understand symptoms and care.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the trachea.
answer_html:
Introduction The trachea (windpipe) is a flexible, tube-like airway that carries air from the larynx to the bronchi.

1. Extent

  • Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at the level of the C6 vertebra
  • Ends at the level of the sternal angle (T4–T5), where it divides into the right and left main bronchi

2. Size

  • Length about 10–12 cm in adults
  • Diameter about 2–2.5 cm; much narrower in infants

3. Position and relations

  • Lies in the midline of the neck and in the superior mediastinum
  • In front: isthmus of the thyroid gland (over the 2nd–4th rings), sternum, arch of the aorta lower down
  • Behind: oesophagus
  • On the sides: lobes of the thyroid gland, carotid sheaths, lungs and pleura in the chest

4. Structure of the wall

  • 16–20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage keep the airway always open
  • The gap at the back of each ring is closed by the trachealis muscle; this allows the oesophagus to expand when food passes
  • Lining: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells – mucus traps particles and the cilia sweep them upwards towards the throat (mucociliary escalator)
  • Submucosa with mucous glands; outer fibrous layer

5. Carina

  • A ridge at the point where the trachea divides
  • Very sensitive – touching it during suction or intubation causes strong coughing

6. Functions

  • Passage of air
  • Cleaning of inspired air by mucus and cilia
  • Cough reflex

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Tracheostomy is usually made through the 2nd–4th tracheal rings
  • The tip of an endotracheal tube should lie a few centimetres above the carina
  • Smoking paralyses the cilia, so mucus collects (smoker's cough)
  • Tracheal suctioning must be sterile, gentle and short (not more than 10–15 seconds)

Conclusion The trachea is a rigid yet flexible airway kept open by cartilage rings and cleaned by its ciliated lining.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a short note on the pleura.
answer_html:
Introduction The pleura is a thin, shiny serous membrane that covers each lung and lines the inside of the chest wall. Each lung has its own pleural sac.

1. Layers of the pleura

  • Visceral (pulmonary) pleura – closely covers the surface of the lung and dips into its fissures; cannot be separated from the lung
  • Parietal pleura – lines the inner surface of the chest wall; named by the part it lines:
    • Costal pleura (ribs)
    • Diaphragmatic pleura
    • Mediastinal pleura
    • Cervical pleura (cupola) – rises above the clavicle into the neck
  • The two layers are continuous with each other at the root (hilum) of the lung

2. Pleural cavity

  • A potential space between the two layers
  • Contains only a few millilitres of pleural fluid
  • Costodiaphragmatic recess – the lowest part, where fluid collects first

3. Functions of the pleura

  • Pleural fluid lets the layers glide smoothly during breathing
  • Surface tension of the fluid keeps the lung stuck to the chest wall, so the lung expands when the chest expands
  • Negative pressure in the cavity keeps the lungs inflated

4. Nerve supply

  • Parietal pleura – pain-sensitive; supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (pleuritic pain may be felt in the shoulder)
  • Visceral pleura – not sensitive to pain

5. Applied / nursing importance

  • Pleurisy – inflamed layers rub; sharp chest pain on breathing; pleural rub heard
  • Pleural effusion – fluid in the cavity; tuberculosis is a common cause in India
  • Pneumothorax – air in the cavity; the lung collapses (sudden breathlessness)
  • Empyema – pus in the cavity
  • Haemothorax – blood in the cavity after chest injury
  • Thoracentesis and chest drains are inserted just above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the intercostal vessels and nerve that run below each rib
  • Care of an underwater-seal drain: keep the bottle below chest level, watch for swinging and bubbling

Conclusion The pleura allows painless breathing movements; fluid or air in the pleural cavity seriously affects breathing.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the larynx.
answer_html:
Introduction The larynx (voice box) is the organ of voice production and the guard of the lower airway. It connects the laryngopharynx above with the trachea below.

1. Position

  • Lies in the front of the neck at the level of the C3–C6 vertebrae
  • Higher in children and women; moves up during swallowing

2. Cartilages (nine)

  • Unpaired (three)
    • Thyroid cartilage – the largest; its front projection forms the Adam's apple (more prominent in men)
    • Cricoid cartilage – the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway; lies below the thyroid cartilage
    • Epiglottis – leaf-shaped elastic cartilage; closes the laryngeal opening during swallowing
  • Paired (three pairs) – arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages; the arytenoids move the vocal cords

3. Membranes and ligaments

  • Thyrohyoid membrane (connects to the hyoid bone)
  • Cricothyroid membrane – between thyroid and cricoid cartilages; site for emergency airway opening

4. Vocal cords (vocal folds)

  • Two folds of mucous membrane stretched from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoids
  • The gap between them is the glottis – the narrowest part of the adult airway
  • Air passing out between them makes them vibrate and produce voice; pitch depends on their tension and length

5. Muscles

  • Intrinsic muscles open and close the glottis and tighten the cords
  • Extrinsic muscles raise and lower the larynx

6. Lining: mostly ciliated columnar epithelium; the vocal cords have stratified squamous epithelium.

7. Nerve supply: branches of the vagus – superior laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

8. Functions

  • Airway
  • Voice production (phonation)
  • Protection of the lower airway during swallowing
  • Cough reflex

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery causes hoarseness – check the voice after thyroidectomy
  • Laryngeal oedema (allergy, burns, infection) can block the airway; an emergency opening can be made through the cricothyroid membrane
  • In children the narrowest part is at the cricoid ring – choose tube size carefully
  • Cancer of the larynx is linked with smoking and tobacco chewing

Conclusion The larynx is a cartilage box that produces voice and protects the airway during swallowing.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the gross anatomy of the lungs with a labelled diagram. Add a note on applied anatomy. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction and location (2 marks)

  • The lungs are the main organs of respiration, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it
  • Two cone-shaped, soft, spongy organs lying in the thoracic cavity, one on each side of the mediastinum (heart and great vessels)
  • Each lung lies in its own pleural sac and rests on the diaphragm
  • Colour: pink in children; becomes greyish and mottled with age and dust, and darker in smokers
  • The lung floats in water because it contains air

(b) External features (3 marks)

1. Apex

  • Rounded upper end
  • Rises about 2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle into the root of the neck

2. Base

  • Concave lower surface resting on the dome of the diaphragm
  • Separates the lung from the liver (right) and the stomach and spleen (left)

3. Surfaces

  • Costal surface – large, smooth, convex; faces the ribs
  • Mediastinal (medial) surface – faces the heart; carries the hilum

4. Borders

  • Anterior border – thin and sharp; on the left side it has a notch for the heart (cardiac notch)
  • Posterior border – thick and rounded
  • Inferior border – separates the base from the costal surface

5. Hilum and root of the lung The hilum is the doorway of the lung through which structures enter and leave. Together they form the root:

  • Main (principal) bronchus
  • Pulmonary artery
  • Two pulmonary veins
  • Bronchial arteries and veins
  • Lymph vessels and lymph nodes
  • Nerves (pulmonary plexus)

(c) Lobes, fissures and differences (3 marks)

Feature Right lung Left lung
Lobes 3 – upper, middle, lower 2 – upper, lower
Fissures 2 – oblique and horizontal 1 – oblique
Size shorter and wider (liver pushes the right dome of the diaphragm up) longer and narrower (heart bulges to the left)
Weight slightly heavier slightly lighter
Cardiac notch absent present, with a tongue-like lingula
Bronchopulmonary segments 10 8–10

Internal structure – the bronchial tree

  • Main bronchus → lobar (secondary) bronchi → segmental (tertiary) bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli
  • There are about 300 million alveoli, giving a surface area of about 70 m²
  • Alveolar wall cells:
    • Type I – thin, flat cells for gas exchange
    • Type II – secrete surfactant, which prevents collapse of alveoli
    • Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) – remove dust and microbes

Bronchopulmonary segment – the area of lung supplied by one segmental bronchus; each is a separate unit with its own artery.

Blood supply

  • Pulmonary arteries bring deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle for gas exchange
  • Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium
  • Bronchial arteries (from the descending aorta) nourish the lung tissue itself

Lymph drainage: to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) and tracheobronchial lymph nodes.

Nerve supply: pulmonary plexus

  • Vagus (parasympathetic) – bronchoconstriction and more mucus
  • Sympathetic – bronchodilation

(d) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Aspiration enters the right lung more often, because the right bronchus is wider and more vertical
  • Auscultation – listen over every lobe; the right middle lobe is heard only from the front
  • Postural drainage positions are planned according to the bronchopulmonary segments involved
  • Lack of surfactant in preterm babies causes respiratory distress syndrome; mothers in preterm labour receive steroids to mature the baby's lungs
  • Tuberculosis often begins at the apex; lobar pneumonia involves a whole lobe
  • Because segments are independent units, a surgeon can remove only a diseased segment (segmentectomy) or lobe (lobectomy)
  • Lung cancer is strongly linked with smoking

Bronchopulmonary segments

  • Each segment is a functionally independent unit supplied by its own segmental bronchus and artery
  • The right lung has 10 segments; the left lung has 8–10 (some segments are fused)
  • Applied: a diseased segment can be removed surgically (segmentectomy); knowledge of segments guides postural drainage

Nerve supply

  • From the pulmonary plexus – vagus nerve (parasympathetic) causes bronchoconstriction and increased secretion; sympathetic fibres (T2–T5) cause bronchodilation

Lymphatic drainage

  • Superficial (subpleural) and deep lymphatics drain to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes, then to the tracheobronchial nodes; these nodes are enlarged in tuberculosis and lung cancer

Conclusion The two lungs differ in lobes, fissures and shape; their division into segments guides physical examination, physiotherapy and surgery.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the cartilages of the larynx.
answer_html:
Introduction The larynx (voice box) has a skeleton of nine cartilages – three unpaired and three paired.

Unpaired cartilages

  1. Thyroid cartilage – the largest; forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple), more prominent in males
  2. Cricoid cartilage – the only complete ring; shaped like a signet ring; lies at the level of C6
  3. Epiglottis – leaf-shaped elastic cartilage; covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing

Paired cartilages

  1. Arytenoid cartilages – the vocal cords are attached to them; their movement changes the tension of the cords
  2. Corniculate cartilages
  3. Cuneiform cartilages

Applied: the cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages is the site for an emergency cricothyroidotomy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the pharynx.
answer_html:
Introduction The pharynx is a muscular tube about 12–14 cm long, extending from the base of the skull to the level of C6, where it continues as the oesophagus. It is a common passage for air and food.

Parts

  1. Nasopharynx – behind the nasal cavity; contains the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) and the openings of the auditory tubes; carries only air
  2. Oropharynx – behind the mouth; contains the palatine tonsils; carries air and food
  3. Laryngopharynx (hypopharynx) – behind the larynx; continues as the oesophagus; carries food

Applied: enlarged adenoids block the nose and auditory tubes, causing mouth breathing and ear infections in children.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the carina? State its importance.
answer_html:
Definition The carina is a ridge of cartilage at the point where the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi. It lies at about the level of the sternal angle (T4–T5).

Importance

  1. Its mucous membrane is very sensitive – touching it with a suction catheter or a foreign body causes violent coughing
  2. Used as a landmark in bronchoscopy
  3. The tip of an endotracheal tube is positioned above the carina; a tube pushed too far usually enters the right main bronchus
  4. Widening or distortion of the carina on bronchoscopy suggests enlarged lymph nodes, often due to lung cancer

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Differentiate between the right and left main bronchi.
answer_html:
Introduction The trachea divides at the carina into the right and left main (primary) bronchi.

Point Right main bronchus Left main bronchus
Length shorter – about 2.5 cm longer – about 5 cm
Width wider narrower
Direction more vertical – in line with the trachea more horizontal (oblique)
Branches gives the upper lobe bronchus before entering the lung enters the lung before dividing
Lobes supplied three (upper, middle, lower) two (upper, lower)

Applied: because the right bronchus is wider and more vertical, inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated material more often enter the right lung, and an endotracheal tube pushed too far usually enters the right bronchus.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the structures in the root (hilum) of the lung.
answer_html:
Introduction The hilum is a depression on the medial (mediastinal) surface of each lung through which structures enter and leave. These structures together form the root of the lung, which attaches the lung to the mediastinum.

Structures in the root of the lung

  1. Pulmonary artery – one
  2. Pulmonary veins – two
  3. Main bronchus (on the right, also the upper lobe bronchus)
  4. Bronchial arteries and veins
  5. Pulmonary plexus of nerves (vagus and sympathetic)
  6. Lymphatics and the bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes

Applied: hilar lymph nodes enlarge in tuberculosis and lung cancer, seen as hilar shadows on a chest X-ray.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the openings in the diaphragm and the structures passing through them.
answer_html:
Introduction The diaphragm separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Three major openings allow structures to pass between them.

Major openings

Opening Vertebral level Main structures
Vena caval opening T8 inferior vena cava, branches of the right phrenic nerve
Oesophageal opening T10 oesophagus, vagal trunks, branches of left gastric vessels
Aortic opening T12 aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein

Memory aid: "I 8 10 eggs at 12" – IVC at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12.

Applied: weakness of the oesophageal opening leads to a hiatus hernia.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is Waldeyer's ring?
answer_html:
Definition Waldeyer's ring is a ring of lymphoid tissue surrounding the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts in the pharynx. It acts as the first line of defence against inhaled and swallowed microorganisms.

Components

  1. Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) – on the roof and back wall of the nasopharynx
  2. Tubal tonsils (two) – near the openings of the auditory tubes
  3. Palatine tonsils (two) – "the tonsils", between the arches of the soft palate
  4. Lingual tonsil – on the back (posterior one-third) of the tongue

Applied: tonsillitis and adenoid enlargement are common in children; enlarged adenoids cause mouth breathing, snoring and ear infections.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of an alveolus.
answer_html:
Introduction Alveoli are tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the ends of the respiratory tree where gas exchange takes place. There are about 300 million alveoli with a total surface area of about 70 square metres.

Structure

  1. Type I pneumocytes (alveolar cells) – thin, flat cells covering most of the surface; allow gas exchange
  2. Type II pneumocytes – cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse
  3. Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) – engulf dust and microbes
  4. Surrounded by a dense network of pulmonary capillaries

Respiratory membrane: the alveolar wall, basement membrane and capillary wall together are only about 0.5 micrometre thick, allowing rapid diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Applied: lack of surfactant in premature babies causes respiratory distress syndrome.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the pharynx.

diagram.caption: Sagittal section showing the parts of the pharynx

answer_html:
Introduction The pharynx (throat) is a funnel-shaped fibromuscular tube that serves as a common passage for air and food. It lies behind the nasal cavity, mouth and larynx, and in front of the cervical vertebrae.

1. Extent and size

  • From the base of the skull above to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (level of C6) below, where it continues as the oesophagus
  • About 12–14 cm long; widest above and narrowest at its lower end

2. Parts

(a) Nasopharynx

  • Lies behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate
  • Contains the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) and the openings of the auditory (Eustachian) tubes
  • Purely respiratory; during swallowing it is closed by the soft palate

(b) Oropharynx

  • Behind the mouth, from the soft palate to the upper border of the epiglottis
  • Contains the palatine tonsils between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
  • Common passage for air and food

(c) Laryngopharynx

  • Behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage
  • Continues as the oesophagus

3. Structure of the wall

  • Mucous membrane – ciliated columnar epithelium in the nasopharynx; stratified squamous epithelium in the oro- and laryngopharynx (to resist friction of food)
  • Fibrous layer (pharyngobasilar fascia)
  • Muscular layer – constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) that push food down, and longitudinal muscles that raise the pharynx during swallowing
  • Outer loose connective tissue (buccopharyngeal fascia)

4. Blood and nerve supply

  • Arteries – branches of the external carotid artery (ascending pharyngeal, facial, maxillary)
  • Nerves – the pharyngeal plexus, formed mainly by the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves

5. Functions

  • Passage for air to the larynx and for food to the oesophagus
  • Swallowing (deglutition)
  • Defence – Waldeyer's ring of lymphoid tissue
  • Resonance for the voice
  • Equalises air pressure in the middle ear through the auditory tube

6. Applied anatomy

  • Pharyngitis and tonsillitis – sore throat
  • Adenoid enlargement – nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, otitis media in children
  • Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
  • Aspiration – in unconscious patients and those with impaired swallowing (stroke), food may enter the larynx; nurses position such patients on their side and check the swallowing reflex before feeding
  • Throat swab is taken from the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway keeps the tongue from blocking the pharynx in unconscious patients

Conclusion The pharynx is a 12–14 cm muscular tube from the skull base to C6, divided into nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx; it conducts air and food, helps in swallowing and defence, and is important in airway care.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the diaphragm.

diagram.caption: Diaphragm seen from below with its openings

answer_html:
Introduction The diaphragm is a dome-shaped musculotendinous partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It is the principal muscle of inspiration.

1. Shape and position

  • Two domes – the right dome is slightly higher (because of the liver below it), reaching the 5th rib; the left dome reaches the 5th intercostal space
