  • Convex upwards towards the thorax, concave towards the abdomen

2. Origin – from the margins of the thoracic outlet

  • Sternal part – back of the xiphoid process
  • Costal part – inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and their cartilages
  • Lumbar (vertebral) part – the right and left crura (from the upper lumbar vertebrae; the right crus is larger) and the arcuate ligaments

3. Insertion

  • All fibres converge on the central tendon – a trefoil-shaped (three-leafed) sheet of tendon

4. Openings

  • Vena caval opening (T8) – inferior vena cava
  • Oesophageal opening (T10) – oesophagus and vagal trunks
  • Aortic opening (T12) – aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein
  • Small openings for nerves and vessels

5. Nerve supply

  • Motor – the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5): "C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive"
  • Sensory – phrenic nerves (central part) and lower intercostal nerves (peripheral part)

6. Blood supply

  • Superior and inferior phrenic arteries, musculophrenic and pericardiophrenic arteries

7. Actions

  • Inspiration – contraction flattens the domes, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax; it is responsible for most of the air moved in quiet breathing
  • Expulsive acts – along with the abdominal muscles, raises intra-abdominal pressure in coughing, sneezing, vomiting, micturition, defecation and childbirth
  • Helps venous return and the flow of lymph by changes in pressure
  • Acts as a sphincter at the oesophageal opening, preventing reflux

8. Applied anatomy

  • Hiccups – involuntary spasms of the diaphragm
  • Hiatus hernia – part of the stomach enters the thorax through the oesophageal opening
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia in newborns
  • Phrenic nerve injury (neck injury, high spinal injury above C3–C5) paralyses the diaphragm; high spinal cord injury needs ventilation
  • Referred pain to the shoulder tip (C4 dermatome) from irritation of the diaphragm – e.g. by blood after rupture of an ectopic pregnancy or gall bladder disease
  • Positioning – breathless patients breathe better sitting up, as the abdominal organs fall away from the diaphragm

Conclusion The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle arising from the sternum, lower ribs and lumbar vertebrae and inserted into the central tendon; supplied by the phrenic nerves (C3–C5), it is the main muscle of inspiration and also helps expulsive acts.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the bronchial tree and the alveoli.

diagram.caption: The bronchial tree from trachea to alveoli

answer_html:
Introduction The bronchial (respiratory) tree is the system of air passages that branches repeatedly, like an upside-down tree, from the trachea to the alveoli. There are about 23 generations of branching. It is divided into a conducting zone (air passages only) and a respiratory zone (gas exchange).

1. Trachea

  • A tube about 10–11 cm long, from the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6) to its bifurcation at the sternal angle (T4–T5)
  • Kept open by 16–20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open at the back where the trachealis muscle lies against the oesophagus
  • Lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells

2. Main (primary) bronchi

  • Right – shorter, wider and more vertical; left – longer, narrower and more horizontal

3. Lobar (secondary) bronchi

  • Three on the right (upper, middle, lower) and two on the left (upper, lower) – one for each lobe

4. Segmental (tertiary) bronchi

  • One for each bronchopulmonary segment – 10 on the right and 8–10 on the left

5. Bronchioles

  • Small airways less than 1 mm wide
  • No cartilage; walls contain smooth muscle – their constriction causes wheezing in asthma

6. Terminal bronchioles

  • The last part of the conducting zone

Conducting zone (nose to terminal bronchioles)

  • Warms, moistens and filters air; no gas exchange; its volume (about 150 ml) is the anatomical dead space

7. Respiratory bronchioles – a few alveoli open from their walls; gas exchange begins here

8. Alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli

Respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles to alveoli)

  • The site of gas exchange

9. Alveoli

  • About 300 million tiny air sacs with a huge surface area (about 70 square metres)
  • Type I cells – thin, flat; gas exchange
  • Type II cells – secrete surfactant
  • Alveolar macrophages – remove dust and microbes
  • Surrounded by pulmonary capillaries; the respiratory membrane is extremely thin (about 0.5 micrometre)

Changes in the wall along the tree

  • Cartilage decreases and disappears at the bronchioles
  • Smooth muscle increases relative to wall thickness
  • Epithelium changes from ciliated columnar to cuboidal and finally to flat cells in the alveoli
  • Goblet cells decrease

Applied anatomy

  • Asthma – spasm of bronchiolar smooth muscle
  • Bronchiectasis – permanent dilatation of bronchi
  • Emphysema – destruction of alveolar walls
  • Pneumonia – alveoli fill with exudate
  • Postural drainage uses gravity to drain secretions from particular segments
  • Smoking paralyses cilia, causing chronic cough

Conclusion The bronchial tree branches from the trachea through main, lobar and segmental bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli; the conducting zone carries and conditions air, and the respiratory zone of respiratory bronchioles and alveoli carries out gas exchange.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the mediastinum.
answer_html:
Introduction The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, lying between the two pleural sacs (lungs). It contains all the thoracic organs except the lungs.

1. Boundaries

  • Anterior – sternum
  • Posterior – bodies of the thoracic vertebrae (T1–T12)
  • Superior – thoracic inlet
  • Inferior – diaphragm
  • Lateral – mediastinal pleura on each side

2. Divisions

  • A horizontal plane passing from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into:
    • Superior mediastinum – above the plane
    • Inferior mediastinum – below, further divided by the pericardium into anterior, middle and posterior parts

3. Contents

(a) Superior mediastinum

  • Arch of the aorta and its three branches (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries)
  • Superior vena cava and the brachiocephalic veins
  • Trachea and oesophagus
  • Thymus (or its remains in adults)
  • Thoracic duct, phrenic and vagus nerves, left recurrent laryngeal nerve

(b) Anterior mediastinum (between sternum and pericardium)

  • Remains of the thymus, lymph nodes, fat and loose connective tissue

(c) Middle mediastinum

  • Heart enclosed in the pericardium
  • Ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk and its branches, lower part of the superior vena cava
  • Bifurcation of the trachea and the main bronchi
  • Phrenic nerves

(d) Posterior mediastinum (behind the pericardium)

  • Descending thoracic aorta
  • Oesophagus
  • Thoracic duct
  • Azygos and hemiazygos veins
  • Vagus nerves, sympathetic trunks (along the sides of the vertebrae) and lymph nodes

4. Applied anatomy

  • Mediastinal shift – in tension pneumothorax or large pleural effusion, the trachea and heart are pushed to the opposite side (trachea felt deviated in the suprasternal notch)
  • Mediastinitis – infection, e.g. after oesophageal rupture or cardiac surgery
  • Mediastinal tumours – thymoma (anterior), lymphoma, neurogenic tumours (posterior)
  • Widened mediastinum on X-ray – aortic aneurysm or dissection
  • Mediastinoscopy – biopsy of lymph nodes
  • Pressure on the superior vena cava by tumours causes swelling of the face and neck (superior vena cava syndrome)

Conclusion The mediastinum is the central space between the lungs, divided at the sternal angle into superior and inferior parts; it contains the heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus, thymus, thoracic duct and important nerves.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the organisation of the respiratory system from the nose to the alveoli and its applications in nursing. (6 + 4)
answer_html:
Introduction The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. It also helps in speech, smell, protection and acid–base balance. It is divided into:

  • Upper respiratory tract – nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx and larynx
  • Lower respiratory tract – trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs
  • Functionally – a conducting portion (nose to terminal bronchioles) and a respiratory portion (respiratory bronchioles to alveoli)

(a) Organisation of the respiratory system (6 marks)

1. Nose and nasal cavity

  • The external nose and the nasal cavity, divided by the nasal septum into two halves
  • The lateral wall has three conchae (turbinates) that increase the surface area
  • Lined by a highly vascular, ciliated mucous membrane that warms, moistens and filters air; the upper part has the olfactory area for smell
  • Paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal, sphenoidal) open into it

2. Pharynx

  • A 12–14 cm muscular tube from the skull base to C6 – nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx; common passage for air and food; contains tonsils

3. Larynx (voice box)

  • From C3 to C6; skeleton of nine cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, arytenoids, corniculates, cuneiforms)
  • Contains the vocal cords; the gap between them is the glottis
  • Functions: passage for air, voice production, protection of the lower airway (epiglottis closes during swallowing; cough reflex)

4. Trachea

  • About 10–11 cm long from C6 to T4–T5; 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings; ciliated epithelium with mucus forms the mucociliary escalator

5. Bronchi and bronchioles

  • Main bronchi → lobar bronchi (3 right, 2 left) → segmental bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles

6. Alveoli

  • About 300 million; type I and type II cells and macrophages; surrounded by capillaries; site of gas exchange

7. Lungs

  • Two cone-shaped organs in the pleural cavities; the right has three lobes (two fissures), the left has two lobes (one fissure) and a cardiac notch
  • Each lung has an apex, base, costal and mediastinal surfaces, and a hilum

8. Pleura

  • A double serous membrane – visceral (on the lung) and parietal (lining the chest wall) – with a thin film of pleural fluid in between that allows smooth movement

9. Muscles of respiration and thoracic cage

  • Diaphragm (main muscle) and external intercostals for inspiration; accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) in forced inspiration; internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration
  • The ribs, sternum and thoracic vertebrae protect the lungs and allow breathing movements

(b) Applications in nursing (4 marks)

1. Airway management

  • In unconscious patients the tongue falls back and blocks the pharynx – head tilt–chin lift, jaw thrust, the recovery position and an oropharyngeal airway keep the airway open
  • Endotracheal intubation passes the tube through the vocal cords; a tube pushed too deep usually enters the right main bronchus, so breath sounds must be checked on both sides

2. Suctioning

  • Oral, nasal and endotracheal suction removes secretions; touching the carina causes coughing; each suction pass is limited to about 10–15 seconds to prevent hypoxia

3. Tracheostomy care

  • A tracheostomy is made through the 2nd–4th tracheal rings; the nurse keeps the tube clean and patent and humidifies the air, because the nose's warming and moistening is bypassed

4. Positioning and breathing exercises

  • Fowler's position lowers the abdominal organs and lets the diaphragm move freely
  • Deep breathing, coughing and incentive spirometry prevent atelectasis and pneumonia after surgery
  • Postural drainage uses knowledge of bronchopulmonary segments

5. Aspiration

  • Inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated feeds more often enter the right lung; check swallowing before oral feeding, keep the head raised during and after feeds, and confirm nasogastric tube position

6. Chest procedures

  • Thoracentesis and chest drains are placed in the 4th–5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line, just above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the intercostal vessels and nerve that run along the lower border

7. Assessment

  • Rate, depth and rhythm of breathing; use of accessory muscles; tracheal position (shift in pneumothorax); breath sounds over each lobe; SpO₂

8. Infection control

  • Cough etiquette, humidification, oral care in ventilated patients to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia

Conclusion The respiratory system is organised from the nose, pharynx and larynx through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli in the lungs, enclosed by the pleura and moved by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Knowledge of this organisation guides airway care, suctioning, tracheostomy care, positioning, prevention of aspiration, chest procedures and respiratory assessment.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the accessory organs of digestion.
answer_html:
Introduction Accessory organs help in digestion, but food does not pass through them. They either break food mechanically or pour secretions into the alimentary canal.

Accessory organs of digestion

  1. Teeth – cut, tear and grind food (20 milk teeth, 32 permanent teeth)
  2. Tongue – mixes food with saliva, helps chewing and swallowing, carries taste buds
  3. Salivary glands – parotid, submandibular and sublingual; secrete saliva with amylase
  4. Liver – secretes bile for fat digestion
  5. Gall bladder – stores and concentrates bile
  6. Pancreas – secretes pancreatic juice containing enzymes for all foods

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the anal canal.
answer_html:
Introduction The anal canal is the terminal part of the large intestine, about 4 cm long, extending from the rectum to the anus.

Structure

  1. Upper part (above the pectinate line) – lined by columnar epithelium; shows vertical folds called anal columns; supplied by autonomic nerves, so not pain-sensitive
  2. Pectinate (dentate) line – the wavy junction between the upper and lower parts
  3. Lower part – lined by stratified squamous epithelium; supplied by somatic nerves, so very painful
  4. Sphincters
    • Internal anal sphincter – involuntary smooth muscle
    • External anal sphincter – voluntary skeletal muscle (pudendal nerve)

Applied: internal piles arise above the dentate line (painless bleeding); external piles and fissures lie below it and are painful.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the muscles of the pharynx.
answer_html:
Introduction The pharynx is a muscular tube behind the nose, mouth and larynx, shared by the digestive and respiratory tracts. Its muscles help in swallowing.

Muscles of the pharynx

  1. Outer circular layer (constrictors)
    • Superior constrictor
    • Middle constrictor
    • Inferior constrictor
    • They contract one after another and squeeze the bolus downwards
  2. Inner longitudinal layer
    • Stylopharyngeus
    • Palatopharyngeus
    • Salpingopharyngeus
    • They raise the pharynx and larynx during swallowing

Nerve supply: pharyngeal plexus (mainly vagus); stylopharyngeus by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the salivary glands and state where their ducts open.
answer_html:
Introduction Salivary glands are exocrine glands that secrete saliva into the mouth – about 1 to 1.5 litres a day.

Major salivary glands

  1. Parotid gland
    • The largest; lies in front of and below the ear
    • Duct: parotid (Stensen's) duct opens on the inner cheek opposite the upper second molar tooth
    • Secretes watery (serous) saliva; swells in mumps
  2. Submandibular gland
    • Lies below the lower jaw
    • Duct: Wharton's duct opens on the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum of the tongue
    • Mixed secretion
  3. Sublingual gland
    • The smallest; lies under the tongue
    • Opens by many small ducts on the floor of the mouth
    • Mainly mucous secretion

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the liver.
answer_html:
Introduction The liver is the largest gland and the largest internal organ of the body. It weighs about 1.5 kg in adults and performs hundreds of functions, which is why it is called the body's "chemical factory".

1. Location

  • Lies in the right hypochondrium, extends across the epigastrium into the left hypochondrium
  • Just below the diaphragm, protected by the lower ribs
  • Moves down with inspiration (felt below the right costal margin in deep breathing)

2. Shape and surfaces

  • Wedge-shaped
  • Diaphragmatic surface – smooth, convex; faces up, front and right
  • Visceral (inferior) surface – faces down and back; related to the stomach, duodenum, gall bladder, right kidney and colon

3. Lobes

  • Right lobe – large
  • Left lobe – small
  • They are separated in front by the falciform ligament
  • On the visceral surface: caudate lobe (behind) and quadrate lobe (in front), both functionally part of the left lobe

4. Porta hepatis

  • A transverse slit on the visceral surface, the "gateway" of the liver
  • Enters: portal vein, hepatic artery, nerves
  • Leaves: right and left hepatic ducts, lymph vessels

5. Coverings and ligaments

  • Covered by peritoneum except the bare area, and by a thin fibrous Glisson's capsule
  • Ligaments: falciform, coronary, right and left triangular, ligamentum teres (remnant of the foetal umbilical vein), ligamentum venosum

6. Blood supply (dual)

  • Portal vein – about 75%; nutrient-rich blood from the gut
  • Hepatic artery – about 25%; oxygenated blood
  • Drained by the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava

7. Microscopic structure

  • Made of about a million hexagonal hepatic lobules
  • Each lobule has a central vein in the middle
  • Plates of hepatocytes radiate from the central vein, separated by sinusoids
  • Sinusoids are lined by phagocytic Kupffer cells
  • At the corners lie portal triads: branch of portal vein, branch of hepatic artery and a bile ductule

8. Main functions (in brief): metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and proteins; bile secretion; detoxification; storage of glycogen, vitamins and iron; formation of plasma proteins and clotting factors.

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Liver biopsy – taken through a lower right intercostal space in the mid-axillary line while the patient holds the breath after breathing out; afterwards the patient lies on the right side to press on the site
  • Hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatomegaly, jaundice, liver abscess (amoebic liver abscess is common in India)
  • Patients with liver disease bleed easily (less clotting factors) – check before injections

Conclusion The liver is a large, vascular gland with a dual blood supply and a lobular structure suited to its many metabolic functions.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the pancreas.
answer_html:
Introduction The pancreas is a soft, pinkish, lobulated gland that is both exocrine (digestive juice) and endocrine (hormones). It is therefore called a mixed gland.

1. Location

  • Lies across the posterior abdominal wall behind the stomach, at the level of L1–L2
  • Retroperitoneal (behind the peritoneum)
  • Extends from the curve of the duodenum on the right to the spleen on the left

2. Size: about 12–15 cm long and weighs about 80–90 g.

3. Parts

  • Head – lies within the C-shaped curve of the duodenum
  • Neck – short; the portal vein forms behind it
  • Body – crosses the vertebral column behind the stomach
  • Tail – reaches the hilum of the spleen

4. Ducts

  • Main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) – runs along the whole gland
  • It joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens into the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla
  • The opening is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi
  • Accessory duct (duct of Santorini) – may open separately at the minor papilla

5. Structure

  • Exocrine part (about 98%) – grape-like groups of cells called acini; secrete pancreatic juice with amylase, lipase and trypsinogen into the duodenum
  • Endocrine part (about 2%) – scattered islets of Langerhans:
    • α (alpha) cells – glucagon (raises blood sugar)
    • β (beta) cells – insulin (lowers blood sugar); the most numerous
    • δ (delta) cells – somatostatin
    • PP cells – pancreatic polypeptide

6. Blood and nerve supply

  • Arteries: branches of the splenic artery and the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries
  • Veins drain into the portal system
  • Nerves: vagus (secretion) and sympathetic fibres (pain)

7. Functions

  • Digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats
  • Neutralises acid chyme (bicarbonate)
  • Control of blood glucose

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • Acute pancreatitis – often from gallstones or alcohol; severe epigastric pain going to the back; patient kept nil by mouth
  • Diabetes mellitus – failure of beta cells
  • Cancer of the head of the pancreas presses on the bile duct → painless, progressive obstructive jaundice
  • Pancreatic injury in abdominal trauma

Conclusion The pancreas is a retroperitoneal mixed gland whose exocrine part digests food and whose islets control blood sugar.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the oesophagus.
answer_html:
Introduction The oesophagus (food pipe) is a muscular tube that carries swallowed food and fluids from the pharynx to the stomach by peristalsis. It does not digest or absorb food.

1. Extent and length

  • About 25 cm long
  • Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6), continuing from the pharynx
  • Ends at the cardiac orifice of the stomach (T11)
  • Passes through the diaphragm at the level of T10

2. Parts and course

  • Cervical part – in the neck, behind the trachea
  • Thoracic part – the longest; in the superior and posterior mediastinum, behind the trachea, left bronchus and heart
  • Abdominal part – short (about 1.25 cm), below the diaphragm

3. Relations

  • In front: trachea, left main bronchus, left atrium (pericardium)
  • Behind: vertebral column, thoracic duct
  • On the left: arch of aorta, thoracic duct

4. Normal constrictions (measured from the incisor teeth)

  1. At its beginning – about 15 cm
  2. Where the arch of the aorta (about 22.5 cm) and left main bronchus (about 27.5 cm) cross it
  3. Where it passes through the diaphragm – about 40 cm - Swallowed foreign bodies tend to stick at these points, and tubes and scopes must be passed gently here

5. Structure of the wall

  • Mucosa – stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, which resists friction from food
  • Submucosa – loose connective tissue with mucous glands
  • Muscle layer – upper third skeletal, middle third mixed, lower third smooth muscle
  • Adventitia – outer fibrous coat (no serosa in the thorax)

6. Sphincters

  • Upper oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus)
  • Lower oesophageal sphincter – a physiological sphincter that prevents acid reflux

7. Blood supply

  • Neck – inferior thyroid artery; thorax – oesophageal branches of the aorta; abdomen – left gastric artery
  • Veins of the lower end connect the portal and systemic systems (important in portal hypertension)

8. Nerve supply: vagus and sympathetic nerves (oesophageal plexus).

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • GERD and heartburn – avoid lying down after meals, raise the head end of the bed
  • Oesophageal varices in portal hypertension can bleed massively (haematemesis)
  • Achalasia cardia – failure of the lower sphincter to relax
  • Carcinoma oesophagus – linked with tobacco, alcohol and very hot drinks
  • Strictures after corrosive (acid/alkali) poisoning – never induce vomiting
  • NG tube length is measured from the nose → earlobe → xiphisternum (NEX)

Conclusion The oesophagus is a 25 cm muscular passage with three natural narrowings and an important lower sphincter that prevents reflux.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the small intestine and its special features for absorption.
answer_html:
Introduction The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal and the main site of digestion and absorption. It extends from the pyloric sphincter to the ileocaecal junction.

1. Length: about 6 metres (shorter in the living body due to muscle tone).

2. Parts

  • Duodenum – about 25 cm, C-shaped, curves around the head of the pancreas; has four parts. The second part receives bile and pancreatic juice through the hepatopancreatic ampulla
  • Jejunum – about two-fifths of the rest
  • Ileum – about three-fifths; ends at the ileocaecal valve

3. Differences between jejunum and ileum

Jejunum Ileum
upper part, left upper abdomen lower part, right lower abdomen
wider lumen, thicker wall narrower lumen, thinner wall
more circular folds and villi fewer folds
fewer Peyer's patches many Peyer's patches

4. Structure of the wall (four layers)

  • Mucosa – simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells
  • Submucosa – vessels, lymphatics; Brunner's glands in the duodenum
  • Muscle layer – inner circular and outer longitudinal
  • Serosa – visceral peritoneum

5. Special features for absorption

  1. Circular folds (plicae circulares) – permanent folds of mucosa and submucosa; slow down chyme
  2. Villi – finger-like projections; each has a capillary network (absorbs sugars and amino acids) and a central lymph vessel called a lacteal (absorbs fat)
  3. Microvilli – tiny projections on each absorptive cell forming the brush border; carry enzymes such as lactase and maltase
  4. Intestinal glands (crypts of Lieberkühn) – secrete intestinal juice and renew the lining
  5. Great length – gives time for absorption - Together these increase the surface area several hundred times (to about the size of a tennis court)

6. Blood supply: superior mesenteric artery; veins drain into the portal vein.

7. Functions

  • Completes digestion (intestinal and pancreatic enzymes, bile)
  • Absorbs nutrients, vitamins, water and electrolytes
  • Immunity – Peyer's patches
  • Secretes hormones (secretin, CCK)

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • Typhoid ulcers form over Peyer's patches and may perforate
  • Malabsorption (coeliac disease), lactose intolerance
  • Intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus after surgery
  • Most oral drugs are absorbed here

Conclusion The small intestine is long, folded and covered with villi and microvilli – a design that gives a huge surface for absorption.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the digestive system. Describe the stomach in detail with a labelled diagram. (2 + 8)
answer_html:
(a) Parts of the digestive system (2 marks)

Introduction: the digestive system breaks food into simple substances that can be absorbed, and removes the waste.

1. Alimentary canal (gastrointestinal tract) – a continuous muscular tube:

  • Mouth (oral cavity)
  • Pharynx
  • Oesophagus
  • Stomach
  • Small intestine – duodenum, jejunum, ileum
  • Large intestine – caecum with vermiform appendix, ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal
  • Anus

2. Accessory organs

  • Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gall bladder, pancreas

(b) Stomach (8 marks)

Introduction The stomach is the most dilated, J-shaped part of the alimentary canal, lying between the oesophagus and the duodenum. It stores food for some hours, churns it and begins protein digestion.

1. Location

  • Upper left part of the abdomen – left hypochondrium, epigastric and umbilical regions
  • Just below the left dome of the diaphragm
  • Its shape and position change with posture, breathing and the amount of food

2. Size and capacity

  • About 25 cm long when moderately full
  • Capacity: about 30 ml at birth, about 1–1.5 litres in adults

3. Parts

  1. Cardia – area around the cardiac orifice where the oesophagus enters
  2. Fundus – dome-shaped part above the level of the cardiac orifice; usually contains a gas bubble (seen on X-ray)
  3. Body – the largest, middle part
  4. Pyloric part – pyloric antrum and the narrow pyloric canal
  5. Pylorus – ends in the pyloric sphincter, a thick ring of circular muscle that controls emptying into the duodenum

4. Curvatures

  • Lesser curvature – short, concave right border; the lesser omentum attaches here; has a notch called the angular incisure
  • Greater curvature – long, convex left border; the greater omentum hangs from it like an apron

5. Orifices

  • Cardiac orifice – at T11; opening of the oesophagus
  • Pyloric orifice – at about L1 (transpyloric plane); opening into the duodenum

6. Surfaces and relations

  • Anterior surface: left lobe of the liver, diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall
  • Posterior surface ("stomach bed"): pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, spleen, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon and diaphragm – separated from the stomach by the lesser sac

7. Structure of the wall (four layers)

  1. Mucosa
    • Simple columnar epithelium that secretes mucus
    • Thrown into folds called rugae when the stomach is empty; they flatten as it fills
    • Has gastric pits leading into gastric glands, which contain:
Cell Secretion
Chief (peptic) cells pepsinogen
Parietal (oxyntic) cells hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor
Mucous neck cells protective mucus
G cells (pyloric region) gastrin (hormone)
  1. Submucosa – loose connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics and the submucous nerve plexus
  2. Muscle coat (muscularis) – three layers: inner oblique, middle circular and outer longitudinal; the extra oblique layer helps the churning of food. The circular layer thickens to form the pyloric sphincter
  3. Serosa – visceral peritoneum

8. Blood supply – all from branches of the coeliac trunk

  • Left gastric artery and right gastric artery – along the lesser curvature
  • Right and left gastro-epiploic arteries – along the greater curvature
  • Short gastric arteries – fundus

9. Venous drainage: the veins accompany the arteries and drain into the portal venous system.

10. Lymphatic drainage: to the gastric nodes and then the coeliac lymph nodes (route of spread of stomach cancer, sometimes to the left supraclavicular node).

11. Nerve supply

  • Parasympathetic – vagus nerves: increase gastric secretion and movement
  • Sympathetic – coeliac plexus (T6–T9): reduce movement; carry pain sensation

12. Functions (in brief)

  • Temporary storage of food
  • Mechanical digestion – churning food into semi-liquid chyme
  • Chemical digestion – pepsin begins protein digestion; gastric lipase acts a little on fats
  • HCl kills swallowed microbes
  • Intrinsic factor – absorption of vitamin B12
  • Absorption of water, alcohol and some drugs (aspirin)
  • Hormone – gastrin

13. Applied anatomy

  • Peptic ulcer – common along the lesser curvature and in the first part of the duodenum
  • Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis – infants (often first-born boys) present with projectile vomiting at 3–6 weeks
  • Carcinoma of the stomach and hiatus hernia
  • Gastric lavage and Ryle's (NG) tube – tube length measured from the nose to the earlobe to the xiphisternum; position is confirmed (aspirate pH) before every feed
  • Vomiting of blood (haematemesis) from bleeding ulcers or varices

Conclusion The stomach is a J-shaped, three-layered muscular bag with specialised glands; its structure suits its roles of storing, churning and beginning the digestion of food.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the large intestine.
answer_html:
Introduction The large intestine is about 1.5 metres long. It extends from the end of the ileum (ileocaecal junction) to the anus.

Parts

  1. Caecum – a blind pouch in the right iliac fossa, with the vermiform appendix attached
  2. Ascending colon – up the right side to the right colic (hepatic) flexure
  3. Transverse colon – across the abdomen to the left colic (splenic) flexure
  4. Descending colon – down the left side
  5. Sigmoid (pelvic) colon – S-shaped, in the pelvis
  6. Rectum – about 12–13 cm
  7. Anal canal – about 3.8 cm, opening at the anus

Special features: taeniae coli (three muscle bands), haustrations (sacculations) and appendices epiploicae (fat tags).

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the layers of the wall of the alimentary canal.
answer_html:
Introduction From the oesophagus to the anal canal, the wall of the gut has the same basic four layers, from inside out:

  1. Mucosa – innermost; lining epithelium, lamina propria and a thin muscle layer (muscularis mucosae); secretes mucus and enzymes and absorbs food
  2. Submucosa – loose connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics, glands and the submucosal (Meissner's) nerve plexus
  3. Muscularis externa – an inner circular and outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle, with the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus between them; produces peristalsis (the stomach has an extra inner oblique layer)
  4. Serosa or adventitia – outermost; serosa (visceral peritoneum) in the abdomen, adventitia (fibrous tissue) in the oesophagus

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is McBurney's point?
answer_html:
Definition McBurney's point is the surface marking of the base of the appendix. It lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and the medial two-thirds of a line joining the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus (spino-umbilical line).

Importance

  1. Maximum tenderness is felt here in acute appendicitis
  2. The classic gridiron (McBurney's) incision for appendicectomy is made through this point
  3. It helps nurses and doctors localise pain in the right iliac fossa during abdominal assessment

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the duodenum.
answer_html:
Introduction The duodenum is the first and shortest part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, C-shaped, curving around the head of the pancreas.

Parts

  1. First (superior) part – about 5 cm; its beginning (duodenal cap) is the commonest site of duodenal ulcer
  2. Second (descending) part – about 7.5 cm; the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open here at the major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater)
  3. Third (horizontal) part – about 10 cm; crosses in front of the aorta and is crossed by the superior mesenteric vessels
  4. Fourth (ascending) part – about 2.5 cm; ends at the duodenojejunal flexure

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the extrahepatic biliary apparatus.
answer_html:
Introduction The extrahepatic biliary apparatus collects bile from the liver, stores it and carries it to the duodenum.

Parts

  1. Right and left hepatic ducts – leave the liver at the porta hepatis
  2. Common hepatic duct – formed by their union
  3. Gall bladder – stores and concentrates bile
  4. Cystic duct – connects the gall bladder to the common hepatic duct
  5. Common bile duct – formed by the union of the cystic and common hepatic ducts; about 7.5 cm long
  6. Hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) – where the common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct; opens at the major duodenal papilla, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi

Applied: gallstones blocking the common bile duct cause obstructive jaundice.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write the dental formula for deciduous and permanent teeth.
answer_html:
Introduction The dental formula shows the number of each type of tooth in one half of the upper and lower jaws, in the order incisors–canine–premolars–molars.

Deciduous (milk) teeth – 20

  • Formula: I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 0/0, M 2/2 in each half
  • Erupt from about 6 months to 2½ years

Permanent teeth – 32

  • Formula: I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3 in each half
  • Erupt from about 6 years (first molar) to 17–25 years (third molar – "wisdom tooth")

Applied: teething in infants; dental caries; nurses inspect teeth in oral assessment and give oral care.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the formation of the portal vein.
answer_html:
Introduction The portal vein carries blood rich in absorbed nutrients from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver.

Formation

  1. Formed behind the neck of the pancreas at the level of L2
  2. By the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein (the inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein)
  3. It is about 8 cm long; it runs up in the free border of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches
  4. It brings about 75% of the blood reaching the liver

Applied: in portal hypertension (e.g. cirrhosis), blood is diverted through portosystemic connections, causing oesophageal varices, haemorrhoid-like rectal varices and caput medusae around the umbilicus.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the large intestine.
answer_html:
Introduction The large intestine is the terminal part of the alimentary canal, about 1.5 metres long and wider than the small intestine. It extends from the ileocaecal junction to the anus. It absorbs water and forms and stores faeces.

1. Parts

  • Caecum – a blind pouch in the right iliac fossa; the ileum opens into it through the ileocaecal valve; the vermiform appendix arises from it
  • Ascending colon – up the right side to the hepatic flexure under the liver
  • Transverse colon – the longest and most mobile part, hanging in a loop, with its own mesentery (transverse mesocolon)
  • Descending colon – down the left side from the splenic flexure
  • Sigmoid colon – S-shaped loop in the pelvis, with a mesentery
  • Rectum – about 12–13 cm, in front of the sacrum; stores faeces before defecation
  • Anal canal – the last 3.8 cm, with internal (involuntary) and external (voluntary) anal sphincters

2. Special features (distinguish it from the small intestine)

  • Taeniae coli – the outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands
  • Haustrations – pouches (sacculations) formed because the taeniae are shorter than the gut
  • Appendices epiploicae – small fat-filled tags of peritoneum
  • Greater width, no villi, many goblet cells

3. Blood supply

  • Superior mesenteric artery – caecum, appendix, ascending colon and the right two-thirds of the transverse colon (midgut)
  • Inferior mesenteric artery – left one-third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon and upper rectum (hindgut)
  • Veins drain into the portal vein

4. Nerve supply

  • Parasympathetic (vagus and pelvic splanchnic nerves) increases peristalsis; sympathetic reduces it

5. Functions

  • Absorption of water and electrolytes – converts liquid chyme into semi-solid faeces
  • Formation, storage and elimination of faeces
  • Secretion of mucus for lubrication
  • Bacterial action – normal flora synthesise vitamin K and some B vitamins and ferment fibre
  • Defecation reflex

6. Applied anatomy

  • Constipation and diarrhoea; colorectal cancer; haemorrhoids; intestinal obstruction
  • Colostomy – an opening of the colon on the abdominal wall
  • Enema and suppositories act in the rectum; the patient lies in the left lateral (Sims') position because the rectum and sigmoid colon lie on the left
  • Per-rectal examination and colonoscopy

Conclusion The large intestine – caecum, colon, rectum and anal canal – has taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae; supplied by the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, it absorbs water, forms and stores faeces and produces vitamin K.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the vermiform appendix.
answer_html:
Introduction The vermiform (worm-like) appendix is a narrow, blind, muscular tube attached to the caecum. Though small, it is clinically very important because appendicitis is a common surgical emergency.

1. Location and size

  • Arises from the posteromedial wall of the caecum, about 2 cm below the ileocaecal junction, where the three taeniae coli meet
  • Average length about 9 cm (varies from 2 to 20 cm)

2. Positions (the tip can point in different directions)

  • Retrocaecal – behind the caecum; the most common
  • Pelvic – hanging into the pelvis; the second most common
  • Subcaecal, pre-ileal and post-ileal, and paracolic

3. Surface marking

  • The base lies at McBurney's point – the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line from the ASIS to the umbilicus

4. Mesoappendix

  • A small triangular fold of peritoneum that attaches it to the mesentery of the ileum and carries its blood vessels

5. Structure

  • Same four layers as the intestine
  • The submucosa contains abundant lymphoid tissue; hence it is called the "abdominal tonsil"

6. Blood supply

  • Appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery)
  • It is an end artery – if it is blocked during inflammation, the appendix becomes gangrenous and may perforate

7. Nerve supply

  • Sympathetic fibres from T10 segment – hence early pain is felt around the umbilicus (T10 dermatome), later shifting to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is involved

8. Function

  • Part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue; may act as a reservoir of normal gut bacteria

9. Applied anatomy

  • Acute appendicitis – periumbilical pain shifting to the right iliac fossa, tenderness at McBurney's point, fever, vomiting
  • Rebound tenderness and Rovsing's sign (pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right)
  • A pelvic appendix may irritate the bladder or rectum
  • Perforation leads to peritonitis or an appendicular abscess
  • Nursing: no heat application to the abdomen in suspected appendicitis (may cause rupture), no laxatives or enemas; nil by mouth, and prepare for appendicectomy

Conclusion The appendix is a 9 cm blind tube from the posteromedial caecum, usually retrocaecal, supplied by an end artery (the appendicular artery), rich in lymphoid tissue and important because of appendicitis.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the gall bladder and the extrahepatic biliary apparatus.
answer_html:
Introduction The biliary apparatus is the system of ducts and the gall bladder that collects, stores, concentrates and delivers bile from the liver to the duodenum.

A. Gall bladder

1. Location and size

  • A pear-shaped sac lying in a fossa on the inferior surface of the liver
  • About 7–10 cm long; capacity about 30–50 ml

2. Parts

  • Fundus – the rounded end projecting below the liver margin; its surface marking is at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the right rectus muscle meets the costal margin
  • Body – the main part
  • Neck – narrow part continuous with the cystic duct; may have a small pouch (Hartmann's pouch) where stones lodge

3. Structure

  • Mucous membrane with folds (lined by tall columnar cells that absorb water), smooth muscle and serosa

4. Functions

  • Stores bile between meals
  • Concentrates bile 5–10 times by absorbing water and salts
  • Contracts after a fatty meal under the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK), releasing bile into the duodenum

5. Blood supply

  • Cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery

B. Extrahepatic bile ducts

  • Right and left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct (about 3 cm)
  • Cystic duct (about 3–4 cm; its mucosa has spiral folds) joins it to form the common bile duct
  • Common bile duct – about 7.5 cm; passes behind the first part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas; joins the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum
  • The sphincter of Oddi controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice

C. Applied anatomy

  • Gallstones (cholelithiasis) – common in "fat, fertile, forty, female"; stones in the common bile duct cause obstructive jaundice (yellow skin, dark urine, pale stools, itching)
  • Cholecystitis – pain in the right hypochondrium, Murphy's sign, pain referred to the right shoulder (via the phrenic nerve)
  • Cholecystectomy (often laparoscopic) and T-tube drainage after bile duct exploration – nurses measure and record bile drainage
  • Low-fat diet after gall bladder disease

Conclusion The gall bladder, a 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac under the liver, stores and concentrates bile, which flows through the hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts to the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater; gallstones and infection are its common problems.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the oral cavity and the teeth.
answer_html:
Introduction The oral cavity (mouth) is the first part of the digestive tract. It receives food, breaks it down by chewing, mixes it with saliva and begins swallowing. It also helps in speech and breathing.

1. Parts

  • Vestibule – the narrow space between the lips and cheeks outside and the teeth and gums inside; the parotid duct opens here opposite the upper second molar tooth
  • Oral cavity proper – the space inside the dental arches

2. Boundaries

  • Roof – the hard palate (front) and the soft palate (back) with the uvula
  • Floor – the tongue and the mylohyoid muscle; the submandibular and sublingual ducts open beneath the tongue
  • Sides – the cheeks (buccinator muscle)
  • Front – the lips
  • Behind – opens into the oropharynx through the oropharyngeal isthmus

3. Lining

  • Stratified squamous epithelium – resists friction; many small salivary glands

4. Teeth

  • Types: incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding)
  • Number: 20 deciduous and 32 permanent teeth
  • Parts of a tooth: crown (above the gum), neck and root (in the socket of the jaw)
  • Structure:
    • enamel – the hardest substance in the body, covering the crown
    • dentine – forms most of the tooth
    • pulp cavity – contains blood vessels and nerves
    • cementum – covers the root and fixes it by the periodontal ligament

5. Gums (gingivae)

  • Fibrous tissue covered by mucous membrane, surrounding the necks of the teeth

6. Functions of the mouth

  • Ingestion and mastication (chewing)
  • Mixing food with saliva to form a bolus; starch digestion begins (salivary amylase)
  • Taste, speech and the first stage of swallowing
  • Helps in breathing when the nose is blocked

7. Applied anatomy and nursing

  • Oral care in unconscious, febrile and critically ill patients prevents stomatitis, parotitis and ventilator-associated pneumonia
  • Dental caries and gingivitis; mouth ulcers after chemotherapy
  • Cleft lip and palate – feeding problems in newborns
  • Oral cancer – common in India due to tobacco chewing; look for white or red patches
  • Teething in infants

Conclusion The oral cavity – vestibule and oral cavity proper, bounded by the palate, tongue, cheeks and lips – contains the teeth (enamel, dentine, pulp, cementum) and receives saliva; it chews and moistens food and begins swallowing, and good oral care is an important nursing duty.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the duodenum.

diagram.caption: Parts of the duodenum and its relation to the pancreas

answer_html:
Introduction The duodenum is the first, shortest and widest part of the small intestine. Its name comes from its length – about twelve finger-breadths (25 cm). It is C-shaped and curves around the head of the pancreas. Most of it is retroperitoneal and fixed.

1. Extent

  • From the pylorus of the stomach to the duodenojejunal flexure, at the level of L1–L3

2. Parts

  • First (superior) part – about 5 cm; the first 2.5 cm is mobile (the duodenal cap) – the commonest site of peptic (duodenal) ulcer
  • Second (descending) part – about 7.5 cm; runs down beside the head of the pancreas; the major duodenal papilla, where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open together, lies on its posteromedial wall; the minor papilla (accessory pancreatic duct) lies above it
  • Third (horizontal) part – about 10 cm; passes horizontally to the left, crossing the IVC and aorta; the superior mesenteric vessels cross in front of it
  • Fourth (ascending) part – about 2.5 cm; rises to the duodenojejunal flexure, which is held by the suspensory ligament (of Treitz)

3. Relations

  • Anteriorly – liver, gall bladder, transverse colon; posteriorly – right kidney, IVC, aorta; medially – head of the pancreas

4. Structure

  • Same four layers as the gut; the submucosa contains special Brunner's glands that secrete alkaline mucus to neutralise acid from the stomach

5. Blood supply

  • Superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (from the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery)

6. Functions

  • Receives acid chyme from the stomach, bile and pancreatic juice
  • Neutralises acid; digestion of fats, proteins and carbohydrates continues
  • Absorbs iron, calcium and some nutrients
  • Secretes hormones – secretin and cholecystokinin

7. Applied anatomy

  • Duodenal ulcer – pain relieved by food, may bleed or perforate
  • Obstruction of the ampulla by stones or cancer of the head of the pancreas → obstructive jaundice
  • Duodenal atresia in newborns – bile-stained vomiting
  • Nasoduodenal and nasojejunal tubes for feeding pass beyond the pylorus
  • The duodenojejunal flexure is a landmark for upper and lower GI bleeding (above it – haematemesis; below – melaena or fresh blood)

Conclusion The duodenum is a 25 cm C-shaped tube around the head of the pancreas, with four parts; its second part receives bile and pancreatic juice at the major duodenal papilla, and its first part is the commonest site of peptic ulcer.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the peritoneum – its layers, folds and pouches – with its functions and applied anatomy. (2 + 4 + 2 + 2)

diagram.caption: Sagittal section showing the peritoneum and its folds

answer_html:
(a) Introduction and layers (2 marks)

  • The peritoneum is the largest serous membrane of the body, lining the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within them
  • Parietal peritoneum – lines the inner surface of the abdominal and pelvic walls; it is sensitive to pain, which is well localised (supplied by somatic nerves)
  • Visceral peritoneum – covers the organs; poorly sensitive (autonomic nerves)
  • Peritoneal cavity – the potential space between the two layers, containing only a small amount of serous fluid that lets organs glide; in females it communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes
  • It consists of a single layer of flat mesothelial cells on loose connective tissue

Intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal organs

  • Intraperitoneal – almost completely covered and usually mobile, with a mesentery: stomach, jejunum, ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon, liver, spleen
  • Retroperitoneal – behind the peritoneum, covered only in front: kidneys, ureters, adrenals, pancreas (most of it), duodenum (2nd–4th parts), ascending and descending colon, aorta, IVC

(b) Folds of the peritoneum (4 marks) Folds are double layers of peritoneum that connect organs to the walls or to each other and carry vessels and nerves.

1. Greater omentum

  • A large apron-like fold hanging from the greater curvature of the stomach in front of the intestines, then turning back up to the transverse colon
  • Contains fat and lymphoid tissue
  • Called the "policeman of the abdomen" because it moves to areas of inflammation and wraps around them (e.g. an inflamed appendix), limiting the spread of infection

2. Lesser omentum

  • From the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum to the liver
  • Parts – hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments
  • Its free right border contains the portal vein, hepatic artery and common bile duct (the portal triad)

3. Mesentery of the small intestine

  • A fan-shaped fold attaching the jejunum and ileum to the posterior abdominal wall
  • Its root is about 15 cm long, running from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac fossa, while its intestinal border is about 6 m long
  • Carries branches of the superior mesenteric vessels, lymphatics and nerves

4. Mesocolons

  • Transverse mesocolon – attaches the transverse colon
  • Sigmoid mesocolon – attaches the sigmoid colon

5. Peritoneal ligaments

  • Falciform ligament (liver to anterior abdominal wall), coronary and triangular ligaments of the liver, gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments, broad ligament of the uterus

(c) Sacs and pouches (2 marks)

  • Greater sac – the main part of the peritoneal cavity
  • Lesser sac (omental bursa) – behind the stomach and lesser omentum; communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (of Winslow)
  • Rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) – between the rectum and uterus in females; the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the erect position, where pus or blood collects
  • Rectovesical pouch – between the rectum and bladder in males
  • Vesicouterine pouch – between the bladder and uterus
  • Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch) – between the liver and right kidney; the lowest point when lying supine

(d) Functions and applied anatomy (2 marks)

Functions

  • Reduces friction and allows organs to move freely
  • Supports and holds organs in position; carries vessels, nerves and lymphatics
  • Defence – the greater omentum and macrophages localise infection
  • Absorption and secretion of fluid – used in peritoneal dialysis
  • Fat storage in the omentum and mesentery
  • Healing – forms adhesions that seal off injured areas

Applied anatomy

  • Peritonitis – inflammation from a perforated appendix, ulcer or bowel; severe pain, rigidity, fever, shock; patient kept in Fowler's position so that pus collects in the pelvis rather than under the diaphragm
  • Ascites – fluid in the peritoneal cavity (cirrhosis, heart failure); drained by paracentesis below the umbilicus or in the flanks, with the bladder emptied first
  • Peritoneal dialysis – dialysis fluid placed in the peritoneal cavity removes wastes in kidney failure
  • Adhesions after surgery may cause intestinal obstruction
  • Spread of cancer across the peritoneum
  • Culdocentesis – aspiration of the pouch of Douglas through the posterior vaginal fornix in suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Conclusion The peritoneum is the largest serous membrane, with parietal and visceral layers enclosing the peritoneal cavity. Its folds – greater and lesser omenta, mesentery, mesocolons and ligaments – support organs and carry vessels, and its pouches collect fluid. It reduces friction, defends against infection and is used in peritoneal dialysis.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the blood supply of the gastrointestinal tract and the portal circulation. (6 + 4)

diagram.caption: Arterial supply of the gut – coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries

answer_html:
Introduction The gastrointestinal tract below the diaphragm receives its arterial blood from three unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta – the coeliac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery – which supply the embryonic foregut, midgut and hindgut respectively. Venous blood from these organs passes to the liver through the portal vein before reaching the heart.

(a) Arterial supply (6 marks)

1. Coeliac trunk – artery of the foregut

  • Arises from the front of the aorta at the level of T12, just below the aortic opening of the diaphragm; very short (about 1 cm)
  • Three branches:
    • Left gastric artery – lesser curvature of the stomach and lower oesophagus
    • Splenic artery – tortuous course along the upper border of the pancreas to the spleen; gives branches to the pancreas, short gastric arteries and the left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery to the stomach
    • Common hepatic artery – gives the gastroduodenal artery (to the duodenum, pancreas, stomach) and continues as the hepatic artery proper to the liver and gall bladder (cystic artery); the right gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature
  • Supplies: lower oesophagus, stomach, first half of the duodenum, liver, gall bladder, pancreas (part) and spleen

2. Superior mesenteric artery – artery of the midgut

  • Arises at the level of L1, behind the neck of the pancreas
  • Branches:
    • Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery – lower duodenum and head of pancreas
    • Jejunal and ileal arteries (about 15–18) – form arcades and straight vessels (vasa recta) in the mesentery
    • Ileocolic artery – terminal ileum, caecum and appendix (appendicular artery)
    • Right colic artery – ascending colon
    • Middle colic artery – transverse colon
  • Supplies: second half of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and the right two-thirds of the transverse colon

3. Inferior mesenteric artery – artery of the hindgut

  • Arises at the level of L3
  • Branches:
    • Left colic artery – descending colon
    • Sigmoid arteries – sigmoid colon
    • Superior rectal artery – upper rectum
  • Supplies: left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and upper anal canal

4. Marginal artery (of Drummond)

  • A continuous arterial channel along the inner border of the colon, formed by branches of the colic arteries; provides a collateral circulation between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries

5. Lower rectum and anal canal

  • Middle and inferior rectal arteries (from the internal iliac and internal pudendal arteries)

Summary

Artery Level Gut segment Main organs
Coeliac trunk T12 foregut stomach, liver, spleen, upper duodenum
Superior mesenteric L1 midgut small intestine, caecum, appendix, right colon
Inferior mesenteric L3 hindgut left colon, sigmoid, rectum

(b) Portal circulation (4 marks)

1. Meaning

  • A portal system is one in which blood passes through two capillary beds before returning to the heart. In the hepatic portal system, blood from the capillaries of the gut, spleen and pancreas passes through the portal vein to the sinusoids of the liver, and then through the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava

2. Formation of the portal vein

  • Formed behind the neck of the pancreas (L2) by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein
  • Tributaries – left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, paraumbilical veins
  • Ascends in the free border of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis

3. Importance

  • Carries absorbed nutrients to the liver for metabolism and storage
  • The liver detoxifies drugs and toxins before they reach the general circulation (first-pass metabolism of oral drugs)
  • The portal vein brings about 75% of the liver's blood; the hepatic artery brings the rest (rich in oxygen)

4. Portosystemic anastomoses – sites where portal and systemic veins meet

  • Lower end of the oesophagus (left gastric vein with oesophageal veins)
  • Anal canal (superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins)
  • Around the umbilicus (paraumbilical veins with veins of the abdominal wall)
  • Retroperitoneal areas

5. Applied – portal hypertension

  • Cirrhosis of the liver obstructs portal flow; the pressure rises and blood is diverted through the anastomoses, producing oesophageal varices (may bleed severely – haematemesis), rectal varices, caput medusae, splenomegaly and ascites
  • Nursing: watch for haematemesis and melaena, monitor vital signs, avoid hard foods and straining, care during variceal banding or balloon tamponade

Other applied points

  • Mesenteric ischaemia – blockage of the superior mesenteric artery causes gangrene of the gut
  • Bleeding from the gastroduodenal artery in a posterior duodenal ulcer
  • Splenic artery may be injured in splenic trauma

Conclusion The gut is supplied by the coeliac trunk (foregut), superior mesenteric artery (midgut) and inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut), linked by the marginal artery. Its venous blood drains through the portal vein to the liver, which processes nutrients and drugs; obstruction of portal flow causes portal hypertension with varices and ascites.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the chambers and valves of the heart.
answer_html:
Introduction The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump. Valves keep blood flowing in one direction.

Chambers (four)

  1. Right atrium – receives deoxygenated blood from the body
  2. Right ventricle – pumps blood to the lungs
  3. Left atrium – receives oxygenated blood from the lungs
  4. Left ventricle – pumps blood to the whole body (thickest wall)

Valves (four)

  1. Tricuspid valve – between right atrium and right ventricle
  2. Pulmonary valve – at the opening of the pulmonary trunk
  3. Mitral (bicuspid) valve – between left atrium and left ventricle
  4. Aortic valve – at the opening of the aorta

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the veins commonly used for intravenous injection.
answer_html:
Introduction Superficial veins that are easy to see, feel and fix are chosen for IV injection, blood sampling and cannulation.

Commonly used veins

  1. Median cubital vein – in front of the elbow (cubital fossa); the most common site for venepuncture
  2. Cephalic vein – on the thumb side of the forearm and arm
  3. Basilic vein – on the little-finger side of the forearm
  4. Dorsal venous network (metacarpal veins) of the back of the hand – common site for an IV cannula
  5. Great saphenous vein – in front of the medial malleolus (used for venous cut-down)
  6. Scalp veins and external jugular vein – in infants
  7. Central veins – internal jugular, subclavian and femoral veins (central lines)

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Differentiate between an artery and a vein.
answer_html:
Introduction Arteries and veins both have three layers (tunica intima, media and adventitia), but they differ in structure and function.

Feature Artery Vein
Direction of blood away from the heart towards the heart
Wall thick, muscular and elastic thin
Lumen narrow, round wide, collapses when empty
Valves absent present (especially in the limbs)
Pressure and flow high pressure; spurts when cut low pressure; steady flow
Blood carried oxygenated (except pulmonary artery) deoxygenated (except pulmonary veins)
Position deep, protected superficial and deep

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a short note on the myocardium.
answer_html:
Introduction The heart wall has three layers – epicardium (outer), myocardium (middle) and endocardium (inner). The myocardium is the thick muscular layer that does the actual work of pumping blood.

1. Structure of cardiac muscle fibres

  • Made of cardiac muscle cells – short, cylindrical and branched
  • Striated (cross-striations like skeletal muscle)
  • Usually one central nucleus in each cell
  • Involuntary – not under our will
  • Contain many mitochondria – the heart depends on a constant oxygen supply

2. Intercalated discs

  • Special junctions joining one cardiac cell to the next, end to end
  • Contain gap junctions that let the impulse pass quickly from cell to cell
  • So the whole muscle contracts as one unit – a functional syncytium
  • Also contain desmosomes that hold the cells firmly together during contraction

3. Thickness of the myocardium

  • Atria – thin, because they pump blood only into the ventricles
  • Right ventricle – moderately thick; pumps blood to the lungs at low pressure
  • Left ventricle – the thickest (about three times the right), because it pumps blood to the whole body against high pressure

4. Arrangement

  • Fibres run in spiral and circular bundles, so contraction wrings the blood out of the ventricles

5. Fibrous skeleton of the heart

  • Rings of dense connective tissue around the valves
  • Separates atrial from ventricular muscle and acts as an electrical insulator
  • The only electrical link between atria and ventricles is the bundle of His

6. Specialised conducting tissue – SA node, AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres are modified myocardial cells.

7. Properties of cardiac muscle

  • Automaticity – produces its own impulses
  • Rhythmicity, excitability, conductivity, contractility
  • Long refractory period – so the heart cannot go into sustained (tetanic) contraction and always gets time to fill

8. Blood supply: right and left coronary arteries.

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Blocked coronary artery → death of a part of the myocardium – myocardial infarction; the dead muscle is replaced by a scar
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy in long-standing hypertension
  • Myocarditis (viral, diphtheria, rheumatic fever) and cardiomyopathy
  • Cardiac enzymes (troponin) leak from damaged myocardium – used for diagnosis

Conclusion The myocardium is striated, branched, involuntary muscle joined by intercalated discs, thickest in the left ventricle, and totally dependent on the coronary blood supply.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the thoracic duct.
answer_html:
Introduction The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel of the body. It collects lymph from most of the body and returns it to the venous blood in the neck.

1. Length: about 45 cm (from the abdomen to the root of the neck).

2. Beginning

  • Begins in the abdomen as a sac-like dilatation called the cisterna chyli, in front of the first and second lumbar vertebrae
  • The cisterna chyli collects lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, abdominal wall and the intestines (milky, fat-rich lymph called chyle)

3. Course

  • Abdomen – runs upwards on the right side of the aorta
  • Enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm (T12), between the aorta and the azygos vein
  • Thorax – ascends in the posterior mediastinum, behind the oesophagus
  • At about the level of T5 it crosses from the right to the left side
  • Continues upwards in the superior mediastinum along the left side of the oesophagus
  • Neck – arches laterally at the level of C7

4. Termination

  • Opens into the junction of the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein (left venous angle)
  • A valve at its end prevents blood entering the duct

5. Tributaries and area drained

  • Drains lymph from the whole body except the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right side of the thorax
  • These right-sided areas drain into the right lymphatic duct, which opens at the junction of the right internal jugular and subclavian veins
  • In the neck it receives the left jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks

6. Special features

  • Thin-walled and has several valves, so it looks beaded when distended
  • Carries about 2–4 litres of lymph a day

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Injury during chest, oesophageal or neck surgery causes chylothorax – milky fluid in the pleural cavity
  • Blockage of lymph flow in filariasis may cause chyluria (milky urine)
  • Cancer cells from the abdomen can spread through it to the left supraclavicular lymph node

Conclusion The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli, crosses from right to left in the chest and ends in the left venous angle, returning most of the body's lymph to the blood.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a short note on the lymphatic system.
answer_html:
Introduction The lymphatic system is a network of vessels, nodes and organs that returns excess tissue fluid to the blood and protects the body against infection. It works alongside the circulatory system.

1. Components

  1. Lymph – clear, watery fluid formed from tissue fluid; contains lymphocytes; lymph from the intestine is milky (chyle)
  2. Lymph capillaries – blind-ended, very permeable tubes in the tissues; in intestinal villi they are called lacteals
  3. Lymph vessels – like thin veins with many valves
  4. Lymph nodes – small filters placed along the vessels
  5. Lymph ducts – thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, emptying into the great veins of the neck
  6. Lymphoid organs – spleen, thymus, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix, red bone marrow

2. Formation and flow of lymph

  • About 2–3 litres of tissue fluid each day is not reabsorbed by capillaries; it enters lymph capillaries
  • Lymph moves by contraction of skeletal muscles, breathing movements, pulsation of nearby arteries and the valves in the vessels
  • Lymph passes through several nodes before reaching the blood

3. Structure of a lymph node

  • Bean-shaped, surrounded by a capsule that sends trabeculae inwards
  • Cortex – lymphoid follicles containing B lymphocytes
  • Paracortex – T lymphocytes
  • Medulla – medullary cords and sinuses with macrophages
  • Several afferent vessels enter on the convex side; one efferent vessel leaves at the hilum

4. Main groups of lymph nodes: cervical, axillary, inguinal, mediastinal, para-aortic and mesenteric.

5. Functions

  • Drains tissue fluid and returns plasma proteins to the blood – prevents oedema
  • Absorbs fat and fat-soluble vitamins from the intestine
  • Filters bacteria, viruses and cancer cells
  • Immunity – produces lymphocytes and antibodies

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Lymphadenitis – tender, swollen nodes near an infection (e.g. groin nodes in a foot infection)
  • Hard, painless, fixed nodes suggest cancer spread; cervical nodes are enlarged in TB (common in India)
  • Lymphoedema – in filariasis (elephantiasis of the leg) and after removal of axillary nodes
  • After mastectomy with axillary clearance: avoid BP measurement, injections and IV lines on that arm; keep the arm elevated and exercised

Conclusion The lymphatic system is the body's drainage and defence network; its nodes are important sites of infection and cancer spread.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the spleen.
answer_html:
Introduction The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ of the body. It is soft, dark purple and highly vascular, and acts as a filter for blood.

1. Location

  • Lies in the left hypochondrium, partly in the epigastrium
  • Behind the stomach and against the diaphragm
  • Lies along the 9th, 10th and 11th ribs; its long axis follows the 10th rib

2. Size (easy "odd number" recall)

  • About 1 inch thick, 3 inches wide and 5 inches long
  • Weighs about 7 ounces (150–200 g)
  • Lies between the 9th and 11th ribs

3. Surfaces and relations

  • Diaphragmatic surface – smooth and convex, faces the diaphragm
  • Visceral surface – related to the stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure of the colon and tail of the pancreas
  • Hilum – where the splenic vessels enter and leave

4. Structure

  • Covered by a fibrous capsule which sends trabeculae inside
  • Red pulp – blood-filled sinusoids and cords; here old red cells are destroyed
  • White pulp – lymphoid tissue around small arteries; contains lymphocytes for immunity

5. Blood supply

  • Splenic artery – a tortuous branch of the coeliac trunk
  • Splenic vein – joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein

6. Functions

  1. Destruction of old RBCs – the "graveyard of RBCs"; iron is recycled
  2. Immunity – forms lymphocytes and antibodies; filters bacteria from blood
  3. Storage – about one-third of the body's platelets and some blood
  4. Blood formation in the foetus (and in some anaemias in adults)

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Splenomegaly – malaria, kala-azar, thalassaemia, leukaemia, portal hypertension (all seen commonly in India)
  • Rupture of the spleen – in blunt abdominal trauma (road accidents); internal bleeding and shock
  • A normal spleen is not palpable; it must enlarge two to three times to be felt below the left costal margin
  • After splenectomy, patients get pneumococcal and other vaccines because of the risk of serious infection

Conclusion The spleen lies under the left 9th–11th ribs, filters blood, destroys old red cells and helps immunity.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the heart under the headings: position, external features, chambers, valves and layers. Add a note on applied anatomy. (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction The heart is a hollow, four-chambered muscular organ that pumps blood throughout the body. It beats about 72 times a minute, about one lakh times a day, from before birth until death.

(a) Position (2 marks)

  • Lies in the middle mediastinum of the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs, behind the sternum
  • Enclosed in the pericardium
  • About two-thirds lies to the left of the midline and one-third to the right
  • Rests on the diaphragm
  • Size: about the size of the person's closed fist – about 12 cm long, 9 cm wide
  • Weight: about 250–300 g
  • Apex points downwards, forwards and to the left; lies in the left 5th intercostal space, about 9 cm from the midline – the apex beat is felt here
  • Base faces backwards; formed mainly by the left atrium

(b) External features (2 marks)

  1. Surfaces
    • Sternocostal (anterior) – formed mainly by the right ventricle
    • Diaphragmatic (inferior) – mainly the left ventricle
    • Left (pulmonary) surface – left ventricle
  2. Borders
    • Right border – right atrium
    • Left border – left ventricle
    • Inferior border – right ventricle
  3. Grooves (sulci)
    • Atrioventricular (coronary) groove – separates atria from ventricles
    • Anterior and posterior interventricular grooves – separate the two ventricles
    • They carry the coronary vessels
  4. Great vessels
    • Superior and inferior venae cavae – into the right atrium
    • Pulmonary trunk – from the right ventricle
    • Four pulmonary veins – into the left atrium
    • Aorta – from the left ventricle

(c) Chambers (2 marks)

  1. Right atrium
    • Receives deoxygenated blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus
    • Contains the SA node (pacemaker)
    • Fossa ovalis on the septum – remnant of the foetal foramen ovale
    • Right auricle – an ear-like pouch
  2. Right ventricle
    • Pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk
    • Inner wall has muscular ridges (trabeculae carneae), papillary muscles, chordae tendineae and the moderator band
  3. Left atrium
    • Receives oxygenated blood from four pulmonary veins
    • Forms most of the base of the heart
  4. Left ventricle
    • Has the thickest wall (about three times the right)
    • Pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta
    • The interatrial and interventricular septa separate the right side from the left side

(d) Valves (2 marks)

Valve Position Cusps Prevents backflow into
Tricuspid right atrium → right ventricle 3 right atrium
Pulmonary right ventricle → pulmonary trunk 3 semilunar right ventricle
Mitral (bicuspid) left atrium → left ventricle 2 left atrium
Aortic left ventricle → aorta 3 semilunar left ventricle
  • Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid, mitral) are held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, which stop the cusps turning inside out
  • Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) have pocket-like cusps; behind the aortic cusps lie the openings of the coronary arteries
  • Heart sounds: closure of the AV valves gives the first sound ("lub"); closure of the semilunar valves gives the second sound ("dub")

(e) Layers of the heart wall

  1. Pericardium – the covering sac
    • Fibrous pericardium – tough outer layer; prevents over-stretching
    • Serous pericardium – parietal layer and visceral layer (epicardium) with a little lubricating fluid between them
  2. Myocardium – thick middle layer of cardiac muscle
  3. Endocardium – smooth inner lining, continuous with the lining of the blood vessels; covers the valves

Course of blood through the heart SVC and IVC → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → whole body

Nerve supply – cardiac plexus: sympathetic fibres increase heart rate and force; vagus fibres slow the heart.

(f) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Apex beat helps to judge heart size; it shifts outwards in cardiac enlargement
  • Apical pulse is counted for a full minute – e.g. before giving digoxin
  • CPR – chest compressions over the lower half of the sternum, directly over the heart
  • Rheumatic heart disease (still common in India) damages the mitral valve – mitral stenosis; prevented by treating sore throats with penicillin
  • Myocardial infarction from coronary artery blockage
  • Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade – fluid in the pericardial sac squeezes the heart; relieved by pericardiocentesis
  • Congenital heart defects – atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot

Conclusion The heart is a four-chambered pump lying in the middle mediastinum, with four valves ensuring one-way flow and three layers in its wall; knowing its structure is the base for understanding heart disease and its nursing care.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the blood supply of the heart.
answer_html:
Introduction The heart muscle works continuously and cannot rest, so it needs its own rich blood supply. This is called the coronary circulation (coronary = crown, because the arteries encircle the heart like a crown). Though the heart is only about 0.5% of body weight, it receives about 5% of the cardiac output (about 250 ml per minute) at rest.

1. Arterial supply – two coronary arteries Both arise from the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve, from small pockets called the aortic sinuses.

A. Right coronary artery (RCA)

  • Origin: anterior (right) aortic sinus
  • Course: passes between the pulmonary trunk and right auricle, then runs in the right atrioventricular groove, curving round the right border to the back of the heart
  • Branches:
    • SA nodal artery – in about 60% of people
    • Right marginal artery – along the inferior border
    • Posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery – in the posterior groove (in most people – "right dominance")
    • AV nodal artery
  • Area supplied:
    • Right atrium
    • Most of the right ventricle
    • Part of the left ventricle on the diaphragmatic surface
    • Posterior one-third of the interventricular septum
    • AV node (and usually the SA node)

B. Left coronary artery (LCA)

  • Origin: left posterior aortic sinus
  • Course: a short main stem (about 1–2 cm) passes between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle, then divides into two:
    1. Anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending, LAD)
      • Runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex
      • Supplies the anterior two-thirds of the septum and the front of both ventricles
      • Its blockage causes large anterior wall infarcts – sometimes called the "widow-maker"
    2. Circumflex artery
      • Runs in the left AV groove round the left border
      • Gives the left marginal artery
      • Supplies the left atrium and the lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle
  • Area supplied: left atrium, most of the left ventricle, anterior two-thirds of the septum and the SA node in about 40%

2. Coronary dominance

  • The artery that gives the posterior interventricular artery is called "dominant"
  • In most people this is the right coronary artery

3. Venous drainage A. Coronary sinus – the main vein of the heart

  • Lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove
  • Opens into the right atrium, between the opening of the IVC and the tricuspid valve
  • Tributaries:
    • Great cardiac vein – runs with the LAD
    • Middle cardiac vein – with the posterior interventricular artery
    • Small cardiac vein – with the right marginal artery
    • Posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium

B. Anterior cardiac veins – drain the front of the right ventricle directly into the right atrium

C. Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins) – tiny veins opening directly into the chambers

4. Special features of coronary circulation
