  • Coronary flow occurs mainly during diastole, because the contracting muscle squeezes the vessels during systole – so a very fast heart rate (short diastole) reduces the supply
  • Coronary arteries behave as functional end arteries – the links between branches are too small to save the muscle when one artery is suddenly blocked
  • The heart extracts most of the oxygen from coronary blood even at rest, so extra demand can be met only by increasing flow

5. Factors affecting coronary blood flow

  • Diastolic blood pressure (the driving pressure)
  • Heart rate (duration of diastole)
  • Local metabolites (low oxygen, adenosine) dilate coronary vessels
  • Nerves – sympathetic and vagal fibres alter coronary tone

6. Applied anatomy

  • Angina pectoris – narrowing of the arteries (atherosclerosis); chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest and nitrates (sublingual nitroglycerine)
  • Myocardial infarction – complete blockage by a clot
Artery blocked Area of infarction
LAD anterior wall and septum
Circumflex lateral wall
RCA inferior wall, often with heart block (supplies the AV node)
  • Coronary angiography, angioplasty and stenting reopen blocked arteries
  • Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) uses the great saphenous vein or the internal thoracic artery as a graft
  • Risk factors to teach: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity, inactivity

7. Nursing points

  • Watch for chest pain, sweating, ECG changes and arrhythmias
  • Give prescribed oxygen, aspirin and nitrates; keep the patient at rest
  • Monitor pulse, BP and urine output

Conclusion The heart is supplied by the right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta and drained mainly by the coronary sinus; because the coronaries act as end arteries, their blockage quickly causes myocardial infarction.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Explain the formation of the circle of Willis with a neat labelled diagram. Add its applied importance.
answer_html:
Introduction The brain is only about 2% of body weight but receives about 15% of the cardiac output and uses about 20% of the body's oxygen. Brain cells die within minutes without blood, so the brain has a special arterial ring at its base – the circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus cerebri) – that links its main supply routes.

1. Location

  • At the base of the brain, in the interpeduncular fossa
  • Surrounds the optic chiasma, the pituitary stalk (infundibulum) and the mammillary bodies
  • Lies in the subarachnoid space

2. Arterial supply of the brain – four arteries reach the brain

  1. Two internal carotid arteries (anterior circulation)
    • Branches of the common carotid arteries in the neck
    • Enter the skull through the carotid canal
  2. Two vertebral arteries (posterior circulation)
    • Branches of the subclavian arteries
    • Pass through the foramina in the cervical transverse processes and enter the skull through the foramen magnum
    • Unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery

3. Formation of the circle (from front to back)

  1. Anterior communicating artery – a short vessel that joins the two anterior cerebral arteries in front
  2. Anterior cerebral arteries (right and left) – branches of the internal carotid arteries
  3. Internal carotid arteries (right and left) – their terminal parts
  4. Posterior communicating arteries (right and left) – connect each internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery
  5. Posterior cerebral arteries (right and left) – the terminal branches of the basilar artery

So the circle joins the carotid system in front with the vertebrobasilar system behind, and the right side with the left side.

Note: the middle cerebral artery is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery, but it is not a part of the circle.

4. Branches and their territories

Artery Area supplied Effect of blockage
Anterior cerebral medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes (leg area of motor and sensory cortex) weakness and numbness of the opposite leg
Middle cerebral most of the lateral surface – motor and sensory areas of face and arm, speech areas, internal capsule (through deep branches) hemiplegia (face and arm more than leg), sensory loss, aphasia if the dominant side
Posterior cerebral occipital lobe (visual cortex), lower temporal lobe, thalamus loss of half of the visual field (hemianopia)
  • Cortical branches supply the surface (cortex)
  • Central (perforating) branches supply deep structures – internal capsule, basal ganglia and thalamus; these are thin and rupture easily in hypertension

5. Functions of the circle of Willis

  • Provides collateral circulation – if one artery is slowly narrowed, blood can come round from another side
  • Equalises blood pressure in the different parts of the brain
  • Distributes blood evenly to both hemispheres

6. Variations

  • The circle shows variations in many people – one vessel may be thin or missing
  • So its protective effect differs from person to person; sudden blockage may not be compensated

7. Applied importance

  • Berry (saccular) aneurysms – small balloon-like swellings at the junctions of the circle, most often at the anterior communicating artery; rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage with a sudden, severe ("worst ever") headache, vomiting and neck stiffness
  • Stroke (cerebrovascular accident) – blockage of the middle cerebral artery is the commonest cause of hemiplegia with aphasia
  • Hypertensive haemorrhage – rupture of the thin perforating branches into the internal capsule
  • Pituitary tumours lie within the circle and may press on nearby vessels and the optic chiasma
  • Doppler and CT/MR angiography study these vessels

8. Nursing care in stroke and subarachnoid haemorrhage

  • Neurological observations – GCS, pupils, limb power – at regular intervals
  • Airway care; lateral position to prevent aspiration
  • Head end raised about 30° when ordered
  • Prevent pressure injuries, contractures and DVT
  • For SAH: complete rest, quiet room, avoid straining (stool softeners), control BP as ordered

Conclusion The circle of Willis is an arterial ring at the base of the brain formed by the anterior and posterior cerebral, anterior and posterior communicating and internal carotid arteries; it protects the brain's blood supply, but aneurysms on it are a major cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the layers of the wall of a blood vessel.
answer_html:
Introduction Arteries and veins have three layers (tunics) in their walls; capillaries have only one.

Layers (from inside out)

  1. Tunica intima (interna) – innermost; a smooth lining of endothelium on a thin layer of connective tissue; reduces friction
  2. Tunica media – middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibres; thickest in arteries; controls the diameter of the vessel (vasoconstriction and vasodilation)
  3. Tunica adventitia (externa) – outer layer of connective tissue; protects and anchors the vessel; thickest in veins; large vessels have small blood vessels (vasa vasorum) in it

Capillaries have only a single layer of endothelium, which allows exchange of gases and nutrients.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the branches of the arch of the aorta.
answer_html:
Introduction The arch of the aorta begins and ends at the level of the sternal angle (T4), curving backwards and to the left over the root of the left lung.

Branches (from right to left)

  1. Brachiocephalic trunk – the largest; divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries
  2. Left common carotid artery – supplies the left side of the head and neck
  3. Left subclavian artery – supplies the left upper limb

Applied: aortic arch aneurysm may press on the trachea, oesophagus or left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness of voice).

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the major arteries of the upper limb.
answer_html:
Introduction The arterial supply of the upper limb is a continuous trunk that changes its name as it passes from one region to the next.

Arteries

  1. Subclavian artery – in the root of the neck, up to the outer border of the first rib
  2. Axillary artery – in the axilla, up to the lower border of the teres major
  3. Brachial artery – in the arm; divides in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius
  4. Radial artery – on the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm; radial pulse at the wrist
  5. Ulnar artery – on the medial side of the forearm
  6. Superficial and deep palmar arches – formed by the radial and ulnar arteries in the hand

Applied: the brachial artery is used for BP measurement; the radial artery for pulse and arterial blood gas sampling.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the great saphenous vein and its importance.
answer_html:
Introduction The great (long) saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body and the main superficial vein of the lower limb.

Course

  1. Begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot
  2. Passes in front of the medial malleolus – a constant position
  3. Ascends along the medial side of the leg and thigh
  4. Ends in the femoral vein at the saphenous opening, about 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
  5. Has many valves and is connected to deep veins by perforating veins

Importance

  • Varicose veins – when its valves fail
  • Venous cut-down in front of the medial malleolus when other veins cannot be found
  • Used as a graft in coronary artery bypass surgery

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the types of capillaries with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, with walls made of a single layer of endothelium. They connect arterioles with venules and are the site of exchange between blood and tissues.

Types

  1. Continuous capillaries – endothelial cells joined tightly without pores; in muscle, skin, lungs and the brain (form the blood–brain barrier)
  2. Fenestrated capillaries – endothelium has small pores (fenestrae); in kidney glomeruli, intestinal villi and endocrine glands, where rapid exchange is needed
  3. Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries – wide, irregular, with large gaps; in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, allowing cells and large proteins to pass

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the lymphoid organs.
answer_html:
Introduction Lymphoid organs produce, store and activate lymphocytes and protect the body against infection.

A. Primary (central) lymphoid organs – where lymphocytes are formed and mature

  1. Red bone marrow – B lymphocytes
  2. Thymus – T lymphocytes

B. Secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs – where lymphocytes meet antigens and respond

  1. Lymph nodes
  2. Spleen – the largest lymphoid organ
  3. Tonsils (Waldeyer's ring)
  4. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) – e.g. Peyer's patches in the ileum and lymphoid tissue in the appendix

Applied: enlargement of lymphoid organs occurs in infections, lymphomas and leukaemia.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is an end artery? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition An end artery is an artery that does not anastomose (connect) with neighbouring arteries, so it is the only source of blood for the area it supplies.

Examples

  1. Central artery of the retina
  2. Appendicular artery (appendix)
  3. Segmental arteries of the kidney
  4. Central branches of the cerebral arteries (e.g. lenticulostriate arteries)
  5. Coronary arteries – functionally behave like end arteries because their connections are too small to help after sudden blockage
  6. Arteries of the spleen and vasa recta of the small intestine

Importance: blockage of an end artery causes death (infarction or gangrene) of the tissue it supplies – e.g. sudden blindness, gangrenous appendicitis, myocardial infarction, stroke.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the pericardium.
answer_html:
Introduction The pericardium is a double-walled fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels. It lies in the middle mediastinum.

1. Fibrous pericardium

  • The outer, tough, inelastic layer of dense fibrous tissue
  • Attachments: its base is fused with the central tendon of the diaphragm; above, it blends with the walls of the great vessels; in front it is attached to the sternum by sternopericardial ligaments
  • Functions: anchors the heart, prevents over-distension of the heart, and protects it

2. Serous pericardium

  • A thin, double-layered serous membrane inside the fibrous pericardium
  • Parietal layer – lines the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium
  • Visceral layer (epicardium) – covers the surface of the heart; forms the outer layer of the heart wall
  • The two layers are continuous with each other around the roots of the great vessels

3. Pericardial cavity

  • The potential space between the parietal and visceral layers
  • Contains a thin film of pericardial fluid (normally about 20–50 ml), which lubricates and allows the heart to beat without friction

4. Pericardial sinuses

  • Transverse sinus – a passage behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk (used by surgeons to clamp these vessels)
  • Oblique sinus – a recess behind the left atrium

5. Blood supply

  • Pericardiophrenic arteries and branches of the internal thoracic artery and aorta

6. Nerve supply

  • Phrenic nerves (C3–C5) – the fibrous and parietal layers are sensitive to pain; pain may be referred to the shoulder
  • The visceral layer is insensitive

7. Functions

  • Protects the heart from infection and injury
  • Anchors the heart in the mediastinum
  • Prevents sudden overfilling of the heart
  • Reduces friction during heartbeats

8. Applied anatomy

  • Pericarditis – inflammation causing sharp chest pain, worse on lying down and relieved by sitting forward; a pericardial friction rub is heard
  • Pericardial effusion – excess fluid
  • Cardiac tamponade – rapid collection of fluid or blood compresses the heart, reducing its filling – falling BP, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad); an emergency
  • Pericardiocentesis – removal of fluid with a needle, usually from below the xiphoid process directed towards the left shoulder
  • Constrictive pericarditis – a thick, rigid pericardium (e.g. after tuberculosis)

Conclusion The pericardium is a fibroserous sac with an outer fibrous layer and an inner serous layer (parietal and visceral) enclosing a small amount of lubricating fluid; it anchors, protects and limits the heart, and its diseases include pericarditis, effusion and tamponade.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the superior and inferior venae cavae and their tributaries.

diagram.caption: Superior and inferior venae cavae and their main tributaries

answer_html:
Introduction The venae cavae are the two largest veins of the body. They return deoxygenated blood from the whole body (except the lungs and heart wall) to the right atrium.

A. Superior vena cava (SVC)

  1. Formation – by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins, behind the lower border of the first right costal cartilage
  2. Each brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins behind the sternoclavicular joint; the left brachiocephalic vein is longer and crosses obliquely behind the manubrium
  3. Course and length – about 7 cm long; descends on the right side of the superior mediastinum and ends in the upper part of the right atrium at the level of the third right costal cartilage
  4. Tributaries – the azygos vein (draining the chest wall), and small pericardial and mediastinal veins
  5. No valves
  6. Drains the head, neck, upper limbs and chest wall

B. Inferior vena cava (IVC)

  1. Formation – by the union of the right and left common iliac veins in front of the L5 vertebra, slightly to the right of the midline
  2. Course and length – the largest vein of the body, about 22 cm long; ascends on the right side of the abdominal aorta, passes through the liver's groove and the caval opening of the diaphragm at T8, and opens into the lower part of the right atrium
  3. Tributaries:
    • common iliac veins (lower limbs and pelvis)
    • lumbar veins
    • right gonadal vein (the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein)
    • renal veins
    • right suprarenal vein (the left drains into the left renal vein)
    • inferior phrenic veins
    • hepatic veins (bringing blood from the liver, including the portal blood)
  4. Drains the lower limbs, pelvis, abdominal walls and abdominal organs

C. Clinical importance

  • Central venous catheters – inserted through the internal jugular or subclavian vein, with the tip lying in the SVC near the right atrium; used for CVP monitoring, long-term drugs and TPN
  • Jugular venous pressure (JVP) – the internal jugular vein reflects right atrial pressure; raised in heart failure
  • Superior vena cava syndrome – compression by lung cancer or lymphoma causes swelling of the face, neck and arms with distended neck veins
  • Supine hypotensive syndrome – in late pregnancy, the uterus compresses the IVC when the woman lies flat on her back, reducing venous return and BP; the left lateral position relieves it
  • IVC filter – placed to prevent pulmonary embolism from leg DVT
  • Air embolism – care when removing central lines (patient lies flat or head-down and holds breath)

Conclusion The SVC, formed by the brachiocephalic veins, drains the upper body, and the IVC, formed by the common iliac veins, drains the lower body; both open into the right atrium and are important in central lines, JVP assessment and the positioning of pregnant women.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the fetal circulation and the changes at birth.
answer_html:
Introduction Before birth, the fetus does not breathe; its lungs are not functioning and its oxygen comes from the placenta. The fetal circulation has special shunts that bypass the lungs and liver. These close after birth.

A. Special features of fetal circulation

  1. Umbilical vein (one) – carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
  2. Ductus venosus – carries most of this blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava
  3. Foramen ovale – an opening in the interatrial septum; lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs
  4. Ductus arteriosus – connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, sending blood from the right ventricle past the lungs
  5. Umbilical arteries (two) – branches of the internal iliac arteries; carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta

B. Course of blood

  • Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → inferior vena cava → right atrium
  • Most of this blood passes through the foramen ovale → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → the head and upper limbs get the best-oxygenated blood
  • Blood from the superior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → most goes through the ductus arteriosus → descending aorta → lower body
  • Deoxygenated blood returns to the placenta through the umbilical arteries

C. Changes at birth

  1. Lungs expand with the first breath; pulmonary resistance falls and blood flows to the lungs
  2. Foramen ovale closes – left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure and pushes the flap shut; it later becomes the fossa ovalis
  3. Ductus arteriosus closes – functionally within a day or so (rise in oxygen, fall in prostaglandins) and anatomically within weeks; becomes the ligamentum arteriosum
  4. Ductus venosus closes → ligamentum venosum
  5. Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres (round ligament) of the liver
  6. Umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments

D. Applied anatomy

  • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) – the duct fails to close (common in premature babies); continuous "machinery" murmur
  • Atrial septal defect – the foramen ovale fails to close
  • Cyanotic heart disease in newborns when shunts persist with abnormal structures (e.g. tetralogy of Fallot)
  • Nursing: observe newborns for cyanosis, breathlessness, poor feeding and murmurs; the umbilical vein is used for exchange transfusion and emergency access in newborns

Conclusion Fetal circulation uses the umbilical vessels, ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus to bypass the liver and lungs; at birth the lungs expand and these shunts close to become ligaments, and failure of closure causes congenital heart defects.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the superficial veins of the upper and lower limbs and their clinical importance.

diagram.caption: Superficial veins of the upper limb

answer_html:
Introduction Superficial veins lie in the subcutaneous tissue and are visible under the skin. They drain into the deep veins through perforating veins and contain valves. Nurses use them daily for venepuncture and IV cannulation.

A. Superficial veins of the upper limb

1. Dorsal venous network of the hand

  • On the back of the hand; drains into the cephalic and basilic veins
  • Dorsal metacarpal veins – good for cannulation; easy to see and secure

2. Cephalic vein

  • Begins on the lateral (thumb) side of the dorsal network
  • Runs up the lateral side of the forearm and arm, in the deltopectoral groove, to join the axillary vein
  • At the wrist it is large and constant – useful for cannulation

3. Basilic vein

  • Begins on the medial (little finger) side
  • Runs up the medial forearm; in the middle of the arm it pierces the deep fascia and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein
  • Used for PICC lines (peripherally inserted central catheters)

4. Median cubital vein

  • Connects the cephalic and basilic veins across the front of the elbow (cubital fossa)
  • Large, superficial and well-supported – the commonest site for venepuncture (blood sampling, blood donation)
  • The brachial artery and median nerve lie deep to it, separated by the bicipital aponeurosis – avoid deep, misdirected punctures

5. Median antebrachial vein

  • Runs up the front of the forearm

B. Superficial veins of the lower limb

1. Great saphenous vein

  • From the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial side of the leg and thigh to the femoral vein
  • Used for venous cut-down and coronary bypass grafts

2. Small saphenous vein

  • From the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, behind the lateral malleolus, up the back of the calf to the popliteal vein

C. Clinical importance

  • Venepuncture and IV cannulation – choose veins of the hand and forearm first (start distally so that proximal sites remain available); avoid joints, the arm on the side of a mastectomy or AV fistula, and paralysed limbs
  • Lower limb veins are avoided in adults because of the risk of thrombophlebitis and deep vein thrombosis
  • Scalp veins and dorsal hand veins are used in infants
  • Varicose veins – failure of valves in the saphenous veins; worsened by long standing (common in nurses, policemen)
  • Thrombophlebitis at cannula sites – check the site every shift and change cannulas as per policy
  • Tourniquet is applied above the site to make veins prominent

Conclusion The cephalic, basilic and median cubital veins of the upper limb and the great and small saphenous veins of the lower limb are the main superficial veins; knowledge of their course guides safe venepuncture, cannulation and the care of varicose veins.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure and functions of a lymph node.
answer_html:
Introduction Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs (a few millimetres to about 2 cm) placed along the course of lymph vessels. They filter lymph and produce immune responses. They occur in groups – cervical, axillary, inguinal, mediastinal and mesenteric.

1. External features

  • A convex surface, where several afferent lymph vessels enter
  • A depression, the hilum, where the efferent lymph vessel leaves and blood vessels enter and leave

2. Capsule and trabeculae

  • A fibrous capsule covers the node and sends trabeculae inwards, dividing it into compartments
  • A network of reticular fibres forms the internal framework

3. Cortex (outer part)

  • Contains lymphoid follicles (nodules), mainly B lymphocytes
  • Active follicles have pale germinal centres where B cells multiply in response to antigens

4. Paracortex (deep cortex)

  • Mainly T lymphocytes; contains special venules through which lymphocytes enter from the blood

5. Medulla (inner part)

  • Medullary cords – containing plasma cells (which make antibodies) and macrophages
  • Medullary sinuses – channels through which lymph flows to the hilum

6. Flow of lymph

  • Afferent vessels → subcapsular sinus → cortical sinuses → medullary sinuses → efferent vessel at the hilum
  • Lymph flows slowly, giving time for filtering

7. Functions

  • Filtration – macrophages remove bacteria, viruses, cancer cells and debris
  • Immune response – antigens are presented to lymphocytes; B cells make antibodies, T cells attack infected cells
  • Production of lymphocytes and plasma cells
  • Return of filtered lymph towards the blood

8. Applied anatomy

  • Lymphadenitis – painful, tender enlarged nodes in infection (e.g. cervical nodes in tonsillitis)
  • Tubercular lymphadenitis – matted cervical nodes, common in India
  • Spread of cancer – cancer cells travel to regional nodes (e.g. axillary nodes in breast cancer); the sentinel node is the first node draining a tumour
  • Lymphoma – cancer of lymphoid tissue
  • Lymph node examination is part of nursing physical assessment; lymphoedema of the arm may follow removal of axillary nodes – avoid BP measurement and injections on that arm

Conclusion A lymph node is a bean-shaped organ with a capsule, cortex (B cells), paracortex (T cells) and medulla (plasma cells), through which lymph flows from afferent to efferent vessels; it filters lymph and produces immune responses, and its enlargement signals infection or cancer.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the major arteries of the upper and lower limbs, with the sites for feeling pulses.
answer_html:
Introduction The limbs are supplied by continuous arterial trunks that change their names as they pass from one region to another. Knowing their course helps nurses to feel pulses, measure BP, assess circulation and control bleeding.

A. Arteries of the upper limb

  1. Subclavian artery – from the brachiocephalic trunk (right) or arch of aorta (left); passes over the first rib
  2. Axillary artery – from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of the teres major, in the axilla
  3. Brachial artery – runs down the medial side of the arm; in the cubital fossa it lies medial to the biceps tendon and divides into:
  4. Radial artery – along the lateral side of the forearm; at the wrist it lies lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon
  5. Ulnar artery – along the medial side of the forearm
  6. Palmar arches – superficial (mainly ulnar) and deep (mainly radial) arches supply the hand

Pulses in the upper limb

  • Brachial pulse – in the cubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon (BP measurement; CPR pulse check in infants)
  • Radial pulse – at the wrist on the thumb side – the commonest site
  • Ulnar pulse – on the little-finger side of the wrist
  • Allen's test – checks the ulnar supply before radial arterial puncture

B. Arteries of the lower limb

  1. External iliac artery – from the common iliac artery; passes under the inguinal ligament to become
  2. Femoral artery – in the femoral triangle; felt at the mid-inguinal point (midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis)
  3. Popliteal artery – deep in the popliteal fossa behind the knee
  4. Anterior tibial artery – front of the leg; continues on the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery
  5. Posterior tibial artery – back of the leg; passes behind the medial malleolus
  6. Peroneal (fibular) artery – branch of the posterior tibial

Pulses in the lower limb

  • Femoral – mid-inguinal point (in shock and cardiac arrest; arterial access)
  • Popliteal – felt with the knee slightly bent
  • Posterior tibial – behind the medial malleolus
  • Dorsalis pedis – on the top of the foot, lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus

C. Clinical importance

  • Circulation checks after fractures, plasters, cardiac catheterisation and vascular surgery – compare pulses on both sides
  • Peripheral vascular disease in diabetics and smokers – weak or absent foot pulses, risk of ulcers and gangrene
  • Pressure points to control severe bleeding – brachial and femoral arteries
  • Arterial blood gas sampling – radial artery
  • Intra-arterial injection must be avoided – check for blood colour and pulsation

Conclusion The upper limb is supplied by the subclavian–axillary–brachial–radial and ulnar arteries, and the lower limb by the femoral–popliteal–tibial arteries; their pulse points help nurses assess circulation, measure BP and control bleeding.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the aorta – its parts and branches – with applied anatomy. (2 + 6 + 2)

diagram.caption: The aorta and its main branches

answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • The aorta is the largest artery of the body; it carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to all parts of the body through its branches
  • It begins at the aortic orifice of the left ventricle (guarded by the aortic valve) and ends in front of the 4th lumbar vertebra by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries
  • Its wall is rich in elastic tissue, which stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, keeping blood flowing between heartbeats
  • It is divided into four parts: ascending aorta, arch of aorta, descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta

(b) Parts and branches (6 marks)

1. Ascending aorta

  • About 5 cm long, within the pericardium, from the left ventricle to the level of the sternal angle
  • Branches: the right and left coronary arteries, arising from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve – they supply the heart muscle

2. Arch of the aorta

  • Begins and ends at the level of the sternal angle (T4); arches backwards and to the left over the root of the left lung
  • Branches:
    • Brachiocephalic trunk → right common carotid and right subclavian arteries
    • Left common carotid artery
    • Left subclavian artery
  • The ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of the ductus arteriosus) connects it to the pulmonary trunk; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks below it

3. Descending thoracic aorta

  • From T4 to the aortic opening of the diaphragm at T12, in the posterior mediastinum
  • Branches:
    • Posterior intercostal arteries (3rd to 11th spaces) and subcostal arteries – chest wall
    • Bronchial arteries – lungs
    • Oesophageal, pericardial and mediastinal branches
    • Superior phrenic arteries – diaphragm

4. Abdominal aorta

  • From T12 to its bifurcation at L4 (at about the level of the umbilicus), lying on the vertebral column, left of the inferior vena cava
  • Branches:
    • Ventral unpaired (to the gut):
    • coeliac trunk (T12)
    • superior mesenteric artery (L1)
    • inferior mesenteric artery (L3)
    • Lateral paired (to organs):
    • inferior phrenic arteries
    • middle suprarenal arteries
    • renal arteries (L1–L2)
    • gonadal arteries – testicular or ovarian (L2)
    • Dorsal: four pairs of lumbar arteries and the median sacral artery
    • Terminal: right and left common iliac arteries, which divide into external iliac (lower limb) and internal iliac (pelvic organs, gluteal region) arteries

Summary

Part Extent Main branches
Ascending left ventricle to sternal angle coronary arteries
Arch at T4 level brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
Descending thoracic T4–T12 intercostal, bronchial, oesophageal arteries
Abdominal T12–L4 coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric, renal, gonadal, common iliac arteries

(c) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Aortic aneurysm – abnormal dilatation, commonest in the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries; felt as a pulsatile abdominal mass; rupture is fatal; risk factors – atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension
  • Aortic dissection – blood tears between the layers of the wall; severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back
  • Coarctation of the aorta – congenital narrowing near the ligamentum arteriosum; high BP in the arms with weak, delayed femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay)
  • Aortic stenosis and regurgitation – valve diseases
  • Atherosclerosis of the aorta and its branches – renal artery stenosis (hypertension), mesenteric ischaemia, leg claudication
  • Nursing: compare BP in both arms and pulses in all limbs; monitor pulses and urine output after aortic surgery

Conclusion The aorta, the largest artery, arises from the left ventricle and runs as the ascending aorta (coronary branches), the arch (three great branches), the descending thoracic aorta (intercostal, bronchial and oesophageal branches) and the abdominal aorta (visceral, renal, gonadal and common iliac branches); aneurysm, dissection and coarctation are important disorders.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the lobes of the pituitary gland and the hormones of each.
answer_html:
Introduction The pituitary gland is a pea-sized gland at the base of the brain, called the master gland because it controls many other endocrine glands.

1. Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) – glandular part; secretes:

  • Growth hormone (GH)
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
  • Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
  • Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
  • Luteinising hormone (LH)
  • Prolactin

2. Posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) – nervous part; stores and releases:

  • ADH (vasopressin)
  • Oxytocin (Both are made in the hypothalamus.)

3. Intermediate part – small; secretes MSH (melanocyte-stimulating hormone).

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a note on the parathyroid glands.
answer_html:
Introduction The parathyroid glands are small endocrine glands that control blood calcium.

Features

  1. Number – usually four (two superior, two inferior)
  2. Location – on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes
  3. Size – each about 6 mm long, yellowish-brown, like a lentil
  4. Cells – chief cells secrete parathormone (PTH); oxyphil cells
  5. Function – PTH raises blood calcium by releasing calcium from bone, increasing reabsorption in the kidney and activating vitamin D

Applied: accidental removal during thyroidectomy causes low calcium and tetany – watch for tingling around the lips, muscle cramps, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs; keep IV calcium gluconate ready.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: State the location and functions of the thymus.
answer_html:
Introduction The thymus is a lymphoid and endocrine organ that trains the body's T lymphocytes.

Location

  • Lies in the superior and anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum and in front of the great vessels
  • Has two lobes

Size changes

  • Large in infancy and childhood
  • Shrinks after puberty and is largely replaced by fat in adults

Functions

  1. Maturation of T lymphocytes – essential for cell-mediated immunity
  2. Secretes the hormone thymosin
  3. Helps the immune system tell "self" from "non-self"

Applied: thymus tumours (thymoma) are linked with myasthenia gravis.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the pituitary gland.
answer_html:
Introduction The pituitary gland (hypophysis cerebri) is a small endocrine gland at the base of the brain. It is called the "master gland" because its hormones control the thyroid, adrenal cortex, ovaries and testes. However, it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus.

1. Location

  • Lies in a depression of the sphenoid bone called the sella turcica (hypophyseal fossa)
  • Hangs from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum (pituitary stalk)

2. Size and weight

  • About the size of a pea – about 1 cm across
  • Weighs about 0.5 g; enlarges slightly in pregnancy

3. Relations

  • Above: optic chiasma and hypothalamus – a pituitary tumour presses on the chiasma and causes loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopia)
  • On each side: cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery
  • Below: sphenoid sinus – surgeons reach the gland through the nose (trans-sphenoidal surgery)

4. Parts

  1. Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis)
    • About 75% of the gland; made of glandular cells
    • Secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin
    • Controlled by releasing and inhibiting hormones from the hypothalamus that reach it through the hypophyseal portal vessels
  2. Posterior lobe (neurohypophysis)
    • Made of nerve fibres and supporting cells (pituicytes)
    • Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and travel down the nerve fibres of the stalk
  3. Pars intermedia – a thin strip; secretes MSH

5. Blood supply

  • Superior and inferior hypophyseal arteries (from the internal carotid)
  • Hypophyseal portal system – a special set of vessels linking the hypothalamus to the anterior lobe

6. Functions (in brief)

  • Growth, metabolism, stress response, reproduction, lactation and water balance

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Gigantism (excess GH in children) and acromegaly (excess GH in adults)
  • Dwarfism – GH deficiency in childhood
  • Diabetes insipidus – ADH deficiency; passing large volumes of dilute urine; keep strict intake–output and daily weight
  • Sheehan's syndrome – pituitary damage after severe postpartum haemorrhage; failure of lactation is the first sign
  • Pituitary tumours – headache and visual field loss

Conclusion The pituitary is a small gland in the sella turcica with an anterior glandular lobe and a posterior nervous lobe; through its hormones it regulates most other endocrine glands.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the suprarenal (adrenal) glands.
answer_html:
Introduction The suprarenal (adrenal) glands are two endocrine glands, one above each kidney. Each gland is really two glands in one – an outer cortex and an inner medulla – with different origins and hormones.

1. Location

  • On the upper pole of each kidney, on the posterior abdominal wall
  • Retroperitoneal (behind the peritoneum)
  • Lie within the renal fascia but in a separate compartment, so the gland stays behind when a kidney is removed

2. Shape and size

  • Right gland – triangular (pyramidal)
  • Left gland – crescent-shaped (semilunar)
  • Each is about 5 cm high, 3 cm wide and 1 cm thick, and weighs about 4–5 g

3. Structure

A. Cortex (outer, yellow) – about 80–90% of the gland; secretes steroid hormones (corticosteroids). It has three zones – remember "GFR – salt, sugar, sex":

  • Zona glomerulosa (outer) → mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone – retains sodium and water, removes potassium ("salt")
  • Zona fasciculata (middle, thickest) → glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol – raises blood sugar, reduces inflammation ("sugar")
  • Zona reticularis (inner) → sex hormones (androgens) ("sex")

B. Medulla (inner, reddish-brown)

  • Made of chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic nerve cells
  • Secretes adrenaline (about 80%) and noradrenaline
  • These are the "fight or flight" hormones – raise heart rate, BP and blood sugar in stress

4. Blood supply

  • Three arteries on each side:
    • Superior suprarenal artery (from the inferior phrenic artery)
    • Middle suprarenal artery (from the aorta)
    • Inferior suprarenal artery (from the renal artery)
  • One vein on each side: right → inferior vena cava; left → left renal vein

5. Nerve supply

  • Preganglionic sympathetic fibres go directly to the medulla (splanchnic nerves) – so the medulla acts like a sympathetic ganglion

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Addison's disease – destruction of the cortex: weakness, low BP, low sodium, darkening of skin
  • Cushing's syndrome – excess cortisol: moon face, buffalo hump, obesity, high sugar and BP
  • Conn's syndrome – excess aldosterone: hypertension, low potassium
  • Phaeochromocytoma – tumour of the medulla: attacks of very high BP, sweating, palpitations
  • Patients on long-term steroids must never stop them suddenly – risk of adrenal crisis (shock)

Conclusion Each adrenal gland sits on the upper pole of a kidney; its cortex makes steroid hormones for salt, sugar and sex functions, and its medulla makes adrenaline for the stress response.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the thyroid gland under the headings: location, structure, blood supply, relations and applied anatomy. (2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2)

diagram.caption: Thyroid gland - front view and follicles

answer_html:
Introduction The thyroid gland is the largest purely endocrine gland in the body. Its hormones control the body's metabolic rate, growth and development, so even small changes in its activity affect almost every organ.

(a) Location (2 marks)

  • A butterfly-shaped (H-shaped) gland in the front and sides of the lower neck
  • Lies at the level of the C5 to T1 vertebrae, in front of the larynx and trachea
  • Two lateral lobes – one on each side of the larynx and trachea
  • The isthmus joins the two lobes and lies over the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings
  • A small pyramidal lobe may rise upwards from the isthmus (a remnant of the thyroglossal duct)
  • Weight: about 25 g; slightly larger in women, and enlarges during puberty, menstruation and pregnancy
  • Enclosed in the pretracheal fascia, which binds it to the larynx – so the gland moves up on swallowing, a useful clinical sign

(b) Structure (3 marks) 1. Capsule

  • A true fibrous capsule surrounds the gland and sends partitions inside, dividing it into lobules
  • Outside it lies a false capsule from the pretracheal fascia

2. Thyroid follicles – the functional units

  • Each follicle is a small hollow sphere lined by a single layer of cuboidal follicular cells
  • The cavity is filled with a jelly-like substance called colloid, which contains thyroglobulin – the stored form of thyroid hormone
  • The gland stores enough hormone to last several weeks
  • Active follicles have tall cells and less colloid; resting follicles have flat cells and more colloid

3. Follicular cells

  • Take up iodine from the blood
  • Make thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which increase the metabolic rate

4. Parafollicular (C) cells

  • Lie between the follicles
  • Secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium

5. Stroma – a rich network of capillaries and connective tissue between the follicles.

(c) Blood supply (2 marks) The thyroid is one of the most vascular organs for its size.

  • Arteries
    • Superior thyroid artery – first branch of the external carotid artery; enters the upper pole
    • Inferior thyroid artery – from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery; enters the back of the lower part
    • Thyroidea ima artery – present occasionally, from the brachiocephalic trunk or arch of aorta
  • Veins
    • Superior and middle thyroid veins → internal jugular vein
    • Inferior thyroid veins → brachiocephalic veins
  • Lymph – to the deep cervical and pretracheal lymph nodes

Nerve supply: sympathetic fibres from the cervical ganglia (mainly control blood vessels).

(d) Relations (1 mark)

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus, close to the inferior thyroid artery
  • External laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery
  • Parathyroid glands lie on the back of the lateral lobes
  • Carotid sheath (common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus) lies on each side
  • Trachea and oesophagus lie behind and medial
  • Covered in front by the strap muscles of the neck and the skin

(e) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  1. Goitre – any enlargement of the thyroid
    • Iodine-deficiency goitre is common in many parts of India, especially hilly areas; prevented by iodised salt under the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme
  2. Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) – weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, bulging eyes
  3. Hypothyroidism
    • Cretinism in infants – mental and physical retardation; newborn screening for TSH helps early treatment
    • Myxoedema in adults – weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, slow pulse
  4. Thyroid nodules and cancer – a swelling that moves on swallowing is examined by ultrasound and needle biopsy (FNAC)
  5. Post-thyroidectomy complications and nursing care
    • Haemorrhage and airway obstruction – keep a tracheostomy tray and suture-cutting set at the bedside; watch for neck swelling and breathlessness
    • Hoarseness or voice change – injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve; ask the patient to speak at intervals
    • Tetany – accidental removal of the parathyroid glands; watch for tingling and spasms, keep calcium gluconate ready
    • Thyroid storm – high fever, tachycardia, agitation
    • Position the patient semi-Fowler's with head and neck supported
  6. Examination – ask the patient to swallow and watch whether the swelling moves upward; a thyroglossal cyst moves on protruding the tongue

Conclusion The thyroid is a highly vascular, butterfly-shaped gland in the lower neck, made of colloid-filled follicles that produce T3, T4 and calcitonin. Its close relation to the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands explains the main complications of thyroid surgery.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the endocrine glands of the body with their location.
answer_html:
Introduction Endocrine glands are ductless glands that pour their secretions (hormones) directly into the blood.

Endocrine glands and location

  1. Hypothalamus – base of the brain, below the thalamus
  2. Pituitary gland – in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
  3. Pineal gland – on the back of the third ventricle of the brain
  4. Thyroid gland – front of the neck, over the trachea (C5–T1)
  5. Parathyroid glands (four) – on the back of the thyroid lobes
  6. Thymus – superior and anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum
  7. Adrenal (suprarenal) glands – on the upper poles of the kidneys
  8. Islets of Langerhans – in the pancreas
  9. Gonads – testes in the scrotum; ovaries in the pelvis - Others: placenta (in pregnancy), kidneys, heart, stomach and intestines also produce hormones

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a note on the pineal gland.
answer_html:
Introduction The pineal gland (pineal body) is a small, pine-cone-shaped gland, about 8 mm long, attached to the posterior wall of the third ventricle of the brain, above the superior colliculi.

Structure

  • Made of pinealocytes and neuroglial cells
  • With age, calcium deposits form ("brain sand"), which make it visible on X-rays and CT – a useful midline landmark

Functions

  1. Secretes melatonin, mainly at night (darkness stimulates and light inhibits its release)
  2. Regulates the sleep–wake cycle (circadian rhythm)
  3. May delay the onset of puberty in childhood

Applied: night-shift work and jet lag disturb melatonin rhythm; melatonin tablets are used for some sleep problems.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the hypophyseal portal system?
answer_html:
Definition The hypophyseal (hypothalamo-hypophyseal) portal system is a special system of blood vessels that carries releasing and inhibiting hormones from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary.

Arrangement

  1. Primary capillary plexus in the median eminence of the hypothalamus receives the hypothalamic hormones
  2. Portal veins run down the pituitary stalk (infundibulum)
  3. Secondary capillary plexus in the anterior pituitary releases them onto the pituitary cells

Importance

  • Allows the hypothalamus to control the anterior pituitary with small amounts of hormones
  • The posterior pituitary is controlled differently – by nerve fibres (hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract) carrying ADH and oxytocin

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the cells of the thyroid gland and the hormones they secrete.
answer_html:
Introduction The thyroid gland is made of many small, round follicles filled with a protein-rich colloid (thyroglobulin).

Cells and hormones

  1. Follicular cells – line the follicles; secrete thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which control the metabolic rate, growth and development; they need iodine
  2. Parafollicular cells (C cells) – lie between the follicles; secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium by depositing calcium in bones

Applied: iodine deficiency causes goitre; deficiency of thyroid hormone in infants causes cretinism – hence newborn screening and iodised salt.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the hypothalamus and its relation with the pituitary gland.
answer_html:
Introduction The hypothalamus is a small but very important part of the diencephalon of the brain. It links the nervous system and the endocrine system, and controls the pituitary gland – the so-called "master gland". Hence the hypothalamus is called the "master of the master gland".

1. Location

  • Lies below the thalamus, forming the floor and lower lateral walls of the third ventricle
  • Its under-surface shows the optic chiasma, the tuber cinereum with the infundibulum (pituitary stalk) and the mammillary bodies

2. Important nuclei and their functions

  • Supraoptic nucleus – produces ADH (vasopressin)
  • Paraventricular nucleus – produces oxytocin (and some ADH)
  • Suprachiasmatic nucleus – the body clock (circadian rhythm)
  • Lateral area – hunger centre; ventromedial nucleus – satiety centre
  • Preoptic and anterior areas – heat loss; posterior area – heat conservation (temperature regulation)
  • Arcuate and other nuclei – produce releasing and inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine)

3. Relation with the pituitary gland

(a) Hypothalamus and anterior pituitary – by blood vessels

  • The hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones travel through the hypophyseal portal system (primary plexus → portal veins → secondary plexus) to the anterior pituitary
  • They stimulate or inhibit the secretion of GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin

(b) Hypothalamus and posterior pituitary – by nerve fibres

  • Axons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei form the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract down the stalk
  • ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus are carried along these axons, stored in the posterior pituitary and released into the blood when needed

4. Other functions of the hypothalamus

  • Control of the autonomic nervous system (heart rate, BP, gut activity)
  • Thirst, hunger, body temperature, sleep–wake cycle
  • Emotional behaviour (with the limbic system) – rage, fear, pleasure
  • Stress response – through CRH → ACTH → cortisol

5. Applied anatomy

  • Diabetes insipidus – lack of ADH; large volumes of dilute urine and thirst
  • Hypothalamic tumours – obesity, abnormal temperature, early or delayed puberty
  • Head injury and brain surgery – disturbances of temperature and fluid balance; nurses monitor intake–output and temperature

Conclusion The hypothalamus, in the floor of the third ventricle, controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep and emotions, and regulates the anterior pituitary through the portal system and the posterior pituitary through nerve fibres carrying ADH and oxytocin.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the endocrine part of the pancreas (islets of Langerhans).

diagram.caption: Islet of Langerhans among pancreatic acini

answer_html:
Introduction The pancreas is a mixed gland. Its exocrine part (acini) produces digestive enzymes, and its endocrine part – the islets of Langerhans – produces hormones that control blood glucose.

1. Structure

  • About 1–2 million islets, scattered like small islands among the acini; they form only about 1–2% of the pancreas
  • More numerous in the tail of the pancreas
  • Each islet is a cluster of pale-staining cells with a rich network of capillaries into which hormones are released

2. Cell types and hormones

Cell Approximate proportion Hormone Main action
Beta (β) cells about 70% (centre) insulin lowers blood glucose – helps glucose enter cells; promotes glycogen, fat and protein formation
Alpha (α) cells about 20% (periphery) glucagon raises blood glucose – glycogen breakdown and glucose formation in the liver
Delta (δ) cells about 5–10% somatostatin inhibits insulin and glucagon secretion
PP (F) cells few pancreatic polypeptide regulates pancreatic secretion and appetite

3. Blood supply

  • Branches of the splenic and pancreaticoduodenal arteries; the islets receive a large share of the pancreatic blood
  • Venous blood goes to the portal vein, so insulin reaches the liver first

4. Nerve supply

  • Sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagus) fibres modify hormone secretion

5. Regulation

  • High blood glucose stimulates beta cells; low blood glucose stimulates alpha cells – a negative feedback system

6. Applied anatomy

  • Diabetes mellitus:
    • type 1 – autoimmune destruction of beta cells; insulin needed from the start (children, young adults)
    • type 2 – insulin resistance and reduced secretion; related to obesity and lifestyle
  • Insulinoma – a tumour of beta cells causing low blood sugar
  • Pancreatitis and pancreatic surgery may cause diabetes
  • Nursing: insulin injection technique and sites, blood glucose monitoring, recognising hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion) and hyperglycaemia, foot care and diet education

Conclusion The islets of Langerhans, forming 1–2% of the pancreas, contain beta cells (insulin), alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin) and PP cells, which together keep blood glucose normal; their failure causes diabetes mellitus.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the endocrine glands. Write their location, structure in brief and the hormones secreted by each. (2 + 8)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction and list (2 marks)

  • Endocrine glands are ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the blood; hormones act on distant target organs and regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction and the internal environment
  • Main endocrine glands: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, adrenals, islets of the pancreas and gonads (testes and ovaries)
  • Other hormone-producing tissues: placenta, kidneys (erythropoietin, renin), heart (atrial natriuretic peptide), gut (gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin) and adipose tissue (leptin)

(b) Location, structure and hormones (8 marks)

1. Hypothalamus

  • Location: base of the brain, forming the floor of the third ventricle
  • Structure: groups of nerve cells (nuclei) in the diencephalon
  • Hormones: releasing and inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) to the anterior pituitary; ADH and oxytocin (stored in the posterior pituitary)

2. Pituitary gland (hypophysis)

  • Location: in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, attached to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum
  • Structure: pea-sized (about 1 cm), with an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) of glandular cells and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) of nerve fibres
  • Hormones:
    • Anterior lobe – growth hormone (GH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinising hormone (LH), prolactin
    • Posterior lobe – releases ADH (water retention) and oxytocin (uterine contraction, milk ejection)

3. Pineal gland

  • Location: posterior wall of the third ventricle
  • Structure: small, cone-shaped; pinealocytes; calcifies with age
  • Hormone: melatonin – sleep–wake rhythm

4. Thyroid gland

  • Location: front of the neck at C5–T1, in front of the trachea
  • Structure: two lobes joined by an isthmus (over the 2nd–4th tracheal rings); made of follicles with colloid; highly vascular
  • Hormones: thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) from follicular cells – metabolism, growth, brain development; calcitonin from C cells – lowers blood calcium

5. Parathyroid glands

  • Location: usually four, on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes
  • Structure: small, yellowish-brown, about the size of a grain of rice; chief cells and oxyphil cells
  • Hormone: parathyroid hormone (parathormone) – raises blood calcium (from bone, kidney and gut, with vitamin D)

6. Thymus

  • Location: superior and anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum
  • Structure: two lobes with cortex and medulla; large in children, replaced by fat after puberty
  • Hormones: thymosin and other factors – maturation of T lymphocytes

7. Adrenal (suprarenal) glands

  • Location: on the upper poles of the kidneys (right – pyramidal, left – crescent-shaped)
  • Structure: outer cortex with three zones and inner medulla
  • Hormones:
    • Zona glomerulosa – aldosterone (salt and water balance)
    • Zona fasciculata – cortisol (glucose, stress, anti-inflammatory)
    • Zona reticularis – sex hormones (androgens)
    • Medulla – adrenaline and noradrenaline (fight-or-flight)

8. Islets of Langerhans (pancreas)

  • Location: scattered in the pancreas, more in the tail
  • Structure: clusters of alpha, beta, delta and PP cells with rich capillaries
  • Hormones: insulin (beta), glucagon (alpha), somatostatin (delta), pancreatic polypeptide

9. Gonads

  • Testes – in the scrotum; Leydig (interstitial) cells secrete testosterone – male characteristics, sperm production
  • Ovaries – in the pelvis; follicles secrete oestrogen, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone; also relaxin and inhibin

10. Placenta (temporary endocrine organ)

  • hCG, oestrogen, progesterone and human placental lactogen – maintain pregnancy

Summary table

Gland Location Main hormones
Pituitary sella turcica GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; ADH, oxytocin
Thyroid front of neck T3, T4, calcitonin
Parathyroid behind thyroid parathormone
Adrenal above kidneys aldosterone, cortisol, androgens, adrenaline
Pancreatic islets pancreas insulin, glucagon
Gonads scrotum / pelvis testosterone; oestrogen, progesterone

Applied importance

  • Disorders of excess or deficiency – diabetes mellitus, hypo- and hyperthyroidism, goitre, Cushing's syndrome, Addison's disease, gigantism and acromegaly, dwarfism, tetany after accidental removal of the parathyroids during thyroid surgery
  • Nursing – monitoring blood sugar, calcium (tingling, carpopedal spasm after thyroidectomy), fluid balance, weight and vital signs; teaching hormone replacement

Conclusion The endocrine glands – hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, adrenals, pancreatic islets and gonads – are located from the brain to the pelvis; through their hormones they control growth, metabolism, salt, water, calcium and glucose balance, stress responses and reproduction.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the layers (coats) of the eyeball.
answer_html:
Introduction The wall of the eyeball is made of three coats (layers), one inside the other.

1. Outer fibrous coat

  • Sclera – white, tough, posterior five-sixths; maintains the shape of the eye
  • Cornea – transparent, anterior one-sixth; lets light in and bends (refracts) it

2. Middle vascular coat (uvea)

  • Choroid – dark, vascular layer that nourishes the retina
  • Ciliary body – controls the shape of the lens
  • Iris – coloured part with the pupil in the centre

3. Inner nervous coat

  • Retina – contains the light-sensitive rods and cones

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the ear ossicles and state their function.
answer_html:
Introduction The ear ossicles are three tiny bones in the middle ear, the smallest bones in the body.

Ossicles (from outside inwards)

  1. Malleus (hammer) – its handle is attached to the tympanic membrane
  2. Incus (anvil) – the middle bone
  3. Stapes (stirrup) – the smallest bone of the body; its footplate fits into the oval window

Function

  • Form a chain of levers that carries sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear
  • Amplify the vibrations so that sound waves can move the fluid of the inner ear

Applied: fixation of the stapes (otosclerosis) causes conductive deafness.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the types of papillae of the tongue.
answer_html:
Introduction Papillae are small projections on the upper surface of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. They give the tongue its rough surface and many carry taste buds.

Types

  1. Filiform papillae – thread-like, the most numerous; give the tongue a velvety feel; no taste buds
  2. Fungiform papillae – mushroom-shaped, seen as red dots at the tip and sides; carry taste buds
  3. Circumvallate (vallate) papillae – the largest; 8–12 in a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis; each has many taste buds
  4. Foliate papillae – leaf-like folds on the sides at the back; poorly developed in humans

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the skin.
answer_html:
Introduction The skin (integument) is the largest organ of the body. In an adult it covers about 1.5–2 square metres and forms a protective barrier between the body and the outside world.

1. Epidermis (outer layer)

  • Made of stratified squamous keratinised epithelium
  • Has no blood vessels – nourished from the dermis
  • Layers (from deep to surface):
    1. Stratum basale (germinativum) – a single layer of dividing cells; contains melanocytes
    2. Stratum spinosum – prickle cells
    3. Stratum granulosum – cells with keratin granules
    4. Stratum lucidum – clear layer, only in thick skin of palms and soles
    5. Stratum corneum – dead, flat, keratin-filled cells that are continuously shed
  • Cells: keratinocytes, melanocytes (make melanin – skin colour and UV protection), Langerhans cells (immunity), Merkel cells (touch)
  • The epidermis is completely renewed about every 4 weeks

2. Dermis (true skin)

  • Dense connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibres – gives strength and elasticity
  • Papillary layer – finger-like dermal papillae that form fingerprints; capillary loops; Meissner's corpuscles (light touch)
  • Reticular layer – thicker; contains blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, Pacinian corpuscles (pressure) and free nerve endings (pain, temperature)

3. Appendages of the skin (lie in the dermis)

  • Hair follicles with arrector pili muscles (cause "goose flesh")
  • Sebaceous glands – secrete oily sebum that keeps skin and hair soft
  • Sweat glands – eccrine (all over the body; temperature control) and apocrine (axilla, groin; body odour)
  • Nails

4. Subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis)

  • Not part of the skin proper; loose areolar and adipose tissue
  • Insulates the body, stores energy, cushions and anchors the skin

5. Functions (in brief): protection, temperature regulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, excretion and absorption.

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Pressure injuries develop over bony prominences (sacrum, heels, hips) where the skin is squeezed against bone – turn patients every 2 hours
  • Burns are classified by depth: superficial (epidermis), partial thickness (part of dermis), full thickness (whole skin)
  • Injection depths: intradermal into the dermis at 10–15° (Mantoux, BCG); subcutaneous into the hypodermis at 45° (insulin, heparin); intramuscular at 90°
  • Skin assessment shows dehydration (poor turgor), cyanosis, jaundice, pallor and rashes

Conclusion The skin has an outer avascular epidermis, an inner vascular dermis containing its appendages, and rests on the subcutaneous fat; its layered structure explains burns, injections and pressure injuries.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the ear.
answer_html:
Introduction The ear is the organ of hearing and balance (equilibrium). It is divided into three parts – the external, middle and inner ear. The middle and inner ear lie inside the temporal bone.

1. External ear – collects sound

  • Auricle (pinna) – a plate of elastic cartilage covered by skin; the lobule has no cartilage
  • External acoustic meatus – about 2.5 cm long and S-shaped
    • Outer one-third cartilaginous, with hairs and ceruminous glands that make wax
    • Inner two-thirds bony
  • Tympanic membrane (eardrum)
    • Thin, pearly-grey, oval membrane, slightly cone-shaped
    • Separates the external from the middle ear
    • Vibrates when sound waves strike it; a bright "cone of light" is seen on otoscopy

2. Middle ear (tympanic cavity) – transmits sound

  • An air-filled space in the temporal bone
  • Ossicles – malleus, incus and stapes – form a chain that carries and amplifies vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window
  • Muscles – tensor tympani and stapedius; they dampen very loud sounds
  • Auditory (Eustachian) tube – connects the middle ear with the nasopharynx; equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum (opens on swallowing and yawning)
  • Communicates behind with the mastoid air cells
  • Windows – oval window (stapes) and round window (releases pressure)

3. Inner ear (labyrinth) – hearing and balance

  • Bony labyrinth filled with perilymph, enclosing the membranous labyrinth filled with endolymph
  • Cochlea – snail-shaped tube of about 2¾ turns; contains the organ of Corti, the receptor for hearing
  • Vestibule – contains the utricle and saccule; sense the position of the head (static balance)
  • Three semicircular canals – at right angles to each other; sense rotation (dynamic balance)
  • Nerve: vestibulocochlear (8th cranial) nerve

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, so throat infections easily cause otitis media
  • Instilling ear drops – pull the pinna up and back in adults and down and back in children under 3 years to straighten the canal
  • Never poke the ear with sticks or pins; wax may be softened with drops
  • Noise-induced hearing loss in industrial workers
  • Vertigo in inner-ear disorders
  • Ototoxic drugs such as streptomycin and gentamicin – ask about ringing in the ears and hearing loss

Conclusion The external ear collects sound, the middle ear amplifies it through three ossicles, and the inner ear converts it into nerve impulses and also maintains balance.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the tongue.
answer_html:
Introduction The tongue is a highly mobile muscular organ in the floor of the mouth, covered by mucous membrane. It is the main organ of taste and is essential for chewing, swallowing and speech.

1. Parts

  • Tip – the free front end
  • Body (oral part) – the anterior two-thirds, lying in the mouth
  • Root (pharyngeal part) – the posterior one-third, facing the oropharynx; carries the lingual tonsil
  • The two parts are separated by a V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, with a small pit, the foramen caecum, at its apex

2. Surfaces

  • Upper surface (dorsum) – rough, covered with papillae
  • Under surface – smooth; shows the frenulum in the midline and large veins on each side (site for sublingual drugs)

3. Papillae: filiform (most numerous, no taste buds), fungiform, circumvallate (largest, many taste buds) and foliate.

4. Muscles

  • Intrinsic muscles – lie wholly within the tongue; change its shape (important for speech)
  • Extrinsic muscles – attach it to bones; change its position:
    • Genioglossus – protrudes the tongue; called the "safety muscle" because it prevents the tongue from falling back
    • Hyoglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus
  • All muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal (12th) nerve, except palatoglossus (vagus)

5. Sensory nerve supply

  • Anterior two-thirds: general sensation – lingual nerve; taste – chorda tympani (facial nerve)
  • Posterior one-third: general sensation and taste – glossopharyngeal nerve
  • Near the epiglottis: vagus nerve

6. Blood supply: lingual artery; veins drain into the internal jugular vein.

7. Functions

  • Taste
  • Chewing – keeps food between the teeth
  • Swallowing – pushes the bolus into the pharynx
  • Speech – articulation of words
  • Cleaning the teeth and mouth

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • In an unconscious patient the tongue falls back and blocks the airway – use head tilt–chin lift, jaw thrust or an oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway
  • Sublingual drugs (nitroglycerine) are absorbed quickly through the thin mucosa under the tongue
  • Oral thermometer is placed in the sublingual pocket
  • Glossitis (red, sore tongue) in iron and B-complex deficiency; central cyanosis is checked on the tongue
  • Coated tongue in fever and dehydration – needs mouth care
  • Damage to the hypoglossal nerve makes the protruded tongue deviate to the affected side

Conclusion The tongue is a muscular organ with intrinsic and extrinsic muscles, covered by papillae carrying taste buds; it is vital for taste, chewing, swallowing and speech.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the eyeball with a labelled diagram. Add a note on applied anatomy.
answer_html:
Introduction The eye is the organ of sight (vision). The eyeball is a nearly spherical organ, about 2.5 cm (24 mm) in diameter, lying in the front part of the bony orbit, cushioned by fat and protected by the eyelids, conjunctiva and tears. Its wall has three coats, and its cavity contains three transparent refractive media.

A. Coats of the eyeball

1. Outer fibrous coat

  • Sclera
    • The white, tough, opaque posterior five-sixths ("white of the eye")
    • Keeps the shape of the eyeball and protects its contents
    • Gives attachment to the extraocular muscles
    • Pierced at the back by the optic nerve
  • Cornea
    • The transparent anterior one-sixth, more curved than the sclera
    • Avascular – nourished by tears and aqueous humour, which is why corneal grafts are rarely rejected
    • Does most of the bending (refraction) of light
    • Richly supplied with nerves – very sensitive (corneal reflex)
    • Junction of cornea and sclera is the limbus

2. Middle vascular coat (uvea or uveal tract)

  • Choroid
    • A thin, dark brown, highly vascular layer lining the sclera
    • Nourishes the outer layers of the retina
    • Its pigment absorbs stray light and prevents reflection inside the eye
  • Ciliary body
    • A thickened ring between the choroid and the iris
    • Ciliary muscle changes the shape of the lens for near vision (accommodation)
    • Ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour
  • Iris
    • The coloured, circular diaphragm in front of the lens, with a central opening called the pupil
    • Sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic – 3rd nerve) constricts the pupil in bright light and near vision
    • Dilator pupillae (sympathetic) dilates the pupil in dim light, fear and excitement
    • Controls the amount of light entering the eye, like the aperture of a camera

3. Inner nervous coat – retina

  • Lines the back two-thirds of the eyeball
  • Contains the photoreceptors:
    • Rods – about 120 million; work in dim light; black-and-white vision; need vitamin A
    • Cones – about 6 million; work in bright light; colour vision and sharp detail
  • Macula lutea (yellow spot) – at the back, in line with the visual axis; its central pit, the fovea centralis, contains only cones – the point of sharpest vision
  • Optic disc – about 3 mm to the nasal side of the macula, where nerve fibres leave as the optic nerve; it has no rods or cones, so it is the blind spot
  • Central retinal artery and vein enter and leave at the optic disc and are seen on ophthalmoscopy

B. Contents (refractive media) of the eyeball

  1. Aqueous humour
    • Clear, watery fluid in the anterior chamber (between cornea and iris) and posterior chamber (between iris and lens)
    • Secreted by the ciliary processes, flows through the pupil and drains through the canal of Schlemm at the angle between the cornea and iris
    • Maintains the intraocular pressure (about 10–21 mm Hg) and nourishes the cornea and lens
  2. Lens
    • Transparent, biconvex, elastic and avascular
    • Held in place by the suspensory ligaments (zonules) attached to the ciliary body
    • Changes its curvature to focus light exactly on the retina
    • Becomes harder and less elastic with age
  3. Vitreous body (humour)
    • Clear, jelly-like substance filling the large space behind the lens (about four-fifths of the eyeball)
    • Keeps the eyeball in shape and holds the retina against the choroid

C. Accessory structures (briefly)

  • Eyelids and eyelashes – protect the eye; blinking spreads tears
  • Conjunctiva – thin mucous membrane lining the lids and covering the front of the sclera
  • Lacrimal apparatus – lacrimal gland (upper outer part of the orbit) → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus of the nose
  • Extraocular muscles – four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two obliques (superior, inferior); remember "LR6 SO4" – lateral rectus by the 6th nerve, superior oblique by the 4th, the rest by the 3rd

Pathway of light: cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous body → retina → optic nerve → optic chiasma → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiation → visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

D. Applied anatomy

  1. Cataract – opacity of the lens; the leading cause of blindness in India, mostly in the elderly; treated by surgery with an intraocular lens (National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment)
  2. Glaucoma – raised intraocular pressure because aqueous humour cannot drain; damages the optic nerve and narrows the field of vision; a "silent thief of sight"
  3. Refractive errors – myopia, hypermetropia, presbyopia and astigmatism; corrected with glasses
  4. Vitamin A deficiency – night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia and keratomalacia in young children; prevented by vitamin A prophylaxis
  5. Conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, retinal detachment, diabetic retinopathy
  6. Instilling eye drops – pull down the lower lid and place drops in the lower conjunctival sac, not on the cornea; then press the inner corner of the eye for a minute so the drug does not drain into the nose
  7. Pupil examination in head injury – size, equality and reaction to light (PERRLA)

Conclusion The eyeball has a protective fibrous coat, a nourishing vascular coat and a light-sensitive retina, with aqueous humour, lens and vitreous focusing light on the retina; most common causes of blindness in India – cataract, glaucoma, refractive errors and vitamin A deficiency – arise from these structures.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the extraocular muscles and their nerve supply.
answer_html:
Introduction The extraocular muscles move the eyeball and the upper eyelid. There are seven in each orbit.

Muscles

  1. Superior rectus
  2. Inferior rectus
  3. Medial rectus
  4. Lateral rectus
  5. Superior oblique
  6. Inferior oblique
  7. Levator palpebrae superioris – raises the upper eyelid

Nerve supply – memory aid "LR6 SO4, rest 3"

  • Lateral rectus – abducent nerve (VI)
  • Superior oblique – trochlear nerve (IV)
  • All the others – oculomotor nerve (III)

Applied: paralysis of these nerves causes squint (strabismus) and double vision; oculomotor palsy also causes ptosis (drooping eyelid).

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the tympanic membrane.
answer_html:
Introduction The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is a thin, semi-transparent, pearly-grey membrane that separates the external ear from the middle ear. It is oval, about 1 cm across, and set obliquely.

Features

  1. Layers – outer skin, middle fibrous layer and inner mucous membrane
  2. Parts – a large tense part (pars tensa) and a small, lax upper part (pars flaccida)
  3. Umbo – the point of maximum depression, where the handle of the malleus is attached
  4. Cone of light – a bright reflection in the antero-inferior part, seen on otoscopy

Functions: transmits sound vibrations to the ear ossicles; protects the middle ear.

Applied: perforation (infection, injury, loud blast); in adults the pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal for otoscopy and ear drops.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the olfactory area of the nose.
answer_html:
Introduction The olfactory area is the part of the nasal cavity concerned with the sense of smell.

Location

  • The roof of the nasal cavity, the upper part of the nasal septum and the superior concha

Structure

  1. Olfactory epithelium – yellowish-brown, containing olfactory receptor cells (bipolar neurons), supporting cells and basal cells
  2. Olfactory glands (Bowman's glands) – keep the surface moist so that odour molecules dissolve
  3. Nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory bulb

Applied: loss of smell (anosmia) after head injury (fracture of the cribriform plate, sometimes with CSF leaking from the nose), common cold and viral infections such as COVID-19.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the accessory structures of the eye.
answer_html:
Introduction Accessory structures protect, support and move the eyeball and keep it moist.

Accessory structures

  1. Eyebrows – shade the eyes and prevent sweat from entering
  2. Eyelids (palpebrae) with eyelashes – protect the eye; blinking spreads tears
  3. Conjunctiva – thin mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the front of the sclera
  4. Lacrimal apparatus – produces and drains tears
  5. Extraocular muscles – move the eyeball and raise the upper eyelid
  6. Orbit and orbital fat – bony protection and cushioning

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the eyelids and the conjunctiva.
answer_html:
Introduction The eyelids are movable folds that protect the front of the eyeball. The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that lines the lids and covers the front of the eye. Both are easily examined and often show signs of general disease.

A. Eyelids

1. Parts

  • Upper and lower eyelids, meeting at the medial and lateral angles (canthi)
  • The gap between them is the palpebral fissure
  • The free margins carry eyelashes; near the medial angle each margin has a small opening, the lacrimal punctum

2. Layers (from outside in)

  • Skin – the thinnest skin in the body
  • Loose subcutaneous tissue – no fat, so swelling (oedema, bleeding) appears easily – "black eye"
  • Orbicularis oculi muscle – closes the eyelids (facial nerve)
  • Tarsal plate – a plate of dense fibrous tissue that gives shape and firmness; contains the tarsal (Meibomian) glands
  • Palpebral conjunctiva – the innermost layer
  • The upper lid also contains the levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve), which raises it

3. Glands of the eyelid

  • Meibomian (tarsal) glands – oily secretion that prevents tears from overflowing and evaporating
  • Glands of Zeis – sebaceous glands of eyelash follicles
  • Glands of Moll – modified sweat glands

4. Functions

  • Protect the eye from injury, dust and bright light
  • Blinking spreads tears and keeps the cornea moist and clean
  • Close during sleep

B. Conjunctiva

1. Parts

  • Palpebral conjunctiva – lines the inner surface of the lids; red and vascular
  • Bulbar conjunctiva – covers the white of the eye (sclera), but not the cornea
  • Conjunctival fornices – the folds where the two parts meet (superior and inferior); eye ointment is placed in the lower fornix

2. Functions

  • Protects the eye; secretes mucus that keeps the surface moist; contains lymphoid tissue for defence

C. Applied anatomy

  • Stye (hordeolum) – infection of a gland of Zeis; chalazion – cyst of a Meibomian gland
  • Ptosis – drooping of the upper lid (oculomotor nerve palsy, myasthenia gravis)
  • Conjunctivitis – red, sticky eye; highly infectious
