  • Subconjunctival haemorrhage – bright red patch after coughing or injury
  • Clinical signs – pallor of the palpebral conjunctiva in anaemia, yellow bulbar conjunctiva and sclera in jaundice
  • Eye care in unconscious patients – the lids may not close fully, so the cornea dries and ulcerates; nurses clean the eyes, instil lubricant drops and tape the lids closed if needed
  • Instilling eye drops – into the lower fornix, avoiding contact of the dropper with the eye

Conclusion The eyelids, with skin, orbicularis oculi, tarsal plate and glands, protect and moisten the eye, while the conjunctiva lines the lids and covers the sclera; their changes reveal anaemia and jaundice, and their care is important in unconscious patients.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the lacrimal apparatus.
answer_html:
Introduction The lacrimal apparatus consists of the structures that produce tears and drain them into the nose. Tears keep the front of the eye moist, clean and protected.

1. Lacrimal gland

  • Lies in the upper outer (lateral) part of the orbit, in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone
  • Has a larger orbital part and a smaller palpebral part
  • Opens by about 12 small ducts into the superior fornix of the conjunctiva

2. Spreading of tears

  • Blinking spreads the tears over the cornea and conjunctiva and moves them towards the medial angle of the eye, where they collect in a small pool (lacus lacrimalis)

3. Drainage pathway

  • Lacrimal puncta – tiny openings on the medial ends of the upper and lower lid margins
  • Lacrimal canaliculi – small channels from the puncta
  • Lacrimal sac – lies in a groove at the medial angle of the orbit
  • Nasolacrimal duct – about 18 mm long; runs down to open into the inferior meatus of the nose
  • This is why the nose runs when we cry and why we can taste eye drops

4. Composition and functions of tears

  • Water, salts, mucus and the antibacterial enzyme lysozyme
  • Keep the cornea moist and transparent
  • Wash away dust and foreign particles
  • Kill bacteria (lysozyme)
  • Supply oxygen and nutrients to the cornea
  • Express emotions (crying)

5. Nerve supply

  • Secretomotor (parasympathetic) fibres come through the facial nerve (via the pterygopalatine ganglion); sympathetic fibres reach it along the blood vessels

6. Applied anatomy

  • Dacryocystitis – infection of the lacrimal sac; swelling at the medial angle
  • Congenital blockage of the nasolacrimal duct in infants – watering and sticky eyes; treated by gentle massage over the sac
  • Dry eye – reduced tear production in the elderly, after facial palsy and in unconscious patients – needs artificial tears
  • Watering of the eye (epiphora) from blocked drainage
  • Instilling eye drops – after instilling, press gently over the inner corner for a minute to reduce drainage into the nose and systemic absorption

Conclusion The lacrimal apparatus – lacrimal gland, ducts, puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct – produces tears that protect and nourish the eye and drains them into the inferior meatus of the nose.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the middle ear.
answer_html:
Introduction The middle ear (tympanic cavity) is a small, air-filled space in the petrous part of the temporal bone, between the external ear and the internal ear. It transmits and amplifies sound from the eardrum to the inner ear.

1. Walls

  • Lateral wall – the tympanic membrane
  • Medial wall – separates it from the internal ear; shows the promontory (bulge of the cochlea), the oval window (fitted with the stapes) and the round window
  • Roof – a thin plate of bone (tegmen tympani) separating it from the middle cranial fossa and brain
  • Floor – thin bone over the internal jugular vein
  • Anterior wall – opening of the auditory (Eustachian) tube
  • Posterior wall – opening (aditus) into the mastoid antrum and air cells

2. Contents

  • Ear ossicles – three small bones forming a chain:
    • Malleus (hammer) – attached to the tympanic membrane
    • Incus (anvil)
    • Stapes (stirrup) – the smallest bone of the body; its footplate fits in the oval window
  • Muscles – tensor tympani (trigeminal nerve) and stapedius (facial nerve) – reduce vibration and protect the ear from very loud sounds
  • Chorda tympani nerve (taste fibres) crossing the membrane
  • Air

3. Auditory (Eustachian) tube

  • About 36 mm long; connects the middle ear with the nasopharynx
  • Equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum (opens during swallowing and yawning) and drains secretions
  • In infants and children it is shorter, wider and more horizontal, so throat infections spread easily to the middle ear

4. Functions

  • Conducts sound from the eardrum to the inner ear through the ossicles
  • Amplifies sound (the large eardrum and small oval window increase pressure)
  • Protects the inner ear from loud sounds (muscle reflex)
  • Equalises pressure through the auditory tube

5. Applied anatomy

  • Acute otitis media – common in children after colds; earache, fever, bulging drum; may perforate the drum
  • Chronic otitis media – discharging ear; can spread to the mastoid (mastoiditis) or through the thin roof to the brain (meningitis, brain abscess)
  • Otosclerosis – fixation of the stapes, causing conductive deafness
  • Barotrauma during flights and diving
  • Nursing: feed infants in a semi-upright position (not lying flat with a bottle) to reduce ear infections; teach patients not to put objects in the ear; dry mopping of discharging ears

Conclusion The middle ear is an air-filled cavity in the temporal bone containing the malleus, incus and stapes and two small muscles; connected to the nasopharynx by the auditory tube, it conducts, amplifies and protects, and its infection is common in children.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the internal ear.
answer_html:
Introduction The internal ear (labyrinth) lies deep in the petrous temporal bone. It contains the receptors for hearing and balance (equilibrium). It consists of a bony labyrinth containing a membranous labyrinth.

1. Bony labyrinth

  • A system of cavities in the bone, filled with a fluid called perilymph
  • Vestibule – the central part; the oval and round windows open on its lateral side
  • Semicircular canals – three (anterior, posterior and lateral), at right angles to each other; each has a swelling, the ampulla
  • Cochlea – snail-shaped, making about 2¾ turns around a central bony pillar (modiolus)

2. Membranous labyrinth

  • A system of membranous sacs and ducts inside the bony labyrinth, filled with endolymph
  • Utricle and saccule – in the vestibule
  • Semicircular ducts – in the semicircular canals
  • Cochlear duct (scala media) – in the cochlea

3. Organ of hearing – the cochlea

  • The cochlea has three channels: scala vestibuli and scala tympani (perilymph) and the cochlear duct (endolymph) between them
  • The organ of Corti, the actual receptor for hearing, rests on the basilar membrane in the cochlear duct
  • It has inner and outer hair cells covered by the tectorial membrane
  • Sound vibrations make the basilar membrane move; the hair cells bend and produce nerve impulses
  • High-pitched sounds are detected near the base of the cochlea, low-pitched sounds near the apex

4. Organ of balance – the vestibular apparatus

  • Semicircular ducts – the crista ampullaris in each ampulla detects rotational (angular) movements of the head
  • Utricle and saccule – the maculae, with tiny calcium crystals (otoliths), detect head position and linear acceleration (moving in a lift or car)

5. Nerve supply

  • Vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) – cochlear part for hearing and vestibular part for balance

6. Applied anatomy

  • Sensorineural deafness – damage to hair cells or the nerve (noise exposure, ageing – presbycusis, meningitis, congenital)
  • Ototoxic drugs – aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin) can damage hair cells; nurses observe for tinnitus and hearing loss
  • Ménière's disease – excess endolymph; vertigo, tinnitus and deafness
  • Vertigo and motion sickness
  • Cochlear implant for profound deafness
  • Newborn hearing screening detects congenital deafness early

Conclusion The internal ear consists of a bony labyrinth with perilymph and a membranous labyrinth with endolymph; its cochlea (organ of Corti) serves hearing and its vestibular apparatus (semicircular ducts, utricle, saccule) serves balance, both connected to the brain by the vestibulocochlear nerve.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the appendages of the skin.
answer_html:
Introduction The appendages of the skin are structures derived from the epidermis that grow down into the dermis. They are hair, nails, sebaceous glands and sweat glands.

1. Hair

  • Found over most of the body except the palms, soles, lips and parts of the genitalia
  • Parts – the shaft (above the skin) and the root (within a hair follicle); the root ends in a swollen bulb into which a papilla of blood vessels projects
  • Arrector pili muscle – a small smooth muscle attached to the follicle; its contraction makes the hair stand up – "goose flesh" in cold or fear
  • Functions – protection (scalp from sun, eyelashes and nose hairs trap dust), sensation of touch, conserving heat

2. Nails

  • Hard plates of keratin on the dorsal surfaces of the ends of fingers and toes
  • Parts – nail plate, nail bed, nail matrix (growing part under the proximal fold), lunula (white half-moon), cuticle
  • Fingernails grow about 0.1 mm a day
  • Functions – protect the fingertips, help in picking up small objects

3. Sebaceous glands

  • Small glands that usually open into hair follicles; absent on the palms and soles
  • Secrete sebum (oily substance) – keeps the skin and hair soft and waterproof; has antibacterial action
  • Become very active at puberty under androgens

4. Sweat (sudoriferous) glands

  • Eccrine sweat glands – all over the body, most numerous on the palms, soles and forehead; open directly on the skin; watery sweat helps temperature regulation and excretes small amounts of salts and urea
  • Apocrine sweat glands – in the axillae, groin and around the nipples; open into hair follicles; thick secretion that causes body odour when acted on by bacteria; active after puberty
  • Modified sweat glands – ceruminous glands (ear wax) and mammary glands

5. Applied anatomy and nursing

  • Acne – blockage and infection of sebaceous glands in adolescents
  • Alopecia (hair loss) – after chemotherapy, in fever and nutritional deficiency
  • Nail signs – clubbing (chronic lung and heart disease), koilonychia (spoon nails in iron deficiency), cyanosis of the nail beds, capillary refill test by pressing a nail
  • Pulse oximetry – remove nail polish for accurate reading
  • Excessive sweating in shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperthyroidism; absence of sweating in heat stroke
  • Hygiene – regular bathing, care of hair and nails; shaving and hair removal before surgery as per policy (clipping preferred to razors)

Conclusion The skin appendages – hair with arrector pili, nails, sebaceous glands and eccrine and apocrine sweat glands – protect the body, help temperature regulation and sensation, and give useful clinical signs.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the retina.

diagram.caption: Fundus of the eye as seen with an ophthalmoscope

answer_html:
Introduction The retina is the innermost, nervous coat of the eyeball. It contains the light-sensitive receptor cells (rods and cones) that convert light into nerve impulses. It lines the back of the eye from the optic disc to the ora serrata.

1. Layers

  • The retina has ten layers, which can be grouped into:
    • outer pigment epithelium – absorbs extra light and nourishes the receptors
    • layer of rods and cones (photoreceptors)
    • bipolar cell layer
    • ganglion cell layer, whose axons form the nerve fibre layer and the optic nerve
  • Light passes through the inner layers to reach the rods and cones

2. Photoreceptors

  • Rods – about 120 million; work in dim light (night vision); contain rhodopsin, which needs vitamin A; more in the periphery
  • Cones – about 6–7 million; work in bright light; give colour vision and sharp vision; concentrated in the fovea

3. Special areas

  • Macula lutea – a yellowish spot at the back of the eye, in line with the visual axis
  • Fovea centralis – a small pit in the centre of the macula; contains only cones; the area of sharpest vision
  • Optic disc (blind spot) – about 3 mm to the nasal side of the macula, where the nerve fibres leave as the optic nerve and the retinal vessels enter; it has no rods or cones, so it cannot detect light

4. Blood supply

  • Central retinal artery (branch of the ophthalmic artery) – supplies the inner layers; it is an end artery
  • Choroid – supplies the outer layers (rods and cones)

5. Functions

  • Receives the image formed by the cornea and lens
  • Converts light into nerve impulses and sends them through the optic nerve to the brain

6. Applied anatomy

  • Night blindness – vitamin A deficiency (rhodopsin)
  • Retinal detachment – flashes of light, floaters and a "curtain" over vision; an emergency
  • Diabetic retinopathy and hypertensive retinopathy – seen on fundoscopy; diabetics need yearly eye check-ups
  • Central retinal artery occlusion – sudden painless loss of vision (end artery)
  • Papilloedema – swelling of the optic disc in raised intracranial pressure
  • Retinopathy of prematurity – in preterm babies given high oxygen; nurses monitor oxygen saturation carefully
  • Colour blindness – defect of cones

Conclusion The retina is the inner nervous coat containing rods (dim light) and cones (colour, sharp vision); its macula and fovea give the sharpest vision, the optic disc is the blind spot, and it is supplied by the central retinal artery and choroid.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the bones of the upper limb.
answer_html:
Introduction Each upper limb has 32 bones, so both limbs together have 64 bones.

Bones of one upper limb

  1. Shoulder girdle – clavicle (collar bone) and scapula (shoulder blade)
  2. Arm – humerus
  3. Forearm – radius (thumb side) and ulna (little-finger side)
  4. Hand
    • 8 carpals – scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
    • 5 metacarpals
    • 14 phalanges (2 in the thumb, 3 in each finger)

Memory aid for carpals: "Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle".

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: List the ligaments of the hip joint.
answer_html:
Introduction The hip joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum. It is very stable because of its deep socket and strong ligaments.

Ligaments of the hip joint

  1. Fibrous capsule (capsular ligament) – encloses the joint
  2. Iliofemoral ligament – Y-shaped; the strongest ligament in the body; prevents over-extension of the hip
  3. Pubofemoral ligament – prevents over-abduction
  4. Ischiofemoral ligament – at the back
  5. Ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres) – carries a small artery to the head of the femur
  6. Transverse acetabular ligament – bridges the notch of the acetabulum
  7. Acetabular labrum – fibrocartilage rim that deepens the socket

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: List the properties of muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction Muscle tissue has special properties that allow it to produce movement.

Properties of muscle

  1. Excitability (irritability) – responds to a stimulus such as a nerve impulse
  2. Contractility – shortens and develops tension when stimulated
  3. Extensibility – can be stretched beyond its resting length
  4. Elasticity – returns to its original length after stretching or contraction
  5. Tonicity – shows a slight continuous contraction even at rest (muscle tone), which maintains posture
  6. Conductivity – spreads the impulse along the muscle fibre

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of a long bone.
answer_html:
Introduction A long bone is longer than it is wide, e.g. femur, humerus, tibia. It has the following parts:

  1. Diaphysis – the shaft; thick compact bone around the medullary cavity
  2. Epiphyses – the two expanded ends; spongy bone covered by articular cartilage
  3. Metaphysis – the flared part of the shaft next to the epiphysis
  4. Epiphyseal (growth) plate – a plate of cartilage where the bone grows in length in children
  5. Periosteum – tough membrane covering the outer surface (except the joint surfaces)
  6. Endosteum – thin membrane lining the medullary cavity
  7. Medullary cavity – contains bone marrow
  8. Nutrient foramen – hole for the nutrient artery

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the fontanelles of the newborn skull and state when they close.
answer_html:
Definition Fontanelles are soft, membrane-covered gaps between the skull bones of a newborn, where ossification is not yet complete. They allow moulding of the head during birth and growth of the brain.

Fontanelles

  1. Anterior fontanelle – diamond-shaped; where the frontal and two parietal bones meet; the largest; closes by 12–18 months
  2. Posterior fontanelle – triangular; between the parietal and occipital bones; closes by 6–8 weeks
  3. Sphenoidal (anterolateral) and mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelles – small, on each side; close during infancy

Applied: a bulging fontanelle suggests raised intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus); a sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the deltoid muscle.

diagram.caption: Deltoid muscle and injection site
labels: injection site 2-3 finger breadths below acromion

answer_html:
Introduction The deltoid is a thick, triangular muscle covering the shoulder joint. It is named after the Greek letter delta (Δ) because of its shape, and it gives the shoulder its rounded contour. It is important for nurses as an intramuscular injection site.

1. Shape and position

  • Triangular muscle with its base above and apex below
  • Covers the shoulder joint from the front, side and back

2. Origin – a V-shaped line on the shoulder girdle

  • Anterior fibres – lateral one-third of the clavicle
  • Middle fibres – lateral border of the acromion process
  • Posterior fibres – lower lip of the spine of the scapula

3. Insertion

  • Deltoid tuberosity on the middle of the lateral surface of the shaft of the humerus

4. Nerve supply

  • Axillary nerve (C5, C6), a branch of the brachial plexus

5. Blood supply

  • Posterior circumflex humeral artery and the deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery

6. Actions

  • Middle fibres – abduct the arm from about 15° to 90° (the first 15° is started by supraspinatus)
  • Anterior fibres – flexion and medial rotation of the arm
  • Posterior fibres – extension and lateral rotation of the arm
  • Stabilises the shoulder joint when carrying weights

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Intramuscular injection site
    • Expose the whole shoulder; locate the acromion process
    • Inject into the thickest central part, about 2–3 finger breadths (2.5–5 cm) below the acromion, in the centre of the triangle
    • Use small volumes only (about 1 ml) – common site for vaccines in adults (hepatitis B, Td)
    • Going too low or too far back risks injury to the radial nerve and the axillary nerve with the posterior circumflex vessels
    • Not suitable for infants and very thin adults (small muscle mass)
  • Axillary nerve injury (fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, dislocation of the shoulder, badly placed crutches) paralyses the deltoid:
    • Loss of abduction of the arm
    • Flattening of the rounded shoulder contour
    • Numbness over the lower part of the deltoid ("regimental badge" area)
  • Wasting of the deltoid in long immobilisation – shoulder exercises are needed

Conclusion The deltoid arises from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula, inserts on the deltoid tuberosity and is supplied by the axillary nerve; its main action is abduction, and it is a common site for small-volume IM injections.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the biceps brachii muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction The biceps brachii is the large, two-headed muscle on the front of the arm ("biceps" means two heads). It is the familiar muscle that bulges when the elbow is bent and is a landmark for blood pressure measurement and venepuncture.

1. Position

  • Lies in the anterior compartment of the arm, superficial to the brachialis

2. Origin – two heads

  • Short head – tip of the coracoid process of the scapula (along with coracobrachialis)
  • Long head – supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; its tendon runs inside the shoulder joint capsule and then down the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus
  • The two heads join in the middle of the arm to form one fleshy belly

3. Insertion

  • Tendon – into the back of the radial tuberosity
  • Bicipital aponeurosis – a flat fibrous sheet that passes downwards and medially into the deep fascia of the forearm

4. Nerve supply

  • Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6)

5. Blood supply

  • Muscular branches of the brachial artery

6. Actions

  • Supination of the forearm – it is the most powerful supinator, especially when the elbow is bent (as in turning a screwdriver or a door key)
  • Flexion of the elbow joint
  • Weak flexion of the shoulder joint
  • The long head helps stabilise the shoulder joint

7. Relations in the cubital fossa

  • The biceps tendon lies in the centre of the cubital fossa
  • Brachial artery lies just medial to the tendon, with the median nerve further medially
  • The median cubital vein lies superficially over the bicipital aponeurosis

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • Blood pressure measurement – feel the brachial pulse just medial to the biceps tendon and place the stethoscope there
  • Venepuncture – the bicipital aponeurosis lies between the median cubital vein (above) and the brachial artery and median nerve (below), protecting them from the needle
  • Biceps reflex – tests the C5–C6 spinal segments
  • Rupture of the long head tendon in the elderly – a bulge appears in the lower arm when the elbow is bent
  • Exercises to strengthen the biceps are part of rehabilitation after immobilisation

Conclusion The biceps brachii has two heads from the scapula, inserts on the radial tuberosity and is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve; it flexes the elbow and is the chief supinator of the forearm.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the components of a synovial joint.
answer_html:
Introduction A synovial joint is a freely movable joint (diarthrosis) in which the bones are separated by a cavity filled with synovial fluid. Most joints of the limbs – shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle – are synovial joints.

1. Articular cartilage

  • A layer of smooth, glassy hyaline cartilage covering the ends of the bones
  • Reduces friction, gives a smooth gliding surface and absorbs shock
  • Has no blood vessels or nerves – nourished by synovial fluid

2. Joint (synovial) cavity

  • A narrow space between the articulating bones
  • Allows free movement

3. Articular capsule – a two-layered sleeve enclosing the joint

  • Fibrous capsule (outer layer) – tough dense connective tissue attached around the bone ends; gives strength and stability
  • Synovial membrane (inner layer) – lines the inside of the capsule and all non-articular surfaces inside the joint (but not the cartilage); rich in blood vessels; secretes synovial fluid

4. Synovial fluid

  • Clear or pale yellow, sticky fluid like egg white
  • Functions: lubricates the joint, nourishes the articular cartilage, absorbs shock, contains phagocytes that remove debris

5. Ligaments

  • Bands of dense fibrous tissue joining bone to bone
  • Capsular (thickening of the capsule), extracapsular (outside the capsule) and intracapsular (inside, e.g. cruciate ligaments of the knee)
  • Hold the bones together and limit unwanted movements

6. Accessory structures

  • Articular discs and menisci – pads of fibrocartilage (knee, temporomandibular joint) that improve fit and absorb shock
  • Labrum – fibrocartilage rim that deepens the socket (shoulder, hip)
  • Bursae – small fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction between tendon and bone
  • Fat pads – fill spaces and cushion

7. Nerve and blood supply

  • Rich nerve supply – the nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply the joint (Hilton's law); joint pain may be felt in nearby areas
  • Articular arteries form an anastomosis around the joint

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • Arthritis – osteoarthritis (wear and tear of cartilage in the elderly) and rheumatoid arthritis (inflammation of the synovial membrane)
  • Joint effusion – excess fluid; may be aspirated (arthrocentesis) under aseptic technique
  • Dislocation and sprain (ligament injury)
  • Bursitis – e.g. housemaid's knee
  • Bedridden patients need regular range-of-motion (ROM) exercises to prevent stiffness and contractures

Conclusion A synovial joint has articular cartilage, a capsule lined by synovial membrane, synovial fluid and supporting ligaments – a design that allows free yet stable movement.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the vertebral column.
answer_html:
Introduction The vertebral column (spine or backbone) is the central bony pillar of the body. It supports the head and trunk, protects the spinal cord and allows movements of the trunk. It is about 70 cm long in adult men.

1. Number of vertebrae – 33

  • Cervical – 7 (neck)
  • Thoracic – 12 (chest; carry the ribs)
  • Lumbar – 5 (lower back; the largest bodies)
  • Sacral – 5, fused to form the sacrum
  • Coccygeal – 4, fused to form the coccyx
  • So the adult column has 26 separate bones

2. Curvatures (seen from the side)

  • Primary curves – thoracic and sacral; concave forwards; present at birth
  • Secondary curves – convex forwards
    • Cervical – develops when the baby holds up its head (about 3–4 months)
    • Lumbar – develops when the child sits and walks (about 12 months)
  • The curves give strength, balance and spring to the column

3. Parts of a typical vertebra

  • Body – the weight-bearing front part
  • Vertebral arch – formed by two pedicles and two laminae; encloses the vertebral foramen
  • Processes – one spinous process, two transverse processes and four articular processes
  • The vertebral foramina together form the vertebral canal, which holds the spinal cord

4. Special vertebrae

  • Atlas (C1) – a ring with no body and no spine; supports the skull; allows the "yes" nodding movement
  • Axis (C2) – has a tooth-like dens (odontoid process) around which the atlas rotates – the "no" movement
  • C7 (vertebra prominens) – long spine felt at the base of the neck; a useful landmark for counting vertebrae

5. Intervertebral discs

  • Pads of fibrocartilage between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae
  • Outer tough annulus fibrosus and inner jelly-like nucleus pulposus
  • Act as shock absorbers and allow movement
  • Make up about one-quarter of the length of the column

6. Functions

  • Supports the head and trunk and transmits body weight to the pelvis
  • Protects the spinal cord and spinal nerve roots
  • Allows bending, twisting and extension of the trunk
  • Gives attachment to muscles and ribs
  • Contains red bone marrow (blood formation)

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Lumbar puncture is done between L3–L4 or L4–L5, because the spinal cord ends at about L1–L2 in adults
  • Disc prolapse ("slipped disc") presses on nerve roots and causes sciatica
  • Abnormal curves – kyphosis (hunchback), lordosis (hollow back), scoliosis (sideways)
  • Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) is still seen in India
  • Spinal injury – log-roll the patient and keep the spine in line; never flex the neck

Conclusion The vertebral column of 33 vertebrae, joined by discs and arranged in four curves, gives support, flexibility and protection to the spinal cord.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the sites for intramuscular injection with their anatomical landmarks.

diagram.caption: Sites of IM injection
labels: vastus lateralis middle third of thigh

answer_html:
Introduction Intramuscular (IM) injections are given into large, well-developed muscles with a good blood supply, away from major nerves, blood vessels and bones. Choosing the right site by its anatomical landmarks prevents nerve injury and abscess.

1. Ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius and minimus) – the safest site for adults and children

  • Landmarks: place the palm on the greater trochanter, the index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and spread the middle finger along the iliac crest
  • Inject into the centre of the V formed between the index and middle fingers
  • Thick muscle, free from major nerves and vessels; less fat

2. Dorsogluteal site (gluteus maximus)

  • Landmarks: divide the buttock into four quadrants (or draw a line from the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter); inject into the upper outer quadrant
  • Risk of injuring the sciatic nerve and the superior gluteal vessels, and thick fat may prevent the drug reaching muscle – now used less

3. Vastus lateralis site – the preferred site in infants (all IM vaccines under the immunisation schedule)

  • Lies on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh
  • Landmarks: inject into the middle third – between a hand's breadth below the greater trochanter and a hand's breadth above the knee
  • Supplied by the femoral nerve; no major nerves or vessels in this area

4. Rectus femoris site

  • Front of the middle third of the thigh
  • Convenient for self-injection, but more painful

5. Deltoid site

  • Landmarks: 2–3 finger breadths (2.5–5 cm) below the acromion process, in the centre of the muscle
  • Small muscle – only about 1 ml; common for adult vaccines
  • Avoid the lower part (radial nerve) and the back (axillary nerve)

6. General principles

  • Needle at 90° to the skin; use a needle long enough to reach muscle
  • Volume: large muscles (ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis) take up to about 3 ml in adults; deltoid about 1 ml; infants – usually 0.5 ml
  • Rotate sites in repeated injections
  • Use the Z-track technique for irritating drugs (iron)
  • Aspirate only if your institution's policy requires it

7. Complications of a wrong site

  • Sciatic nerve injury → foot drop (from a badly placed gluteal injection)
  • Injection abscess, haematoma, broken needle, injection into a vessel

Conclusion Ventrogluteal is the safest IM site, vastus lateralis is preferred for infants and the deltoid takes only small volumes; correct landmarks protect the sciatic, radial and axillary nerves.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a short note on the pelvic floor muscles.
answer_html:
Introduction The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is a funnel-shaped sheet of muscles that closes the outlet of the pelvis and supports the pelvic organs. It is especially important in women because of childbirth.

1. Muscles forming the pelvic floor

  • Levator ani – the main muscle; has three parts:
    • Pubococcygeus – from the back of the pubis to the coccyx
    • Iliococcygeus – from the tendinous arch to the coccyx
    • Puborectalis – loops round the anorectal junction like a sling; important for faecal continence
  • Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) – the posterior part, from the ischial spine to the sacrum and coccyx

2. Attachments

  • Origin: back of the pubis, a tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia, and the ischial spine
  • Insertion: perineal body, anococcygeal raphe, coccyx

3. Openings in the pelvic floor

  • Urethra
  • Vagina (in females)
  • Anal canal

4. Nerve supply

  • Branches of the sacral nerves S3, S4 and the pudendal nerve

5. Functions

  • Supports the pelvic organs – bladder, uterus, vagina and rectum
  • Helps maintain urinary and faecal continence
  • Resists the rise of intra-abdominal pressure in coughing, sneezing, lifting and straining
  • In labour, it guides the rotation of the baby's head and forms part of the birth canal
  • Supports the foetus in pregnancy

6. Perineal body

  • A fibromuscular mass between the vagina and the anal canal, where many perineal muscles meet
  • Key support of the pelvic organs; often torn in childbirth

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Stretching or tearing in childbirth weakens the pelvic floor → uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele and stress incontinence
  • Episiotomy – a planned cut of the perineum to prevent uncontrolled tears; needs proper repair and perineal care
  • Kegel (pelvic floor) exercises – repeated tightening of the pelvic floor muscles; taught after delivery, in the elderly and after prostate surgery
  • Repeated heavy lifting and chronic cough worsen prolapse

Conclusion The pelvic floor, formed mainly by levator ani and coccygeus, supports the pelvic organs and maintains continence; protecting and strengthening it is an important part of maternity nursing.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Classify joints with examples. Describe the knee joint. (4 + 6)

diagram.caption: Knee joint - opened from the front

answer_html:
Introduction A joint (articulation) is a place where two or more bones meet. Joints hold bones together and allow movement; some allow no movement, some a little and some a great deal.

(a) Classification of joints (4 marks)

A. Structural classification – based on the tissue joining the bones

  1. Fibrous joints – bones joined by fibrous tissue; no joint cavity; little or no movement
    • Sutures – between skull bones
    • Syndesmosis – bones joined by a ligament or membrane, e.g. lower tibiofibular joint, interosseous membrane of the forearm
    • Gomphosis – a peg in a socket, e.g. a tooth in its socket
  2. Cartilaginous joints – bones joined by cartilage; slight movement
    • Primary (synchondrosis) – hyaline cartilage, often temporary, e.g. epiphyseal plate, first sternocostal joint
    • Secondary (symphysis) – fibrocartilage, e.g. pubic symphysis, joints between vertebral bodies (intervertebral discs)
  3. Synovial joints – have a joint cavity with synovial fluid; freely movable

B. Functional classification – based on the amount of movement

  • Synarthrosis – immovable, e.g. sutures
  • Amphiarthrosis – slightly movable, e.g. pubic symphysis, intervertebral joints
  • Diarthrosis – freely movable, e.g. all synovial joints

C. Types of synovial joints

Type Movement Example
Plane (gliding) sliding of flat surfaces intercarpal, acromioclavicular
Hinge flexion and extension in one plane elbow, interphalangeal, ankle
Pivot rotation around one axis atlanto-axial ("no" movement), superior radio-ulnar
Condyloid (ellipsoid) flexion, extension, abduction, adduction wrist, metacarpophalangeal
Saddle like condyloid plus some rotation carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
Ball and socket movement in all directions, including rotation shoulder, hip

(b) Knee joint (6 marks)

1. Introduction and type

  • The largest and most complex synovial joint of the body
  • A modified hinge (condylar) joint – mainly flexion and extension, with slight rotation when bent
  • Carries the full weight of the body and is often injured in sports and accidents

2. Bones forming the joint

  • Femur – medial and lateral condyles
  • Tibia – medial and lateral condyles
  • Patella – articulates with the front of the lower end of the femur
  • The fibula does not take part
  • So the knee has three articulations: medial and lateral tibiofemoral and the patellofemoral joint

3. Articular capsule

  • Thin and incomplete in front, where it is replaced by the patella, the quadriceps tendon and the patellar ligament
  • Lined by a large synovial membrane

4. Ligaments

  • Extracapsular ligaments
    • Patellar ligament – continuation of the quadriceps tendon from the patella to the tibial tuberosity
    • Medial (tibial) collateral ligament – broad band on the inner side; attached to the medial meniscus
    • Lateral (fibular) collateral ligament – cord-like band on the outer side
    • Oblique and arcuate popliteal ligaments – at the back
  • Intracapsular ligaments
    • Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) – prevents the tibia slipping forward on the femur; commonly torn in sports
    • Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) – prevents the tibia slipping backward; the stronger of the two
    • They cross each other like the letter X (cruciate = cross-shaped)

5. Menisci (semilunar cartilages)

  • Two C-shaped plates of fibrocartilage on the upper surface of the tibia
  • Medial meniscus – larger, C-shaped, less mobile and more often injured (attached to the medial collateral ligament)
  • Lateral meniscus – smaller, nearly circular, more mobile
  • Functions: deepen the tibial surfaces, absorb shock, spread the load, help lubrication

6. Bursae – the knee has about a dozen bursae

  • Suprapatellar bursa – communicates with the joint cavity, so knee effusions extend above the patella
  • Prepatellar bursa – inflamed in "housemaid's knee" (kneeling)
  • Infrapatellar bursae

7. Movements and muscles

  • Extension – quadriceps femoris (femoral nerve)
  • Flexion – hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus), gastrocnemius
  • Rotation – only when the knee is bent
  • Locking and unlocking – in full extension the femur rotates slightly on the tibia and "locks" the knee for standing; the popliteus muscle "unlocks" it to begin flexion

8. Blood and nerve supply

  • Blood: genicular arteries from the popliteal artery, forming an anastomosis around the knee
  • Nerves: branches of the femoral, obturator, tibial and common peroneal nerves

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Osteoarthritis of the knee – very common in the elderly and the obese; pain, stiffness, crepitus; total knee replacement in severe cases
  • Meniscus tears and ACL injuries in sports – knee "gives way"
  • Knee effusion – detected by the "patellar tap" test; aspirated under strict asepsis
  • Knee-jerk reflex – tests the L2–L4 segments
  • In bedridden patients, avoid keeping a pillow under the knees for long periods – it causes flexion contracture; do knee ROM and quadriceps exercises
  • Prepatellar bursitis in people who kneel for long periods

Conclusion Joints are classified as fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial; the knee is a large modified hinge joint stabilised by collateral and cruciate ligaments and cushioned by menisci, which explains its common sports injuries and degenerative disease.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Classify bones. Describe the structure of a long bone and the process of ossification. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
Introduction Bone (osseous tissue) is a hard, living connective tissue whose matrix is hardened by calcium salts. The adult skeleton has 206 bones that support the body, protect organs, allow movement, store minerals and form blood cells.

(a) Classification of bones (2 marks)

1. According to shape

  • Long bones – longer than wide; e.g. femur, humerus, radius, tibia, phalanges
  • Short bones – cube-shaped; e.g. carpals, tarsals
  • Flat bones – thin and flat; e.g. bones of the skull vault, sternum, ribs, scapula
  • Irregular bones – complex shapes; e.g. vertebrae, facial bones, hip bone
  • Sesamoid bones – develop inside tendons; e.g. patella, pisiform
  • Pneumatic bones – contain air spaces; e.g. maxilla, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid

2. According to region

  • Axial skeleton – 80 bones (skull, hyoid, ear ossicles, vertebral column, ribs, sternum)
  • Appendicular skeleton – 126 bones (limbs with their girdles)

3. According to development

  • Membrane bones – formed directly in membrane (skull vault)
  • Cartilage bones – formed by replacing cartilage (long bones)

4. According to structure

  • Compact bone – dense; forms the shaft of long bones
  • Spongy (cancellous) bone – a network of thin plates; in the ends of long bones and inside flat bones

(b) Structure of a long bone (4 marks)

1. Gross structure

  • Diaphysis (shaft)
    • A tube of thick compact bone
    • Encloses the medullary cavity, which contains yellow bone marrow (mainly fat) in adults
  • Epiphyses (ends)
    • Expanded ends made of spongy bone filled with red bone marrow, which forms blood cells
    • Covered by hyaline articular cartilage where they form joints
  • Metaphysis – flared part of the shaft next to the epiphysis
  • Epiphyseal (growth) plate
    • A plate of hyaline cartilage between the metaphysis and epiphysis in children
    • Site of growth in length; replaced by an epiphyseal line after growth stops
  • Periosteum
    • Tough membrane covering the outer surface except at the joints
    • Outer fibrous layer and inner osteogenic (bone-forming) layer
    • Anchored to bone by Sharpey's fibres
    • Rich in blood vessels and nerves – this is why fractures are so painful
    • Essential for growth in thickness, nutrition and fracture healing
  • Endosteum – thin membrane lining the medullary cavity
  • Nutrient artery – enters the shaft through the nutrient foramen and supplies the marrow and inner bone

2. Microscopic structure

  • Compact bone is built of cylindrical units called Haversian systems (osteons):
    • A central (Haversian) canal containing blood vessels and nerves
    • Concentric rings of bone matrix called lamellae
    • Small spaces (lacunae) between lamellae, each holding an osteocyte
    • Tiny channels (canaliculi) connecting lacunae, through which cells receive nutrients
    • Volkmann's canals – connect neighbouring Haversian canals and the periosteum
  • Spongy bone – a lattice of thin plates (trabeculae) with red marrow in the spaces; light but strong

3. Bone cells

  • Osteoblasts – bone-forming cells; lay down new matrix
  • Osteocytes – mature bone cells trapped in lacunae; maintain the bone
  • Osteoclasts – large multinucleated cells that break down (resorb) bone; important in remodelling

4. Bone matrix

  • Organic part (about one-third) – mainly collagen fibres; gives flexibility
  • Inorganic part (about two-thirds) – mainly calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite); gives hardness
  • A bone soaked in acid becomes rubbery; a burnt bone becomes brittle

(c) Ossification (4 marks)

Definition: ossification (osteogenesis) is the process of formation of bone. It begins in the early weeks of foetal life (the clavicle is the first bone to start ossifying) and continues till about 25 years, when the last growth plates fuse.

1. Intramembranous ossification

  • Bone forms directly in a sheet of mesenchyme (membrane), without a cartilage stage
  • Steps:
    1. Mesenchymal cells cluster and become osteoblasts – an ossification centre appears
    2. Osteoblasts lay down osteoid (unmineralised matrix)
    3. Calcium salts are deposited; osteoblasts trapped in the matrix become osteocytes
    4. Spongy bone forms; the outer and inner surfaces become compact bone
    5. The surrounding mesenchyme forms the periosteum
  • Examples: flat bones of the skull vault, facial bones, most of the clavicle and mandible
  • The fontanelles are areas of membrane not yet ossified at birth

2. Endochondral (intracartilaginous) ossification

  • Bone replaces a model made of hyaline cartilage
  • Forms most bones of the body – long bones, vertebrae, pelvis and the base of the skull
  • Steps:
    1. A cartilage model of the future bone forms in the embryo
    2. A primary ossification centre appears in the middle of the shaft (diaphysis): cartilage cells enlarge and die, the matrix calcifies, blood vessels invade and osteoblasts lay down bone
    3. A bone collar forms around the shaft from the periosteum
    4. Osteoclasts hollow out the centre to form the medullary cavity
    5. Secondary ossification centres appear in the epiphyses – most of them after birth
    6. A plate of cartilage – the epiphyseal plate – remains between the shaft and each epiphysis and keeps growing, so the bone grows in length
    7. When growth ends, the plate turns into bone and the epiphysis fuses with the shaft; growth in height stops (usually by 18–25 years)
  • Growth in thickness occurs by new bone laid down under the periosteum (appositional growth), while osteoclasts enlarge the marrow cavity

3. Factors necessary for normal bone growth

  • Nutrients: calcium, phosphorus, protein, vitamin D (calcium absorption), vitamin C (collagen), vitamin A
  • Hormones: growth hormone, thyroid hormones, insulin, sex hormones (cause the pubertal growth spurt and later closure of growth plates), parathormone and calcitonin
  • Exercise and weight-bearing – strengthen bone

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Bone age – an X-ray of the wrist shows which ossification centres have appeared; used to assess growth in children
  • Rickets – lack of vitamin D in children; soft, bent bones, bow legs; prevented by sunlight and diet
  • Osteoporosis – loss of bone mass in the elderly and after menopause; fractures of the hip and spine; prevention by calcium, vitamin D, exercise and fall prevention
  • Fracture healing depends on the periosteum and a good blood supply; it occurs by callus formation
  • Injury to the growth plate in children can stop growth of that bone or cause deformity
  • Bone marrow aspiration – from the sternum or iliac crest, where red marrow persists in adults

Conclusion Bones are classified by shape, region, development and structure. A long bone has a compact shaft with a marrow cavity and spongy ends with growth plates; it develops by endochondral ossification, while flat skull bones develop in membrane. Adequate nutrition, hormones and exercise are needed for healthy bone growth.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the bones of the lower limb.
answer_html:
Introduction Each lower limb, with its share of the pelvic girdle, has 31 bones.

Bones

  1. Hip bone (os coxae) – formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis
  2. Femur – thigh bone; the longest and strongest bone of the body
  3. Patella – kneecap; the largest sesamoid bone
  4. Tibia – the medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg
  5. Fibula – the thin lateral bone of the leg
  6. Tarsal bones (7) – talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms
  7. Metatarsal bones (5)
  8. Phalanges (14) – two in the big toe and three in each of the other toes

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the bones of the skull.
answer_html:
Introduction The skull has 22 bones (excluding the ear ossicles) – 8 cranial and 14 facial.

A. Cranial bones (8) – enclose the brain

  1. Frontal (1)
  2. Parietal (2)
  3. Temporal (2)
  4. Occipital (1)
  5. Sphenoid (1)
  6. Ethmoid (1)

B. Facial bones (14)

  1. Nasal (2)
  2. Maxillae (2)
  3. Zygomatic (2)
  4. Lacrimal (2)
  5. Palatine (2)
  6. Inferior nasal conchae (2)
  7. Vomer (1)
  8. Mandible (1) – the only movable bone of the skull

The hyoid bone and the six ear ossicles are counted separately.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Differentiate between the axial and appendicular skeleton.
answer_html:
Introduction The adult human skeleton has 206 bones, divided into two parts.

Axial skeleton Appendicular skeleton
forms the central axis of the body forms the limbs and their girdles
80 bones 126 bones
skull (22), ear ossicles (6), hyoid (1), vertebral column (26), sternum (1) and ribs (24) shoulder girdles (4), upper limbs (60), pelvic girdle (2), lower limbs (60)
protects the brain, spinal cord and thoracic organs concerned with movement and handling objects

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of a typical vertebra.
answer_html:
Introduction A typical vertebra (e.g. a thoracic or lumbar vertebra) has the following parts.

Parts

  1. Body – the large, cylindrical, weight-bearing part in front
  2. Vertebral (neural) arch – behind the body, made of:
    • two pedicles (joining the arch to the body)
    • two laminae (forming the back of the arch)
  3. Vertebral foramen – the opening enclosed by the body and arch; together these form the vertebral canal for the spinal cord
  4. Processes (seven):
    • one spinous process (felt in the midline of the back)
    • two transverse processes
    • four articular processes (two superior, two inferior)
  5. Intervertebral foramina – between adjacent vertebrae, for the spinal nerves

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the curvatures of the vertebral column.
answer_html:
Introduction The adult vertebral column is not straight; it has four curvatures that give it strength, flexibility and balance.

A. Primary curvatures – present at birth; concave forwards

  1. Thoracic
  2. Sacral

B. Secondary curvatures – develop after birth; convex forwards

  1. Cervical – develops when the infant starts holding up the head (about 3–4 months)
  2. Lumbar – develops when the child starts sitting, standing and walking

Abnormal curvatures

  • Kyphosis – excessive backward curve of the thoracic spine (hunchback)
  • Lordosis – excessive forward curve of the lumbar spine (seen in pregnancy)
  • Scoliosis – sideways curve

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Classify the ribs.
answer_html:
Introduction There are 12 pairs of ribs. They form the side walls of the thoracic cage.

Classification according to their anterior attachment

  1. True ribs (vertebrosternal) – 1st to 7th; attached directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages
  2. False ribs – 8th to 12th; do not reach the sternum directly:
    • vertebrochondral (8th–10th) – their cartilages join the cartilage above
    • floating ribs (11th and 12th) – free anterior ends; attached only to the vertebrae

According to features

  • Typical ribs – 3rd to 9th
  • Atypical ribs – 1st, 2nd, 10th, 11th and 12th

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the rotator cuff muscles.
answer_html:
Introduction The rotator cuff is a group of four short muscles whose tendons blend with the capsule of the shoulder joint. They hold the head of the humerus in the shallow glenoid cavity and give stability to the joint.

Muscles – memory aid "SITS"

  1. Supraspinatus – starts abduction of the arm
  2. Infraspinatus – lateral rotation
  3. Teres minor – lateral rotation
  4. Subscapularis – medial rotation

Applied: rotator cuff tears and tendinitis (especially of the supraspinatus) cause shoulder pain and weakness, common in the elderly and in people who do repeated overhead work.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Differentiate between the male and female pelvis.
answer_html:
Introduction The female pelvis is adapted for childbirth, so it differs from the male pelvis.

Point Female pelvis Male pelvis
General build light, smooth heavy, rough (strong muscle markings)
Pelvic inlet round or oval heart-shaped
Cavity wide and shallow narrow and deep
Subpubic angle wide – about 90° or more narrow – about 50–60°
Sacrum short, wide, less curved long, narrow, more curved
Ischial spines less prominent more prominent
Greater sciatic notch wide narrow

Applied: the shape and size of the pelvis are assessed in pregnancy to predict normal delivery.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the triceps brachii muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction The triceps brachii is the large muscle on the back of the arm. As the name shows, it has three heads. It is the main extensor of the elbow.

1. Origin

  • Long head – infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (just below the shoulder joint)
  • Lateral head – back of the humerus, above the radial (spiral) groove
  • Medial head – back of the humerus, below the radial groove

2. Insertion

  • The three heads join into a common tendon that is inserted into the olecranon process of the ulna (point of the elbow)

3. Nerve supply

  • Radial nerve (C6, C7, C8 – mainly C7)

4. Blood supply

  • Profunda brachii artery and branches of the brachial artery

5. Actions

  • Extension of the elbow – pushing, doing push-ups, pushing oneself up from a chair or bed
  • The long head also helps to extend and adduct the shoulder and supports the shoulder joint

6. Applied anatomy

  • Triceps reflex – tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon causes extension of the elbow; tests the C7 segment
  • Radial nerve injury (fracture of the shaft of the humerus, pressure in the axilla from crutches – "crutch palsy") – the triceps may be weak or spared depending on the level, while wrist drop is characteristic
  • Triceps skinfold thickness – measured over the back of the mid-arm with calipers to assess nutritional status (body fat)
  • Weakness of the triceps makes it difficult for patients to use walking aids or push themselves up in bed; strengthening exercises are given before crutch walking

Conclusion The triceps brachii, with long, lateral and medial heads inserted into the olecranon and supplied by the radial nerve, extends the elbow; it is tested by the triceps reflex (C7) and used to assess nutritional status.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the gluteal muscles and their importance in nursing.

diagram.caption: Gluteal region showing the muscles, sciatic nerve and safe injection sites

answer_html:
Introduction The gluteal muscles form the buttock and attach the pelvis to the femur. They are important for walking, standing up and maintaining posture, and the gluteal region is a common site for intramuscular injections.

1. Gluteus maximus

  • The largest and most superficial muscle of the buttock
  • Origin – back of the ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament
  • Insertion – the iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur
  • Nerve – inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2)
  • Actions – powerful extension of the hip (rising from sitting, climbing stairs, running) and lateral rotation; it is not much used in ordinary walking on level ground

2. Gluteus medius

  • Lies partly under the gluteus maximus
  • Origin – outer surface of the ilium; insertion – the greater trochanter of the femur
  • Nerve – superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1)
  • Actions – abduction and medial rotation of the hip; keeps the pelvis level when the opposite foot is lifted during walking

3. Gluteus minimus

  • The deepest and smallest; same nerve and actions as the gluteus medius

4. Tensor fasciae latae

  • From the iliac crest to the iliotibial tract; superior gluteal nerve; helps abduction and steadies the knee

5. Deep muscles

  • Piriformis and other small lateral rotators; the sciatic nerve usually emerges below the piriformis

6. Importance in nursing

  • Intramuscular injections:
    • Ventrogluteal site – in the gluteus medius and minimus; located by placing the palm on the greater trochanter, the index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine and the middle finger along the iliac crest; it is the safest gluteal site because it is away from major nerves and vessels and has less fat
    • Dorsogluteal site – the upper outer quadrant of the buttock; carries a risk of injuring the sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels if given wrongly, so many guidelines prefer the ventrogluteal site
  • Pressure ulcers – bony points under the buttocks (sacrum, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters) need frequent turning and padding
  • Trendelenburg sign – if the gluteus medius is weak (e.g. after hip surgery or nerve injury), the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on one leg; patients walk with a lurching gait
  • Rehabilitation – gluteal setting exercises (squeezing the buttocks) keep the muscles strong during bed rest and after hip surgery

Conclusion The gluteus maximus extends the hip, while the gluteus medius and minimus abduct it and keep the pelvis level; the gluteal region provides important injection sites, with the ventrogluteal site the safest and the sciatic nerve the structure to avoid.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall.

diagram.caption: Muscles of the anterior abdominal wall

answer_html:
Introduction The anterior abdominal wall is made mainly of four pairs of muscles arranged in layers, with fibres running in different directions like plywood, which makes the wall strong yet flexible.

1. External oblique

  • The largest and most superficial flat muscle
  • Fibres run downwards and forwards ("hands in the pockets")
  • Its lower border forms the inguinal ligament; its aponeurosis forms the front of the rectus sheath

2. Internal oblique

  • Lies under the external oblique; fibres run upwards and forwards, at right angles to the external oblique

3. Transversus abdominis

  • The deepest flat muscle; fibres run horizontally, like a belt

4. Rectus abdominis

  • A long, strap-like vertical muscle on each side of the midline, from the pubic symphysis and crest to the xiphoid process and 5th–7th costal cartilages
  • Crossed by three tendinous intersections – the "six-pack"
  • Enclosed in the rectus sheath, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles

5. Pyramidalis

  • A small triangular muscle in front of the lower rectus (may be absent)

6. Linea alba

  • A tendinous band in the midline from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, formed by the meeting of the aponeuroses; the umbilicus lies in it

7. Nerve supply

  • Lower six thoracic nerves (T7–T12) and the first lumbar nerve (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves)

8. Functions

  • Support and protect the abdominal organs
  • Raise intra-abdominal pressure – in coughing, sneezing, vomiting, defecation, micturition and the second stage of labour (bearing down)
  • Forced expiration
  • Movements of the trunk – flexion (sit-ups), lateral bending and rotation
  • Maintain posture

9. Applied anatomy

  • Hernias – weak areas allow abdominal contents to bulge out: inguinal, umbilical, epigastric (linea alba) and incisional (through a surgical scar)
  • Surgical incisions – midline (through the linea alba), paramedian, Pfannenstiel (low transverse incision for caesarean section and gynaecological surgery), gridiron (appendicectomy)
  • Divarication of recti – separation of the recti after pregnancy; post-natal exercises help
  • Post-operative care – patients splint the incision with a pillow while coughing; avoid heavy lifting for some weeks to prevent incisional hernia
  • Subcutaneous injections (insulin, heparin) are given into the fat of the abdominal wall, away from the umbilicus

Conclusion The anterior abdominal wall consists of the external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis and rectus abdominis (in the rectus sheath) with the linea alba in the midline; supplied by T7–L1, these muscles protect the viscera, raise intra-abdominal pressure and move the trunk, and their weak points lead to hernias.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the shoulder joint.
answer_html:
Introduction The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint. It is the most mobile joint of the body, but for the same reason the least stable and the most commonly dislocated.

1. Articular surfaces

  • Head of the humerus – large, rounded (the "ball")
  • Glenoid cavity of the scapula – small and shallow (the "socket"), slightly deepened by a fibrocartilaginous rim, the glenoid labrum
  • Only a small part of the head touches the glenoid at any time

2. Ligaments

  • Fibrous capsule – thin and lax, especially below (allowing wide movement)
  • Glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior) – thickenings of the capsule in front
  • Coracohumeral ligament – from the coracoid process to the humerus
  • Transverse humeral ligament – holds the tendon of the long head of the biceps in its groove
  • Coraco-acromial arch – formed by the coracoid process, acromion and coraco-acromial ligament; prevents upward displacement of the head

3. Bursae

  • The subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa reduces friction between the rotator cuff and the acromion and deltoid

4. Factors giving stability

  • Mainly muscles – the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), the long head of the biceps and the deltoid; the glenoid labrum and ligaments help a little

5. Movements

  • Flexion (pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, coracobrachialis)
  • Extension (latissimus dorsi, posterior deltoid)
  • Abduction (supraspinatus starts it, deltoid continues; scapular rotation helps above 90°)
  • Adduction (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi)
  • Medial and lateral rotation, and circumduction

6. Blood and nerve supply

  • Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral and suprascapular arteries
  • Axillary, suprascapular and lateral pectoral nerves

7. Applied anatomy

  • Dislocation – usually anterior (inferior and forward), due to a fall on the outstretched hand; the axillary nerve may be injured (loss of sensation over the deltoid, weakness of abduction)
  • Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) – painful stiffness, common in diabetics and after immobilisation
  • Rotator cuff tears and subacromial bursitis
  • Shoulder subluxation in hemiplegia – support the paralysed arm on pillows and avoid pulling the patient up by the arm
  • Deltoid IM injection site lies over this region (2.5–5 cm below the acromion)

Conclusion The shoulder joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the head of the humerus and the shallow glenoid cavity, with a lax capsule and stability mainly from the rotator cuff; it allows the widest range of movement but dislocates easily.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the elbow joint.
answer_html:
Introduction The elbow joint is a hinge-type synovial joint between the lower end of the humerus and the upper ends of the radius and ulna. It allows bending and straightening of the forearm.

1. Articular surfaces

  • Trochlea of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna
  • Capitulum of the humerus with the head of the radius
  • The joint cavity is continuous with that of the proximal radio-ulnar joint, where pronation and supination occur

2. Ligaments

  • Fibrous capsule
  • Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament – triangular, on the medial side
  • Radial (lateral) collateral ligament – blends with the annular ligament
  • Annular ligament – holds the head of the radius against the ulna (part of the radio-ulnar joint)

3. Movements

  • Flexion – brachialis, biceps brachii, brachioradialis
  • Extension – triceps, anconeus

4. Carrying angle

  • When the extended forearm is supinated, it deviates laterally from the arm by about 10–15° – the carrying angle; it is greater in females and keeps the forearm clear of the hip while carrying objects

5. Important relations

  • In front – the brachialis, the tendon of the biceps, the brachial artery and the median nerve (in the cubital fossa)
  • Behind – the triceps
  • Medially – the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone" – hitting it causes tingling in the little finger)

6. Blood and nerve supply

  • Anastomosis around the elbow from branches of the brachial, radial and ulnar arteries
  • Musculocutaneous, radial, median and ulnar nerves

7. Applied anatomy

  • Supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children – may injure the brachial artery, leading to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture; nurses check the radial pulse, colour, warmth and finger movements, and watch for severe pain on passive finger extension
  • Dislocation of the elbow – usually posterior
  • Pulled elbow – subluxation of the radial head from the annular ligament in young children lifted by the hand
  • Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) and golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis)
  • Venepuncture in the cubital fossa (median cubital vein); BP cuff placed above the elbow

Conclusion The elbow is a hinge joint between the humerus and the ulna and radius, strengthened by collateral ligaments, allowing flexion and extension; its carrying angle, close relation to the brachial artery and ulnar nerve, and common injuries in children are important clinically.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the thoracic cage.
answer_html:
Introduction The thoracic cage is the bony and cartilaginous framework of the chest. It is shaped like a truncated cone – narrow above and broad below – and encloses the thoracic cavity.

1. Components

  • Behind – the 12 thoracic vertebrae and intervertebral discs
  • Sides – the 12 pairs of ribs and their costal cartilages
  • In front – the sternum

2. Sternum (breastbone)

  • A flat bone about 15–17 cm long, in three parts:
    • Manubrium – upper part; its upper border shows the suprasternal (jugular) notch; it articulates with the clavicles and first ribs
    • Body – the longest part; the 2nd to 7th costal cartilages join its sides
    • Xiphoid process – the small lower tip, cartilaginous in youth
  • Sternal angle (angle of Louis) – the junction of the manubrium and body, at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage; used to count ribs

3. Ribs

  • True ribs (1–7) join the sternum directly; false ribs (8–10) join the cartilage above; floating ribs (11–12) are free in front
  • A typical rib has a head, neck, tubercle and a curved shaft with a costal groove on the lower inner border

4. Openings

  • Thoracic inlet (superior aperture) – small; bounded by T1, the first ribs and the manubrium; transmits the trachea, oesophagus, great vessels and nerves
  • Thoracic outlet (inferior aperture) – large; closed by the diaphragm

5. Intercostal spaces

  • Eleven spaces between the ribs, filled by the external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles
  • The neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery and nerve, from above downwards – "VAN") runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib

6. Functions

  • Protects the heart, lungs, great vessels, liver and spleen
  • Breathing – movements of the ribs and sternum change the size of the thorax
  • Supports the shoulder girdle and upper limbs
  • Gives attachment to muscles of respiration, the back and the abdomen
  • Red bone marrow in the sternum and ribs forms blood cells

7. Applied anatomy

  • Rib fractures – painful breathing; multiple fractures may cause a flail chest
  • CPR – compressions on the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid process (may injure the liver)
  • Sternal puncture for bone marrow aspiration
  • Chest drains and thoracentesis – inserted just above the upper border of a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle
  • Chest deformities – pigeon chest, funnel chest, barrel chest in emphysema
  • Counting ribs from the sternal angle to locate the apex beat and ECG lead positions

Conclusion The thoracic cage, formed by the thoracic vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs with costal cartilages and the sternum, protects the thoracic and upper abdominal organs, supports breathing and the upper limbs, and guides CPR, chest drains and ECG placement.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the quadriceps femoris muscle and the vastus lateralis injection site.

diagram.caption: Quadriceps femoris and the vastus lateralis injection site

answer_html:
Introduction The quadriceps femoris is the large muscle on the front of the thigh. It has four parts and is the main extensor of the knee. Its lateral part, the vastus lateralis, is an important intramuscular injection site, especially in infants.

1. Parts and origin

  • Rectus femoris – from the anterior inferior iliac spine and above the acetabulum; the only part that crosses the hip joint
  • Vastus lateralis – the largest part; from the greater trochanter and the lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur
  • Vastus medialis – from the intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera
  • Vastus intermedius – from the front and lateral surfaces of the shaft of the femur

2. Insertion

  • All four parts join to form the quadriceps tendon, which encloses the patella and continues as the ligamentum patellae to the tibial tuberosity

3. Nerve supply

  • Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4)

4. Actions

  • Extension of the knee – standing up, walking, climbing stairs, kicking
  • Rectus femoris also flexes the hip
  • The vastus medialis stabilises the patella

5. Vastus lateralis injection site

  • Location – the middle third of the anterolateral aspect of the thigh, between a hand-breadth below the greater trochanter and a hand-breadth above the knee
  • Advantages – a thick, well-developed muscle free of major nerves and blood vessels; easily reached
  • Preferred IM site for infants and young children, whose gluteal muscles are poorly developed (used for vaccines such as pentavalent and hepatitis B in infants)
  • Technique – position the patient lying down or sitting; in infants hold the leg firmly; insert the needle at 90° (or angled slightly towards the knee in infants)

6. Applied anatomy

  • Knee jerk (patellar reflex) – tapping the ligamentum patellae causes extension of the knee; tests L3–L4
  • Wasting of the quadriceps after knee injury and prolonged bed rest – static quadriceps exercises (tightening the thigh muscle with the knee straight) are taught after knee surgery and fractures
  • Rupture of the quadriceps tendon or ligamentum patellae
  • Femoral nerve injury – inability to extend the knee
  • The rectus femoris site on the front of the thigh is used for self-injection

Conclusion The quadriceps femoris – rectus femoris and the three vasti – inserts through the patella into the tibial tuberosity, is supplied by the femoral nerve and extends the knee; its vastus lateralis is a safe intramuscular site, especially in infants.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of skeletal muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction Skeletal muscle is the voluntary, striated muscle attached to bones. It makes up about 40% of body weight. Its structure is organised in levels, from the whole muscle down to the protein filaments that produce contraction.

1. Connective tissue coverings

  • Epimysium – dense connective tissue around the whole muscle
  • Perimysium – surrounds bundles of fibres called fascicles
  • Endomysium – surrounds each muscle fibre
  • These coverings join at the ends to form tendons that attach the muscle to bone

2. Muscle fibre (muscle cell)

  • Long, cylindrical, multinucleated cells (nuclei at the periphery), up to several centimetres long
  • Sarcolemma – cell membrane; sarcoplasm – cytoplasm with many mitochondria and myoglobin (stores oxygen)
  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum – stores calcium
  • T-tubules – inward extensions of the sarcolemma that carry the impulse deep into the fibre

3. Myofibrils

  • Each fibre contains many myofibrils, which show cross-striations

4. Sarcomere – the unit of contraction

  • The part of a myofibril between two Z lines
  • A band (dark) – contains thick myosin filaments
  • I band (light) – contains thin actin filaments; bisected by the Z line
  • H zone – the central part of the A band with only myosin; M line in its centre
  • Contraction – actin filaments slide over myosin (sliding filament mechanism); the sarcomere shortens, the I band and H zone narrow, while the A band stays the same

5. Contractile and regulatory proteins

  • Actin and myosin (contractile); troponin and tropomyosin (regulatory, controlled by calcium)

6. Blood and nerve supply

  • Rich blood supply; each muscle is supplied by a motor nerve
  • A motor unit – one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies; small units for fine movements (eye), large units for powerful movements (thigh)
  • The nerve meets the fibre at the neuromuscular junction

7. Types of fibres

  • Red (slow, type I) – rich in myoglobin and mitochondria; resist fatigue; for posture (back muscles)
  • White (fast, type II) – contract quickly, tire easily; for quick powerful actions

8. Applied anatomy

  • Atrophy – wasting from disuse, immobilisation or nerve injury; hypertrophy – increase in size with exercise
  • Cramps, strains and muscular dystrophy
  • Rhabdomyolysis – muscle breakdown after crush injury; myoglobin can damage the kidneys (dark urine)
  • Rigor mortis after death – lack of ATP keeps actin and myosin locked
  • IM injections are given into well-vascularised skeletal muscles for faster absorption

Conclusion Skeletal muscle is organised from the whole muscle (epimysium) to fascicles (perimysium), fibres (endomysium), myofibrils and sarcomeres, where actin slides over myosin to produce contraction; its nerve supply forms motor units.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the hip joint under the headings: type, articular surfaces, ligaments, blood and nerve supply, movements and applied anatomy. (1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction The hip joint connects the lower limb to the pelvis. It carries the weight of the body in standing and walking, so it is built for stability as well as movement. Unlike the shoulder, it rarely dislocates in adults except with great force.

(a) Type (1 mark)

  • A ball-and-socket variety of synovial joint

(b) Articular surfaces (1 mark)

  • Head of the femur – about two-thirds of a sphere, covered with hyaline cartilage except at a small pit (fovea)
  • Acetabulum of the hip bone – a deep, cup-shaped socket formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis
  • The acetabular labrum, a fibrocartilaginous rim, deepens the socket and grips the head of the femur; the transverse acetabular ligament bridges the notch at its lower part

(c) Ligaments (3 marks)

  • Fibrous capsule – strong and thick; attached to the margin of the acetabulum and to the neck of the femur (in front along the intertrochanteric line)
  • Iliofemoral ligament (Y-shaped ligament of Bigelow) – in front; the strongest ligament in the body; prevents hyperextension and helps us stand upright with little muscular effort
  • Pubofemoral ligament – below and in front; prevents excessive abduction
  • Ischiofemoral ligament – behind; limits medial rotation
  • Ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres) – inside the joint, from the acetabular notch to the fovea; carries a small artery to the head
  • Transverse acetabular ligament

(d) Blood and nerve supply (1 mark)

  • Arteries – medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, which form a ring at the base of the neck and send retinacular branches up along the neck to the head (the main supply of the head); a small branch of the obturator artery through the ligament of the head; branches of the gluteal arteries
  • Nerves – femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves (nerve to quadratus femoris) and the superior gluteal nerve; the obturator nerve also supplies the knee – hence hip disease may cause pain felt in the knee

(e) Movements (2 marks)

  • Flexion – iliopsoas (main), rectus femoris, sartorius
  • Extension – gluteus maximus, hamstrings
  • Abduction – gluteus medius and minimus, tensor fasciae latae
  • Adduction – adductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis
  • Medial rotation – gluteus medius and minimus (anterior fibres)
  • Lateral rotation – piriformis, obturator muscles, quadratus femoris, gluteus maximus
  • Circumduction – a combination of all these

Factors giving stability

  • Deep acetabulum with labrum, strong capsule and ligaments (especially the iliofemoral), powerful surrounding muscles and atmospheric pressure

Relations

  • In front – the femoral artery, vein and nerve (in the femoral triangle)
  • Behind – the sciatic nerve, separated by the small lateral rotators

(f) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Fracture of the neck of the femur – common in elderly women with osteoporosis after a minor fall; the limb is shortened and externally rotated; the retinacular arteries may be torn, causing avascular necrosis of the head and non-union; treated by fixation or hip replacement
  • Posterior dislocation – in road accidents (knee hitting the dashboard); the limb is shortened, flexed, adducted and medially rotated; the sciatic nerve may be injured
  • Developmental dysplasia (congenital dislocation) of the hip – screened in newborns by Ortolani and Barlow tests; asymmetric thigh folds; treated with abduction splints
  • Osteoarthritis of the hip in the elderly – pain and stiffness; total hip replacement
  • Perthes disease in children
  • Nursing after hip replacement – avoid bending the hip beyond 90°, crossing the legs and turning the leg inwards; keep an abduction pillow between the legs; use raised toilet seats; early mobilisation with a walker; prevent pressure ulcers and DVT
  • Referred pain – hip disease may present as pain in the knee (obturator nerve)

Conclusion The hip joint is a stable ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the femur and the deep acetabulum, strengthened by the labrum, a strong capsule and the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments; supplied mainly by the circumflex femoral arteries, it allows all movements and is clinically important for neck-of-femur fractures, dislocation and hip replacement.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the skull – its bones, sutures, fontanelles and foramina – with applied anatomy. (3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2)

diagram.caption: Superior view of the newborn skull

answer_html:
Introduction The skull is the skeleton of the head. It protects the brain and the organs of special sense, forms the framework of the face and gives passage to cranial nerves and vessels. It consists of the cranium (brain-box) and the facial skeleton.

(a) Bones of the skull (3 marks)

1. Cranial bones (8)

  • Frontal (1) – forehead and the roof of the orbits; contains the frontal sinuses
  • Parietal (2) – the sides and roof of the cranium
  • Temporal (2) – the sides and base; contain the middle and internal ear; the mastoid process lies behind the ear
  • Occipital (1) – back and base; contains the foramen magnum
  • Sphenoid (1) – butterfly-shaped, in the middle of the base; contains the sella turcica for the pituitary
  • Ethmoid (1) – between the orbits; forms part of the nasal cavity; its cribriform plate transmits the olfactory nerves

2. Facial bones (14)

  • Nasal (2), maxillae (2), zygomatic (2), lacrimal (2), palatine (2), inferior nasal conchae (2), vomer (1) and mandible (1)
  • The mandible (lower jaw) is the only movable bone; it forms the temporomandibular joint
  • The maxillae carry the upper teeth and contain the largest paranasal sinuses

Parts of the cranium

  • Vault (calvaria) – the roof
  • Base – divided internally into anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae, which hold the frontal lobes, temporal lobes and the cerebellum and brainstem respectively

(b) Sutures (2 marks)

  • Sutures are immovable fibrous joints between the skull bones
  • Coronal suture – between the frontal and the two parietal bones
  • Sagittal suture – between the two parietal bones in the midline
  • Lambdoid suture – between the parietal and occipital bones
  • Squamous suture – between the parietal and temporal bones
  • Frontal (metopic) suture – between the two halves of the frontal bone in infants; usually fuses in infancy or early childhood
  • Pterion – the H-shaped meeting point of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones on the side of the skull; the bone is thin here and the middle meningeal artery lies beneath it

(c) Fontanelles (2 marks)

  • Fontanelles are membrane-covered gaps between the skull bones of the newborn, at the meeting of sutures
  • Anterior fontanelle – diamond-shaped, at the junction of the coronal, sagittal and frontal sutures; the largest; closes at about 18 months
  • Posterior fontanelle – triangular, at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures; closes at about 2–3 months
  • Sphenoidal (anterolateral) and mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelles – small; close within the first year or so
  • Functions – allow moulding of the head during birth and growth of the brain after birth

(d) Important foramina (1 mark)
