  • Foramen magnum – medulla oblongata, vertebral arteries, spinal accessory nerve roots
  • Cribriform plate – olfactory nerves
  • Optic canal – optic nerve, ophthalmic artery
  • Superior orbital fissure – nerves to the eye muscles (III, IV, VI) and ophthalmic nerve
  • Foramen ovale – mandibular nerve
  • Carotid canal – internal carotid artery
  • Jugular foramen – internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX, X and XI
  • Internal acoustic meatus – facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves
  • Hypoglossal canal – hypoglossal nerve (XII)

(e) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Fontanelle assessment in infants – a bulging anterior fontanelle suggests raised intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus); a sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration; delayed closure occurs in rickets and hypothyroidism
  • Moulding – overlapping of skull bones during labour; disappears in a few days
  • Fracture of the vault – linear or depressed fractures; a blow at the pterion may tear the middle meningeal artery, causing an extradural haematoma (lucid interval, then deterioration)
  • Fracture of the base of the skull – CSF leaking from the nose (rhinorrhoea) or ear (otorrhoea), bruising around the eyes ("raccoon eyes") or behind the ear (Battle's sign); nurses must not pack the nose or ear or pass a nasogastric tube through the nose
  • Craniosynostosis – early fusion of sutures, causing an abnormal head shape
  • Head circumference is measured in children to monitor brain growth (microcephaly, hydrocephalus)

Conclusion The skull has 8 cranial and 14 facial bones joined by sutures; in the newborn, fontanelles allow moulding and brain growth; its foramina transmit nerves and vessels, and nurses use this knowledge in assessing fontanelles and caring for head injuries.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Define Bowman's capsule.
answer_html:
Definition Bowman's (glomerular) capsule is the cup-shaped, double-walled, blind beginning of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus.

Features

  1. Parietal (outer) layer – simple squamous epithelium
  2. Visceral (inner) layer – special cells called podocytes, whose foot processes wrap around the glomerular capillaries and leave filtration slits
  3. Capsular (Bowman's) space – between the two layers; receives the glomerular filtrate
  4. Continues into the proximal convoluted tubule
  5. Bowman's capsule and the glomerulus together form the renal (Malpighian) corpuscle, the site of filtration of blood

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Write a note on the ureter.
answer_html:
Introduction The ureters are two narrow muscular tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.

Features

  1. Length – about 25–30 cm; diameter about 3 mm
  2. Course – begin at the renal pelvis, run down behind the peritoneum on the psoas muscle, cross the pelvic brim and enter the back of the bladder obliquely – this oblique entry acts as a valve and prevents back-flow
  3. Wall – lined by transitional epithelium; smooth muscle moves urine by peristalsis
  4. Three narrow points – pelviureteric junction, crossing of the pelvic brim, and entry into the bladder; stones commonly get stuck here

Applied: ureteric colic (pain from loin to groin); the ureter lies close to the uterine artery and can be injured in hysterectomy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Draw a labelled diagram of the gross structure of the kidney.
answer_html:
How to draw Draw a bean-shaped outline with the hilum facing medially. Inside, shade an outer band (cortex) and draw triangular pyramids in the inner zone (medulla), with their tips pointing to the hilum.

Labels

  1. Fibrous capsule
  2. Cortex – outer, granular zone
  3. Medulla with triangular renal pyramids
  4. Renal columns – cortex dipping between the pyramids
  5. Renal papillae – tips of the pyramids
  6. Minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis
  7. Ureter leaving the hilum
  8. Renal artery and renal vein at the hilum

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the urinary bladder.
answer_html:
Introduction The urinary bladder is a hollow, muscular, distensible organ that acts as a reservoir for urine until it is convenient to pass it.

1. Location

  • In the pelvic cavity, just behind the pubic symphysis
  • When empty it lies wholly in the pelvis; when full it rises into the abdomen and can be felt above the pubis

2. Capacity

  • About 500 ml in adults (can stretch further in retention)
  • The desire to pass urine starts at about 200–300 ml

3. Shape and parts

  • Empty bladder is shaped like a three-sided pyramid; full bladder becomes oval
  • Apex – points forward towards the pubic symphysis
  • Base (fundus) – faces backwards
  • Body – between apex and base
  • Neck – the lowest part, continuous with the urethra

4. Trigone

  • A smooth triangular area on the inner surface of the base
  • Its three corners are the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral orifice
  • Its lining does not form folds; it is very sensitive and a common site of infection

5. Structure of the wall

  • Mucosa – transitional epithelium; thrown into folds (rugae) when empty
  • Submucosa – connective tissue
  • Muscle coat – detrusor muscle – smooth muscle in three layers; contracts to empty the bladder
  • Serous coat – peritoneum on the upper surface only

6. Sphincters

  • Internal urethral sphincter – at the neck; smooth muscle; involuntary
  • External urethral sphincter – around the urethra below; skeletal muscle; voluntary

7. Relations

  • Females – uterus and vagina lie behind the bladder
  • Males – rectum, seminal vesicles and vas deferens behind; prostate below the neck

8. Nerve supply

  • Parasympathetic (pelvic nerves, S2–S4) – contracts the detrusor → micturition
  • Sympathetic (T11–L2) – relaxes the detrusor and tightens the internal sphincter (storage)
  • Pudendal nerve – controls the external sphincter

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Retention of urine (after surgery, enlarged prostate) – relieved by catheterisation
  • Urinary tract infection – commoner in women
  • Bladder training after catheter removal; intake–output charting
  • A full bladder lifts the peritoneum away from the front of the abdomen, so suprapubic puncture or catheterisation can be done without entering the peritoneal cavity
  • A full bladder must be emptied before pelvic surgery and delivery

Conclusion The urinary bladder is a muscular reservoir behind the pubic symphysis with a sensitive trigone, a detrusor muscle and two sphincters, controlled by autonomic and voluntary nerves.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Compare the male and female urethra.
answer_html:
Introduction The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside. It is very different in the two sexes, which is important for catheterisation and urinary infections.

1. Comparison

Feature Female urethra Male urethra
Length about 4 cm about 18–20 cm
Course short, straight, runs downward and forward long, S-shaped with two bends
Parts one part three parts – prostatic, membranous, spongy (penile)
Widest part – prostatic part
Narrowest part external meatus membranous part (and external meatus)
External opening in the vestibule, between the clitoris and the vaginal opening tip of the glans penis
Function urine only urine and semen
External sphincter in the urogenital diaphragm around the membranous part
Infection UTI much more common – short, close to the vagina and anus less common

2. Parts of the male urethra

  • Prostatic part (about 3 cm) – passes through the prostate; widest and most dilatable; receives the ejaculatory ducts and prostatic ducts
  • Membranous part (about 1–2 cm) – the shortest and narrowest; passes through the urogenital diaphragm, surrounded by the external sphincter
  • Spongy (penile) part (about 15 cm) – the longest; runs in the corpus spongiosum of the penis

3. Lining: transitional epithelium near the bladder, changing to stratified columnar and then stratified squamous near the outer opening.

4. Applied – catheterisation

  • Female: insert about 5–7.5 cm (until urine flows); clean the perineum from front to back; identify the meatus carefully (it may be confused with the vagina)
  • Male: insert about 17.5–22.5 cm; hold the penis upwards at about 60–90° to straighten the first bend; use plenty of lubricant; never force against resistance (prostate enlargement, stricture)
  • Strict aseptic technique – catheter-associated UTI is a common hospital infection

5. Other applied points

  • Urethral stricture and urethral injury (pelvic fracture) are more common in men
  • Enlarged prostate narrows the prostatic urethra in elderly men
  • Women should be taught perineal hygiene and to drink enough water to prevent UTI

Conclusion The female urethra is short and straight, so infection is common; the male urethra is long, curved and has three parts, so catheterisation needs more skill.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of a nephron with a labelled diagram.

diagram.caption: Structure of a nephron
labels: descending limb of loop of Henle
ascending limb of loop of Henle

answer_html:
Introduction The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney – the smallest part that can form urine. Each kidney has about one million nephrons, and together they filter the whole blood volume many times a day.

1. Renal corpuscle (Malpighian corpuscle) – in the cortex

  • Glomerulus – a tuft of capillaries
    • Blood enters by the afferent arteriole (wider) and leaves by the efferent arteriole (narrower)
    • This difference keeps the pressure in the glomerulus high, which drives filtration
  • Bowman's capsule – a double-walled cup around the glomerulus that collects the filtrate

2. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) – in the cortex

  • Coiled tube lined by cuboidal cells with a brush border (microvilli)
  • Reabsorbs about two-thirds of the water and sodium, all the glucose and amino acids, and most of the bicarbonate

3. Loop of Henle – dips into the medulla

  • Descending limb – thin; permeable to water
  • Ascending limb – the thick part pumps out sodium and chloride but is impermeable to water
  • Creates a salty medulla that helps concentrate the urine (countercurrent mechanism)

4. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) – back in the cortex

  • Fine-tunes the reabsorption of sodium and the secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions under aldosterone
  • Passes close to its own glomerulus

5. Collecting duct (not strictly part of the nephron)

  • Several DCTs drain into one collecting duct, which runs through the medulla to open at a renal papilla
  • ADH makes its wall permeable to water – concentrated urine is produced when the body needs water

6. Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)

  • Where the DCT touches the afferent arteriole of its own nephron
  • Juxtaglomerular cells (in the arteriole wall) secrete renin – blood pressure control
  • Macula densa (in the DCT wall) senses sodium in the tubular fluid

7. Blood supply of the nephron

  • Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (around the tubules) and vasa recta (around the loops in the medulla)

8. Types of nephrons

  • Cortical nephrons – about 85%; short loops
  • Juxtamedullary nephrons – about 15%; long loops reaching deep into the medulla; important for concentrating urine

9. Functions – filtration, reabsorption, secretion and concentration of urine.

10. Applied / nursing importance

  • Glomerulonephritis damages glomeruli → protein and blood in urine, oedema, hypertension
  • Diuretics act at different sites – furosemide on the loop of Henle, thiazides on the DCT
  • Loss of nephrons in chronic kidney disease is permanent

Conclusion The nephron consists of a renal corpuscle and a long tubule (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT) draining into a collecting duct; its parts work in sequence to form urine and keep the body's fluids balanced.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the kidney under the headings: location, external features, coverings, internal structure, blood supply and applied anatomy. (2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs that form urine. By doing so they remove waste products and keep the volume, composition and pH of the body fluids constant. They also produce hormones, so they are vital organs – life is not possible without at least one working kidney or dialysis.

(a) Location (2 marks)

  • On the posterior abdominal wall, one on each side of the vertebral column
  • Retroperitoneal – behind the peritoneum
  • Extend from about T12 to L3 vertebrae
  • The right kidney lies slightly lower than the left because the large liver lies above it
  • The upper poles are protected by the 11th and 12th ribs
  • They move up and down slightly with breathing
  • Relations
    • In front of the right kidney: liver, duodenum, hepatic flexure of the colon
    • In front of the left kidney: stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, descending colon
    • Behind both: diaphragm, 12th rib, psoas major and quadratus lumborum muscles
    • On top of each: the suprarenal gland

(b) External features (1 mark)

  • Size: about 11 cm long, 6 cm wide and 3 cm thick
  • Weight: about 150 g (a little less in women)
  • Colour: reddish-brown
  • Two poles – upper and lower
  • Two surfaces – anterior and posterior
  • Two borders – convex lateral border and concave medial border
  • Hilum – a slit on the medial border; transmits, from front to back, the renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis (remember "VAP"), along with lymph vessels and nerves

(c) Coverings of the kidney (1 mark) – from inside out

  1. Fibrous (true) capsule – thin, tough, easily stripped from a healthy kidney
  2. Perirenal (perinephric) fat – a cushion of fat around the kidney
  3. Renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) – encloses the kidney, its fat and the suprarenal gland
  4. Pararenal (paranephric) fat – outside the renal fascia

These coverings hold the kidney in place; loss of the fat (in severe weight loss) can cause a "floating kidney".

(d) Internal structure (3 marks) Seen on a coronal (lengthwise) section:

1. Cortex

  • Outer reddish-brown, granular layer just under the capsule
  • Contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules of nephrons
  • Extends between the pyramids as renal columns (of Bertin)

2. Medulla

  • Inner zone made of 8–18 cone-shaped renal pyramids, which look striped because of straight tubules and vessels
  • The base of each pyramid faces the cortex; the apex forms a renal papilla that projects into a minor calyx

3. Collecting system

  • Urine drips from the papillae into minor calyces (7–13)
  • Minor calyces join to form major calyces (2–3)
  • Major calyces join to form the funnel-shaped renal pelvis
  • The renal pelvis narrows at the hilum to become the ureter

4. Renal sinus – the space inside the hilum containing the pelvis, calyces, vessels and fat.

5. Microscopic structure

  • Each kidney has about one million nephrons
  • Each nephron has a glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule, draining into collecting ducts
  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus secretes renin

(e) Blood supply (1 mark)

  • Renal artery – a direct branch of the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2
  • Course inside the kidney: renal artery → segmental arteries → interlobar arteries (between pyramids) → arcuate arteries (at the base of pyramids) → interlobular arteries (in the cortex) → afferent arterioles → glomerulus → efferent arterioles → peritubular capillaries and vasa recta → veins → renal vein → inferior vena cava
  • The kidneys receive about 20–25% of the cardiac output – about 1.2 litres of blood per minute – far more than their size suggests
  • Nerve supply: renal plexus (mainly sympathetic) – controls blood flow
  • Lymph drainage: to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes

(f) Applied anatomy (2 marks)

  • Renal angle tenderness – tenderness in the angle between the 12th rib and the spine in pyelonephritis
  • Renal stones – cause renal colic radiating from the loin to the groin; may block the ureter
  • Kidney biopsy – done with the patient lying prone, through the back; afterwards the patient lies flat and pulse, BP and urine colour are watched for bleeding
  • Polycystic kidney disease, hydronephrosis, renal tumours
  • Acute and chronic kidney disease – may need dialysis or kidney transplantation (the donor kidney is placed in the iliac fossa)
  • Renal injury in road accidents – watch for blood in urine
  • Nursing: strict intake–output charting, daily weight, watching for oedema, hypertension and changes in the colour and amount of urine

Conclusion The kidneys are retroperitoneal, bean-shaped organs from T12 to L3, covered by capsule, fat and fascia. Each has an outer cortex, inner pyramids and a collecting system draining into the ureter, and receives a very rich blood supply through the renal artery; this structure enables them to form urine and maintain the internal environment.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the urinary system.
answer_html:
Introduction The urinary system forms, stores and eliminates urine, and helps keep the internal environment constant.

Parts

  1. Two kidneys – form urine; lie on the posterior abdominal wall on either side of the vertebral column (T12–L3)
  2. Two ureters – muscular tubes about 25 cm long that carry urine to the bladder by peristalsis
  3. Urinary bladder – a muscular reservoir in the pelvis that stores urine (capacity about 400–600 ml in adults)
  4. Urethra – carries urine from the bladder to the exterior; about 4 cm in females and 18–20 cm in males

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the sites of normal constriction of the ureter.
answer_html:
Introduction The ureter is about 25 cm long and 3 mm wide, but it is narrower at three places.

Sites of constriction

  1. Pelvi-ureteric junction – where the renal pelvis joins the ureter
  2. Pelvic brim – where the ureter crosses the common or external iliac artery
  3. Uretero-vesical junction – where it passes obliquely through the bladder wall; the narrowest part

Applied: kidney stones commonly get stuck at these points, causing severe colicky pain (renal or ureteric colic) radiating from the loin to the groin.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the trigone of the urinary bladder?
answer_html:
Definition The trigone is a smooth, triangular area on the inner surface of the base (posterior wall) of the urinary bladder.

Features

  1. Its three angles are formed by the two ureteric openings (above) and the internal urethral orifice (below)
  2. Its mucous membrane is firmly attached to the muscle below, so it remains smooth even when the bladder is empty (the rest of the mucosa forms folds)
  3. It is very sensitive – stretching it gives the desire to pass urine

Applied: a common site for bladder stones, infection and tumours; seen on cystoscopy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the coverings of the kidney.
answer_html:
Introduction Each kidney is surrounded by layers that support and protect it.

Coverings (from inside out)

  1. Fibrous (true) capsule – a thin, tough membrane closely covering the kidney; can be stripped off easily from a healthy kidney
  2. Perirenal (perinephric) fat – a layer of fat around the kidney and adrenal gland
  3. Renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) – a fibrous sheath enclosing the kidney, the perirenal fat and the adrenal gland
  4. Pararenal (paranephric) fat – fat outside the renal fascia, more behind the kidney

Applied: loss of fat in rapid weight loss may let the kidney move down (floating kidney – nephroptosis); infection may form a perinephric abscess.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
answer_html:
Definition The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a small, specialised structure at the vascular pole of each glomerulus, where the distal convoluted tubule comes into contact with the afferent arteriole.

Components

  1. Juxtaglomerular cells – modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole; secrete renin
  2. Macula densa – special cells of the distal tubule that sense the sodium chloride content of the tubular fluid
  3. Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells

Function: regulates blood pressure and the glomerular filtration rate through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the structures at the hilum of the kidney.
answer_html:
Introduction The hilum is a vertical slit on the medial, concave border of the kidney, at about the level of L1. It leads into a space called the renal sinus.

Structures (from front to back)

  1. Renal vein – in front
  2. Renal artery – in the middle
  3. Renal pelvis – behind (continues as the ureter)

Memory aid – "VAP" (vein, artery, pelvis – front to back).

Lymph vessels and sympathetic nerves also pass through the hilum.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the blood supply of the kidney.
answer_html:
Introduction The kidneys receive about 20–25% of the cardiac output – about 1,200 ml of blood per minute – although they form less than 1% of body weight. This large supply is needed not for their own nutrition but for filtering the blood.

1. Renal artery

  • Arises from the abdominal aorta at about the level of L1–L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery
  • The right renal artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava
  • Enters the kidney at the hilum, between the renal vein (in front) and the pelvis (behind)

2. Branches inside the kidney (arterial pathway)

  • Segmental arteries (usually five) – supply separate segments; they are end arteries (no connections with each other)
  • Lobar arteries → interlobar arteries – run between the renal pyramids in the renal columns
  • Arcuate arteries – arch over the bases of the pyramids at the cortico-medullary junction
  • Interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries – run outwards into the cortex
  • Afferent arterioles – one to each nephron
  • Glomerular capillaries – where filtration occurs
  • Efferent arterioles – leave the glomerulus; narrower than the afferent arterioles, which keeps the filtration pressure high

3. Second capillary network

  • Peritubular capillaries – around the convoluted tubules of cortical nephrons; absorb reabsorbed water and solutes
  • Vasa recta – long, straight vessels running beside the loops of Henle of juxtamedullary nephrons; help in concentrating urine
  • The kidney is thus a special example of an arterial portal system (two capillary beds in series)

4. Venous drainage

  • Interlobular veins → arcuate veins → interlobar veins → renal vein → inferior vena cava
  • The left renal vein is longer; it crosses in front of the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery and receives the left testicular (or ovarian) and left suprarenal veins

5. Applied anatomy

  • Renal artery stenosis – reduced blood flow stimulates renin release, causing hypertension (renovascular hypertension)
  • Segmental arteries are end arteries – their blockage causes infarction of a segment; this also guides partial nephrectomy
  • Shock and haemorrhage reduce renal blood flow, leading to acute kidney injury – nurses monitor urine output (less than 0.5 ml/kg/hour is a warning sign)
  • Left varicocele – the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein
  • Kidney transplant – the donor renal artery and vein are joined to the recipient's iliac vessels

Conclusion The kidney receives a quarter of the cardiac output through the renal artery, which branches into segmental, interlobar, arcuate and interlobular arteries and afferent arterioles to the glomeruli; efferent arterioles form peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, and blood returns through the renal vein to the IVC.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Explain the anatomical basis of urinary catheterisation in males and females.
answer_html:
Introduction Urinary catheterisation is the insertion of a tube through the urethra into the bladder to drain urine. Knowledge of the length, curves, narrow points and opening of the urethra in males and females makes catheterisation safe, comfortable and infection-free.

A. Female urethra

  • Length – short, about 4 cm
  • Course – almost straight, running downwards and forwards behind the pubic symphysis, embedded in the front wall of the vagina
  • Opening (external meatus) – in the vestibule, about 2.5 cm behind the clitoris and just in front of the vaginal opening
  • Catheterisation points:
    • Position the patient in the dorsal recumbent position with knees bent and apart; good light is essential
    • Separate the labia and identify the meatus; in elderly women it may be hidden near the vaginal opening
    • Insert the catheter about 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) until urine flows, then a little further before inflating the balloon
    • If the catheter enters the vagina by mistake, leave it there as a guide and insert a new sterile catheter into the urethra
  • Short urethra close to the anus means women get urinary tract infections more easily – clean from front to back

B. Male urethra

  • Length – about 18–20 cm
  • Parts:
    • Prostatic urethra – about 3 cm; passes through the prostate; the widest and most dilatable part
    • Membranous urethra – about 1.5–2 cm; passes through the urogenital diaphragm, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter; the narrowest part apart from the external meatus and the least dilatable
    • Spongy (penile) urethra – about 15 cm; in the corpus spongiosum of the penis
  • Two curves (S-shaped):
    • Subpubic curve – fixed, below the pubic symphysis
    • Prepubic curve – mobile; straightened by holding the penis upwards, at about 60–90° to the body
  • Narrowest point – the external urethral meatus
  • Catheterisation points:
    • Hold the penis upright to straighten the prepubic curve; retract the foreskin and clean the glans
    • Instil lignocaine gel into the urethra for lubrication and comfort
    • Insert about 17.5–22.5 cm (7–9 inches) until urine flows, then advance a little further before inflating the balloon (never inflate in the urethra)
    • Resistance at the external sphincter – ask the patient to breathe deeply or bear down gently; never force
    • Enlarged prostate in elderly men may block the catheter – a special catheter or a doctor's help may be needed
    • Replace the foreskin after the procedure to prevent paraphimosis

C. General anatomical points

  • The bladder lies behind the pubic symphysis; a full bladder rises into the abdomen and can be felt above the pubis
  • Aseptic technique is essential because the bladder is normally sterile
  • Secure the catheter and keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder

Conclusion The female urethra is short (4 cm), straight and opens in front of the vagina, while the male urethra is long (18–20 cm), S-shaped and narrowest at the external meatus and membranous part; holding the penis upright, using lubrication, gentle insertion and asepsis make catheterisation safe.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the lobes of the prostate gland.
answer_html:
Introduction The prostate is a walnut-sized male accessory gland lying below the neck of the urinary bladder, surrounding the first part of the urethra. It weighs about 20 g.

Lobes of the prostate (five)

  1. Anterior lobe (isthmus) – in front of the urethra; contains little glandular tissue
  2. Posterior lobe – behind the urethra; felt on rectal examination; common site of carcinoma
  3. Median (middle) lobe – between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts; enlarges in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and blocks the bladder neck
  4. Two lateral lobes – right and left; form the bulk of the gland

(Modern descriptions divide it into zones – peripheral, central and transition.)

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: List the ligaments that support the uterus.
answer_html:
Introduction The uterus is held in its normal anteverted, anteflexed position by ligaments and the pelvic floor.

Ligaments of the uterus

  1. Transverse cervical (cardinal or Mackenrodt's) ligaments – from the cervix to the side walls of the pelvis; the main support
  2. Uterosacral ligaments – from the cervix backwards to the sacrum
  3. Pubocervical ligaments – from the cervix forwards to the pubis
  4. Round ligaments – from the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia majora; maintain anteversion
  5. Broad ligaments – double folds of peritoneum on each side; give little real support

Other supports: pelvic floor muscles (levator ani) and the perineal body.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the fallopian tube.
answer_html:
Introduction Each fallopian (uterine) tube is about 10 cm long and carries the ovum from the ovary to the uterus.

Parts (from the uterus outwards)

  1. Interstitial (intramural) part – lies within the wall of the uterus; the narrowest part
  2. Isthmus – narrow, straight part next to the uterus; site of tubal ligation (sterilisation)
  3. Ampulla – the widest and longest part; usual site of fertilisation and of ectopic pregnancy
  4. Infundibulum – funnel-shaped outer end opening into the peritoneal cavity; has finger-like fimbriae that catch the ovum

Lining: ciliated columnar epithelium – cilia and peristalsis move the ovum towards the uterus.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the ovary.
answer_html:
Introduction The ovaries are the two female gonads (primary sex organs). They produce ova (eggs) and the female sex hormones oestrogen and progesterone.

1. Location

  • In the pelvic cavity, one on each side of the uterus
  • Lie in a shallow depression on the side wall of the pelvis called the ovarian fossa

2. Shape and size

  • Almond-shaped, about 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 1 cm thick
  • Smooth before puberty; becomes scarred and irregular after repeated ovulation; shrinks after menopause

3. Attachments

  • Mesovarium – a fold attaching the ovary to the back of the broad ligament
  • Suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament – attaches it to the pelvic wall; carries the ovarian vessels
  • Ovarian ligament – attaches it to the side of the uterus, just below the tube

4. Structure (from outside inwards)

  1. Germinal epithelium – a single layer of cuboidal cells on the surface
  2. Tunica albuginea – dense connective tissue capsule
  3. Cortex – the outer part, containing ovarian follicles in different stages:
    • Primordial follicles – present from birth (about 1–2 million at birth, about 4 lakh at puberty)
    • Primary and secondary follicles – growing under FSH
    • Mature (Graafian) follicle – ruptures at ovulation to release the ovum
    • Corpus luteum – yellow body formed from the ruptured follicle; secretes progesterone
    • Corpus albicans – white scar left when the corpus luteum degenerates
  4. Medulla – the inner part; loose connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves, entering at the hilum

5. Blood supply

  • Ovarian artery – from the abdominal aorta
  • Branches of the uterine artery
  • Veins: right ovarian vein → IVC; left ovarian vein → left renal vein
  • Lymph: to the para-aortic nodes

6. Functions

  • Oogenesis – formation and release of ova (usually one each month)
  • Endocrine – oestrogen (from follicles), progesterone (from corpus luteum), small amounts of inhibin, relaxin and androgens

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Ovarian cysts and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) – irregular periods, infertility
  • Ovarian torsion – sudden severe lower abdominal pain; a surgical emergency
  • Ovarian cancer – often detected late
  • Oophorectomy causes surgical menopause
  • Ovarian pain may be referred to the inner thigh (obturator nerve)

Conclusion The ovary is an almond-shaped gland in the ovarian fossa with a follicle-rich cortex and a vascular medulla; it produces ova and the hormones that control the menstrual cycle and pregnancy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure of the breast.
answer_html:
Introduction The breast (mammary gland) is a modified sweat gland that produces milk to nourish the newborn. It is an accessory organ of the female reproductive system; in men it remains rudimentary.

1. Location and extent

  • Lies in the superficial fascia of the front of the chest
  • Vertically: from the 2nd to the 6th rib
  • Horizontally: from the side of the sternum to the mid-axillary line
  • Rests on the pectoralis major (two-thirds) and serratus anterior (one-third), separated from them by loose tissue called the retromammary space (allows the breast to move)
  • Axillary tail (of Spence) – an extension into the axilla; the upper outer quadrant has the most glandular tissue and is where most cancers arise

2. Structure

  • Glandular tissue
    • 15–20 lobes, arranged like the spokes of a wheel
    • Each lobe is made of lobules, which contain milk-secreting alveoli (acini)
  • Ducts
    • Each lobe drains by a lactiferous duct
    • Each duct widens under the areola into a lactiferous sinus (stores milk)
    • Opens on the tip of the nipple
  • Fibrous tissue
    • Suspensory ligaments of Cooper – fibrous bands from the skin to the deep fascia; support the breast
  • Fat – fills the spaces between lobes; decides the size of the breast (not the milk-producing capacity)

3. Nipple and areola

  • Nipple – a projection at about the 4th intercostal space (in men and young women), with 15–20 duct openings; contains smooth muscle that makes it erect
  • Areola – pigmented circle of skin around the nipple; contains Montgomery's glands (areolar glands) that lubricate during feeding; becomes darker in pregnancy

4. Blood supply

  • Internal thoracic (mammary) artery – medial part
  • Branches of the axillary artery (lateral thoracic, thoracoacromial)
  • Intercostal arteries

5. Lymph drainage (important in cancer spread)

  • About 75% to the axillary lymph nodes
  • Most of the rest to the internal mammary (parasternal) nodes
  • Some to the opposite breast and the abdomen

6. Changes: enlarges at puberty (oestrogen), during pregnancy and lactation (progesterone, prolactin); shrinks after menopause.

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in Indian women – teach breast self-examination every month, about a week after the period
  • Dimpling and "orange-peel" skin (peau d'orange) occur when cancer pulls on Cooper's ligaments or blocks lymphatics; nipple retraction
  • Breastfeeding problems – engorgement, cracked nipples, mastitis, breast abscess; good attachment prevents most of them
  • After mastectomy, care of the arm on the operated side (lymphoedema risk)

Conclusion The breast is a modified sweat gland of 15–20 lobes draining through lactiferous ducts to the nipple, supported by Cooper's ligaments and drained mainly to the axillary nodes – facts that matter in lactation and in breast cancer.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the testis and the male genital ducts.
answer_html:
Introduction The testes are the male gonads (primary sex organs). They produce sperm and the male hormone testosterone. A system of ducts carries the sperm to the outside.

1. Location

  • Two oval glands lying in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity
  • The scrotum keeps them about 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for sperm production
  • They descend from the abdomen into the scrotum before birth

2. Size: about 4–5 cm long, 2.5 cm wide and 3 cm thick.

3. Coverings

  • Tunica vaginalis – a double serous sac around the front and sides
  • Tunica albuginea – a tough fibrous capsule
  • Tunica vasculosa – the inner vascular layer

4. Internal structure

  • Fibrous septa divide each testis into 200–300 lobules
  • Each lobule contains 1–4 highly coiled seminiferous tubules, which contain:
    • Spermatogenic cells – go through stages to form sperm
    • Sertoli cells – support and nourish developing sperm
  • Leydig (interstitial) cells – lie between the tubules; secrete testosterone

5. Genital ducts (path of sperm)

  1. Seminiferous tubules → straight tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules
  2. Epididymis – a highly coiled tube about 6 m long, lying on the back of the testis (head, body, tail); stores sperm and helps them mature and become motile
  3. Vas deferens (ductus deferens) – about 45 cm long; runs in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal into the pelvis
  4. Joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra
  5. Urethra – carries semen to the outside

6. Spermatic cord – contains the vas deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform plexus of veins, lymph vessels and nerves.

7. Accessory glands

  • Seminal vesicles – produce most of the seminal fluid (rich in fructose)
  • Prostate gland – thin, milky, alkaline fluid
  • Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands – mucus

8. Blood supply: testicular artery from the abdominal aorta; veins form the pampiniform plexus.

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Undescended testis – should be corrected early; otherwise risk of infertility and cancer
  • Torsion of the testis – sudden severe pain; surgery within hours
  • Hydrocele (fluid in tunica vaginalis), varicocele (dilated veins)
  • Vasectomy – cutting and tying the vas deferens; a simple, permanent method of male sterilisation
  • Mumps orchitis can cause infertility

Conclusion The testes in the scrotum produce sperm in the seminiferous tubules and testosterone in the Leydig cells; sperm travel through the epididymis, vas deferens and ejaculatory duct to the urethra.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the uterus under the headings: location and position, parts, structure of the wall, supports, blood supply and applied anatomy. (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1)

diagram.caption: Uterus, tubes and ovaries - front view

answer_html:
Introduction The uterus (womb) is a hollow, thick-walled, muscular organ of the female reproductive system. It receives the fertilised ovum, nourishes and protects the developing foetus for nine months, and expels it at birth. Every month, in the absence of pregnancy, its lining is shed as menstruation.

(a) Location and position (2 marks)

  • Lies in the true pelvis
  • In front: urinary bladder (separated by the uterovesical pouch)
  • Behind: rectum (separated by the rectouterine pouch – pouch of Douglas, the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity)
  • On each side: broad ligaments, fallopian tubes and ovaries
  • Below: continuous with the vagina
  • Size in an adult woman who has not given birth: about 7.5 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick (remember 3 × 2 × 1 inches)
  • Weight: about 50–60 g; increases to about 1 kg at the end of pregnancy
  • Normal position:
    • Anteverted – the long axis of the uterus is tilted forward on the vagina (about 90°)
    • Anteflexed – the body is bent forward on the cervix
  • In about one in five women the uterus is retroverted (tilted backward), usually harmless

(b) Parts (2 marks)

  1. Fundus – the dome-shaped upper part above the openings of the fallopian tubes
  2. Body (corpus) – the main part; its cavity is triangular when seen from the front
  3. Cornua – the upper corners where the tubes enter
  4. Isthmus – a narrow part about 0.5 cm long between body and cervix; becomes the lower uterine segment in late pregnancy (site of the incision in caesarean section)
  5. Cervix – the lower, cylindrical neck, about 2.5 cm long
    • Supravaginal part and vaginal part (projects into the vagina)
    • Internal os – opens into the uterine cavity
    • External os – opens into the vagina; round in women who have not given birth and slit-like after vaginal delivery
    • The cervical canal is lined by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium; the vaginal part by squamous epithelium

(c) Structure of the wall (2 marks)

  1. Endometrium – inner mucous membrane
    • Simple columnar epithelium with uterine glands
    • Functional layer – thickens each month and is shed during menstruation
    • Basal layer – remains and regenerates the functional layer
    • In pregnancy it becomes the decidua
  2. Myometrium – thick middle layer of smooth muscle in three layers
    • The middle layer has criss-cross fibres around blood vessels that act as "living ligatures" – after delivery they contract and squeeze the vessels shut, controlling bleeding
    • Contractions expel the foetus during labour
  3. Perimetrium – outer serous covering of peritoneum

(d) Supports of the uterus (2 marks) 1. Ligaments

  • Transverse cervical (cardinal or Mackenrodt's) ligaments – the main support; from the cervix to the side walls of the pelvis
  • Uterosacral ligaments – hold the cervix back towards the sacrum
  • Pubocervical ligaments – from the cervix to the pubis
  • Round ligaments – keep the uterus anteverted; pass through the inguinal canal
  • Broad ligaments – peritoneal folds containing the tubes, vessels and ovarian ligament; little support

2. Pelvic floor

  • Levator ani muscles and the perineal body support the uterus from below

3. Position – anteversion places the uterus over the bladder, which helps prevent it slipping down

(e) Blood and nerve supply (1 mark)

  • Uterine artery – a branch of the internal iliac artery; runs in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter about 2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge") – a danger point during hysterectomy
  • Ovarian artery anastomoses with it
  • Veins drain into the internal iliac veins
  • Lymph: to the internal and external iliac and para-aortic nodes
  • Nerves: autonomic fibres through the pelvic plexuses; pain of labour travels with sympathetic fibres

(f) Functions and applied anatomy (1 mark) Functions: menstruation, receiving and implanting the fertilised ovum, nourishing and protecting the foetus (with the placenta), expelling the foetus and placenta in labour.

Applied

  • Uterine prolapse – weakness of the cardinal ligaments and pelvic floor (multiple deliveries, heavy work)
  • Fibroids (leiomyomas) – common benign tumours; heavy periods
  • Carcinoma of the cervix – a leading cancer in Indian women; screened by Pap smear or VIA; HPV vaccination prevents it
  • Postpartum haemorrhage – when the uterus fails to contract after delivery; fundal massage and oxytocin help the "living ligatures" work
  • Fundal height is measured in pregnancy to judge foetal growth
  • Procedures: D&C, hysterectomy, caesarean section through the lower uterine segment

Conclusion The uterus is a pear-shaped muscular organ in the true pelvis, normally anteverted and anteflexed, with a fundus, body, isthmus and cervix. Its three-layered wall, strong ligamentous supports and rich blood supply from the uterine arteries suit it for menstruation, pregnancy and labour, and explain conditions such as prolapse and postpartum haemorrhage.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the accessory glands of the male reproductive system.
answer_html:
Introduction The accessory glands add secretions to the sperm to form semen.

Glands

  1. Seminal vesicles (two) – behind the bladder; produce about 60–70% of semen; secretion contains fructose (energy for sperm) and prostaglandins
  2. Prostate gland (one) – surrounds the beginning of the urethra; produces about 20–30% of semen; thin, milky fluid with enzymes (including prostate-specific antigen), citric acid and zinc
  3. Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands (two) – below the prostate; secrete a clear mucus that lubricates the urethra and neutralises acidity before ejaculation

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the coverings of the testis.
answer_html:
Introduction Each testis is covered by three layers (tunics), and it lies inside the scrotum with additional coverings derived from the abdominal wall.

Coverings of the testis (from outside in)

  1. Tunica vaginalis – a closed serous sac with parietal and visceral layers; it is a remnant of the peritoneum that came down with the testis
  2. Tunica albuginea – a thick, white, dense fibrous capsule; sends septa inwards to divide the testis into lobules
  3. Tunica vasculosa – the innermost, vascular layer

Layers of the scrotum – skin, dartos muscle, external spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia, internal spermatic fascia.

Applied: fluid collecting in the tunica vaginalis forms a hydrocele.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the pouch of Douglas? State its importance.
answer_html:
Definition The pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) is the fold of peritoneum between the rectum (behind) and the uterus (in front) in females.

Features

  1. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the upright position
  2. Its floor is close to the posterior fornix of the vagina

Importance

  • Pus, blood or fluid in the peritoneal cavity collects here – e.g. blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, pus in pelvic infection
  • Fluid can be aspirated through the posterior vaginal fornix (culdocentesis), and pelvic abscesses can be drained this way
  • It can be felt on vaginal and rectal examination
  • Prolapse of bowel into it causes an enterocele

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the fallopian (uterine) tube.
answer_html:
Introduction The fallopian (uterine) tubes are two muscular tubes, each about 10 cm long, that extend from the upper angles of the uterus to the ovaries. They lie in the upper free border of the broad ligament. They carry the ovum to the uterus and are the usual site of fertilisation.

1. Parts (from the uterus outwards)

  • Interstitial (intramural) part – about 1–2 cm, within the wall of the uterus; the narrowest part
  • Isthmus – about 2–3 cm; narrow, thick-walled; the site usually chosen for tubectomy
  • Ampulla – about 5 cm; the widest and longest part; the usual site of fertilisation and of most ectopic pregnancies
  • Infundibulum – the funnel-shaped outer end; its opening (abdominal ostium) is surrounded by finger-like fimbriae; one long fimbria (the ovarian fimbria) is attached to the ovary

2. Structure of the wall

  • Mucous membrane – folded, lined by ciliated columnar cells (cilia beat towards the uterus) and secretory (peg) cells
  • Muscular layer – inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle; produces peristalsis
  • Serous layer – peritoneum

3. Blood supply

  • Branches of the uterine and ovarian arteries; veins follow the arteries

4. Nerve supply

  • Autonomic nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic)

5. Functions

  • Picks up the ovum at ovulation – the fimbriae sweep over the ovary
  • Site of fertilisation (ampulla)
  • Transports the fertilised ovum to the uterus (about 3–4 days) by ciliary action and peristalsis
  • Nourishes the ovum and early embryo with its secretions
  • Provides a passage for sperm towards the ovum

6. Applied anatomy

  • Ectopic (tubal) pregnancy – implantation in the tube, usually the ampulla; rupture causes severe pain and internal bleeding – an emergency
  • Salpingitis and pelvic inflammatory disease – may block the tubes, causing infertility and ectopic pregnancy
  • Tubectomy (female sterilisation) – a segment of the isthmus is tied and cut, or blocked by rings or clips (laparoscopic)
  • Hysterosalpingography (HSG) – tests tubal patency in infertility
  • IVF bypasses blocked tubes

Conclusion The fallopian tube is a 10 cm tube with interstitial, isthmus, ampulla and infundibulum parts, lined by ciliated epithelium; it picks up the ovum, is the site of fertilisation and transports the zygote to the uterus, and it is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the vagina.
answer_html:
Introduction The vagina is a fibromuscular canal that extends from the vestibule (external opening) to the cervix of the uterus. It is the female organ of copulation, the outlet for menstrual flow and the birth canal.

1. Position and direction

  • Lies in the pelvis between the urinary bladder and urethra in front and the rectum and anal canal behind
  • Directed upwards and backwards, making an angle of about 45° with the horizontal

2. Size

  • The anterior wall is about 7.5 cm and the posterior wall about 9 cm long, because the cervix projects into the upper part of the anterior wall
  • Normally the walls are in contact, but it can stretch greatly during childbirth

3. Fornices

  • The recesses around the projecting cervix: anterior, posterior and two lateral fornices
  • The posterior fornix is the deepest; it is close to the pouch of Douglas

4. Structure of the wall

  • Mucous membrane – stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium arranged in transverse folds (rugae); it has no glands – it is moistened by cervical mucus
  • Muscular layer – smooth muscle; at the lower end, the bulbospongiosus muscle acts like a sphincter
  • Outer fibrous (adventitia) layer
  • The hymen – a thin fold of mucous membrane partly closing the external opening

5. Vaginal environment

  • The epithelium contains glycogen (under the influence of oestrogen), which Doderlein's bacilli (lactobacilli) convert into lactic acid, keeping the vaginal pH acidic (about 4–4.5) – this protects against infection

6. Relations

  • Anterior – base of the bladder and the urethra
  • Posterior – pouch of Douglas (above), rectum (middle) and anal canal with the perineal body (below)
  • Lateral – the levator ani muscles; the ureters lie close to the lateral fornices

7. Blood and nerve supply

  • Vaginal artery and branches of the uterine artery (from the internal iliac artery)
  • Upper part – autonomic nerves (less pain-sensitive); lower part – pudendal nerve (sensitive)

8. Applied anatomy

  • Vaginal examination in labour to assess cervical dilatation and descent
  • Culdocentesis through the posterior fornix
  • Prolapse – cystocele, rectocele
  • Vesicovaginal and rectovaginal fistulae after obstructed labour
  • Vaginal infections – candidiasis and trichomoniasis, more common when the acidity is lost (antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy)
  • Pap smear is taken from the cervix through the vagina; perineal care and avoiding douching preserve normal flora

Conclusion The vagina is a fibromuscular canal from the vestibule to the cervix, with a posterior wall of 9 cm, fornices around the cervix and an acidic environment maintained by Doderlein's bacilli; it serves as the birth canal and is examined in pregnancy and gynaecology.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the prostate gland.

diagram.caption: Prostate gland in relation to the bladder and urethra

answer_html:
Introduction The prostate is a fibromuscular and glandular organ of the male reproductive system that surrounds the beginning of the urethra. It adds a milky secretion to semen.

1. Location and size

  • Lies in the pelvis below the neck of the bladder, behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the rectum (it can be felt by a finger in the rectum)
  • Shaped like an inverted cone, about the size of a walnut (about 4 × 3 × 2 cm; weight about 20 g)

2. Parts

  • Base (upper, against the bladder neck), apex (lower), and anterior, posterior and two inferolateral surfaces
  • Pierced by the prostatic urethra and the two ejaculatory ducts

3. Lobes and zones

  • Lobes – anterior, posterior, median and two lateral lobes
  • Zones (clinical division):
    • Peripheral zone – the largest; the commonest site of cancer
    • Central zone
    • Transition zone – around the urethra; the site of benign enlargement

4. Capsules

  • A true capsule (fibrous) and an outer false capsule (prostatic sheath) of pelvic fascia, between which lies a venous plexus

5. Structure

  • Many tubulo-alveolar glands embedded in fibromuscular tissue; the smooth muscle helps expel the secretion during ejaculation

6. Blood supply and venous drainage

  • Branches of the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries
  • Veins form the prostatic venous plexus, which communicates with the vertebral venous plexus – this explains the spread of prostate cancer to the vertebrae

7. Functions

  • Secretes a thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid (about 20–30% of semen) containing citric acid, enzymes, zinc and prostate-specific antigen (PSA), which liquefies semen and helps sperm motility
  • Its muscle helps close the bladder neck during ejaculation

8. Applied anatomy

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) – enlargement in older men (especially the median lobe and transition zone), causing frequency, nocturia, poor stream and retention of urine; difficult catheterisation
  • Carcinoma of the prostate – usually in the peripheral zone; felt as a hard, irregular nodule on rectal examination; PSA is a screening test; may spread to the spine
  • Prostatitis – painful infection
  • TURP (transurethral resection of prostate) – nurses manage continuous bladder irrigation and watch for bleeding and clot retention

Conclusion The prostate is a walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the prostatic urethra below the bladder, in front of the rectum; it secretes a milky part of semen, and its enlargement (BPH) and cancer are common in elderly men.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the perineum and its importance in obstetrics.

diagram.caption: Female perineum – urogenital and anal triangles

answer_html:
Introduction The perineum is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani), between the thighs. In obstetrics, the term "perineum" often refers to the perineal body – the area between the vaginal opening and the anus – which stretches and may tear during childbirth.

1. Boundaries (anatomical perineum)

  • In front – pubic symphysis
  • Behind – tip of the coccyx
  • On each side – the ischial tuberosities and the ischiopubic rami and sacrotuberous ligaments

2. Divisions

  • A line joining the two ischial tuberosities divides it into:
    • Urogenital triangle (in front) – contains the external genitalia, the urethral opening and, in females, the vaginal opening
    • Anal triangle (behind) – contains the anal canal and the external anal sphincter

3. Perineal body (central tendon of the perineum)

  • A pyramid-shaped fibromuscular mass in the midline between the vagina and the anal canal (in males, between the bulb of the penis and the anus)
  • Many muscles meet here – bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter and fibres of the levator ani
  • Function – supports the pelvic organs (vagina, uterus, rectum); its damage leads to prolapse

4. Nerve and blood supply

  • Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) – supplies the muscles and skin; it is blocked by a pudendal nerve block for perineal anaesthesia
  • Internal pudendal artery

5. Importance in obstetrics

  • Stretching during the second stage of labour – the perineum thins and bulges as the head is delivered ("crowning")
  • Perineal tears:
    • first degree – skin and vaginal mucosa
    • second degree – also the perineal muscles
    • third degree – also the anal sphincter
    • fourth degree – also the rectal mucosa
  • Episiotomy – a planned incision to enlarge the outlet when needed; a mediolateral cut (directed away from the anus) is preferred because it is less likely to extend into the anal sphincter
  • Perineal support during delivery of the head reduces tears
  • Repair and care – suturing in layers; perineal care with clean water after each void and defecation, sitz baths, pain relief, cold packs in the first 24 hours, observation for haematoma and infection
  • Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises after delivery restore muscle tone and prevent incontinence and prolapse
  • Damaged perineal body in multiparous women leads to genital prolapse

Conclusion The perineum is a diamond-shaped region divided into urogenital and anal triangles, with the perineal body as its central support; in obstetrics it stretches during delivery and may tear, so perineal support, timely episiotomy, careful repair and perineal care are essential.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the spermatic cord and the scrotum.
answer_html:
Introduction The scrotum is the pouch of skin that holds the testes, and the spermatic cord is the bundle of structures that suspends each testis and carries its vessels, nerves and duct.

A. Spermatic cord

1. Extent

  • From the deep inguinal ring (in the abdominal wall), through the inguinal canal and superficial inguinal ring, to the posterior border of the testis

2. Contents

  • Ductus (vas) deferens – carries sperm; felt as a firm cord
  • Testicular artery (from the abdominal aorta), artery to the ductus deferens and cremasteric artery
  • Pampiniform plexus of veins – a network of veins around the artery
  • Nerves – genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (to the cremaster muscle), sympathetic fibres
  • Lymph vessels
  • Remnant of the processus vaginalis

3. Coverings

  • External spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia, internal spermatic fascia – derived from the layers of the abdominal wall

B. Scrotum

1. Structure

  • A pouch of thin, pigmented skin with sweat and sebaceous glands and a midline raphe
  • Dartos muscle – smooth muscle under the skin that wrinkles the scrotum
  • Divided by a septum into two compartments, one for each testis

2. Temperature regulation for sperm production

  • Sperm are best produced at about 2–3 °C below body temperature
  • In cold, the dartos wrinkles the skin and the cremaster pulls the testes up towards the body; in heat they relax
  • The pampiniform plexus cools the arterial blood going to the testis (counter-current exchange)

C. Applied anatomy

  • Varicocele – dilated pampiniform veins ("bag of worms"), commoner on the left (the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein); may reduce fertility
  • Testicular torsion – twisting of the cord cuts off blood supply; sudden severe pain; a surgical emergency (surgery within about 6 hours saves the testis)
  • Vasectomy – the vas deferens is felt in the cord, cut and tied (male sterilisation)
  • Inguinal hernia – bowel descends along the cord
  • Hydrocele – fluid in the tunica vaginalis
  • Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) – the testis stays in the abdomen or canal; higher risk of infertility and cancer; checked in newborn examination
  • Nursing – scrotal support after hernia and hydrocele surgery; teach testicular self-examination

Conclusion The spermatic cord runs from the deep inguinal ring to the testis, carrying the vas deferens, testicular artery and pampiniform plexus; the scrotum, with the dartos and cremaster muscles, keeps the testes cooler than the body for sperm production, and both are involved in varicocele, torsion, hernia and vasectomy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the female external genitalia.
answer_html:
Introduction The female external genitalia, together called the vulva (pudendum), are the structures outside the vagina. They protect the internal organs, contain the openings of the urethra and vagina and are sensitive to touch.

1. Mons pubis

  • A rounded pad of fat over the pubic symphysis, covered with hair after puberty

2. Labia majora

  • Two large folds of skin and fat extending back from the mons pubis; outer surface hairy, inner surface smooth with sebaceous glands
  • Homologous to the scrotum in males

3. Labia minora

  • Two thin folds of skin inside the labia majora, without fat or hair
  • In front they enclose the clitoris (forming the prepuce and frenulum); behind they join to form the fourchette

4. Clitoris

  • A small, highly sensitive erectile organ at the front meeting point of the labia minora
  • Homologous to the penis

5. Vestibule

  • The space between the labia minora; contains:
    • External urethral meatus – about 2.5 cm behind the clitoris
    • Vaginal opening (introitus) – behind the urethral opening, partly closed by the hymen in virgins
    • Openings of the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands – at about the 5 and 7 o'clock positions, lateral to the vaginal opening; they secrete mucus for lubrication
    • Openings of the paraurethral (Skene's) glands

6. Vestibular bulbs

  • Erectile tissue on either side of the vaginal opening

7. Perineum

  • The area between the fourchette and the anus

8. Blood and nerve supply

  • Internal and external pudendal arteries
  • Pudendal nerve, ilioinguinal nerve and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve

9. Applied anatomy and nursing

  • Bartholin's cyst and abscess – painful swelling of the lower labium
  • Vulvovaginitis – itching and discharge; good perineal hygiene
  • Catheterisation – the urethral meatus lies just in front of the vaginal opening
  • Perineal tears and episiotomy during delivery involve the fourchette and perineum
  • Perineal care – cleaning from front to back; privacy and dignity during examinations
  • Signs of sexual abuse must be recorded carefully and reported as per law (medico-legal)

Conclusion The vulva consists of the mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris and vestibule with the urethral and vaginal openings and Bartholin's glands; knowledge of these structures is essential for catheterisation, delivery care and perineal hygiene.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Draw a labelled diagram of a neuron.
answer_html:
Introduction The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

How to draw

  • Draw a star-shaped cell body with a large central nucleus
  • From it draw several short, branching dendrites
  • From one side draw a single long axon starting at a cone-shaped axon hillock
  • Cover the axon with segments of myelin sheath, leaving small gaps (nodes of Ranvier)
  • End the axon in branched axon terminals with small synaptic knobs

Labels: dendrites, cell body, nucleus, Nissl granules, axon hillock, axon, myelin sheath, Schwann cell, node of Ranvier, axon terminals.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the cranial nerves.
answer_html:
Introduction There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain. They are numbered in Roman numerals from front to back.

No. Name Type
I Olfactory sensory
II Optic sensory
III Oculomotor motor
IV Trochlear motor
V Trigeminal mixed
VI Abducens motor
VII Facial mixed
VIII Vestibulocochlear sensory
IX Glossopharyngeal mixed
X Vagus mixed
XI Accessory motor
XII Hypoglossal motor

Memory aid for type: "Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More" (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both).

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the meninges and the spaces related to them.
answer_html:
Definition The meninges are three protective membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord.

Meninges (from outside inwards)

  1. Dura mater – thick, tough outer layer; forms folds (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli) and encloses the venous sinuses
  2. Arachnoid mater – thin, web-like middle layer
  3. Pia mater – delicate, vascular inner layer, closely attached to the brain and spinal cord

Spaces

  • Epidural (extradural) space – outside the dura; used for epidural anaesthesia
  • Subdural space – between dura and arachnoid; site of subdural haematoma
  • Subarachnoid space – between arachnoid and pia; contains CSF; used for spinal anaesthesia and lumbar puncture

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the ventricles of the brain and how they are connected.
answer_html:
Introduction The ventricles are cavities inside the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

Ventricles

  1. Two lateral ventricles – one in each cerebral hemisphere; the largest
  2. Third ventricle – a narrow slit between the two thalami
  3. Fourth ventricle – between the pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind

Connections

  • Lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (of Monro) → third ventricle
  • Third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) → fourth ventricle
  • Fourth ventricle → median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka) → subarachnoid space; it also continues into the central canal of the spinal cord

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the structure and types of neurons.
answer_html:
Introduction The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It is specialised to receive stimuli and to conduct nerve impulses. There are billions of neurons in the brain. Mature neurons do not divide, so neurons lost through injury or disease are not replaced.

1. Cell body (soma or perikaryon)

  • Contains a large, central nucleus with a prominent nucleolus
  • Cytoplasm contains Nissl granules (rough ER that makes proteins), neurofibrils and many mitochondria
  • The cell bodies form the grey matter of the brain and spinal cord and the ganglia outside

2. Dendrites

  • Many short, branched processes
  • Receive stimuli and carry impulses towards the cell body

3. Axon (nerve fibre)

  • A single long process arising from the axon hillock; may be over a metre long
  • Carries impulses away from the cell body
  • Myelin sheath – a fatty covering formed by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves and oligodendrocytes in the CNS; insulates the axon
  • Nodes of Ranvier – gaps in the myelin; the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), so myelinated fibres conduct much faster
  • Neurilemma – the outer Schwann cell sheath; helps regeneration of peripheral nerves
  • Ends in axon terminals with synaptic knobs containing neurotransmitters

4. Classification of neurons

A. According to the number of processes

  • Multipolar – many dendrites and one axon; e.g. motor neurons
  • Bipolar – one dendrite and one axon; e.g. retina, olfactory epithelium, inner ear
  • Unipolar (pseudo-unipolar) – a single process that divides into two; e.g. sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia

B. According to function

  • Sensory (afferent) neurons – carry impulses from receptors to the CNS
  • Motor (efferent) neurons – carry impulses from the CNS to muscles and glands
  • Interneurons (association neurons) – connect neurons within the CNS; the most numerous

5. Neuroglia (supporting cells)

  • Astrocytes – support neurons and help form the blood–brain barrier
  • Oligodendrocytes – form myelin in the CNS
  • Microglia – phagocytes of the CNS
  • Ependymal cells – line the ventricles; help form CSF
  • Schwann cells and satellite cells – in the peripheral nervous system
  • Most brain tumours (gliomas) arise from neuroglia, not from neurons

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Demyelinating diseases (multiple sclerosis, Guillain–Barré syndrome) slow or block conduction
  • Injured peripheral nerves can regrow slowly (about 1 mm a day) because of the neurilemma; central neurons cannot – so spinal cord injury and stroke cause permanent damage
  • Neurons are very sensitive to lack of oxygen and glucose – brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes of cardiac arrest

Conclusion A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and a single axon; neurons are classified by their processes and function, and are supported by neuroglia.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the cerebral hemisphere with its sulci, gyri and lobes.

diagram.caption: Lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere

answer_html:
Introduction The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, forming about 85% of its weight. It is the seat of intelligence, memory, voluntary movement and conscious sensation. It consists of two cerebral hemispheres.

1. General features

  • The two hemispheres are separated by a deep longitudinal fissure
  • They are joined in the depth by a thick band of fibres, the corpus callosum
  • Each hemisphere has three surfaces – lateral (superolateral), medial and inferior
  • Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body

2. Surface: gyri and sulci

  • The surface is folded into ridges called gyri separated by grooves called sulci
  • This folding greatly increases the area of the cortex inside the skull

3. Important sulci

  • Central sulcus (of Rolando) – runs from the top of the hemisphere downwards and forwards; separates the frontal and parietal lobes
  • Lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) – a deep cleft on the lateral surface; separates the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above; the insula lies hidden in its depth
  • Parieto-occipital sulcus – on the medial surface; separates the parietal and occipital lobes
  • Calcarine sulcus – on the medial surface of the occipital lobe; the visual cortex lies around it
  • Cingulate sulcus – on the medial surface, above the cingulate gyrus

4. Important gyri

  • Precentral gyrus – just in front of the central sulcus; the primary motor area
  • Postcentral gyrus – just behind the central sulcus; the primary sensory area
  • Superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri – Broca's speech area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus
  • Superior temporal gyrus – contains the auditory area
  • Cingulate gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus – part of the limbic system (emotion and memory)

5. Lobes

  • Frontal lobe – movement, speech, personality, judgement
  • Parietal lobe – body sensation
  • Temporal lobe – hearing, memory, understanding speech
  • Occipital lobe – vision
  • Insula – taste and visceral sensations

6. Internal structure

  • Grey matter on the outside – the cerebral cortex, a few millimetres thick, made of nerve cell bodies
  • White matter inside – nerve fibres:
    • Association fibres – connect areas within one hemisphere
    • Commissural fibres – connect the two hemispheres (corpus callosum)
    • Projection fibres – connect the cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord; they pass through the internal capsule
  • Basal ganglia – masses of grey matter deep in the white matter (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus); control of movement
  • Lateral ventricle – inside each hemisphere

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • A stroke in the left hemisphere causes right-sided weakness (and speech problems if it is the dominant side)
  • Bleeding into the internal capsule is a common cause of hemiplegia in hypertensive patients
  • Damage to the basal ganglia causes Parkinson's disease
  • Head injuries may damage the frontal lobe and change personality

Conclusion Each cerebral hemisphere is folded into gyri and sulci, divided into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes by the central, lateral and parieto-occipital sulci, with grey matter outside and white matter inside.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the spinal cord.
answer_html:
Introduction The spinal cord is the part of the central nervous system lying in the vertebral canal. It is the main pathway between the brain and the body and the centre for spinal reflexes.

1. Extent

  • Begins at the foramen magnum as the continuation of the medulla oblongata
  • Ends at the lower border of L1 (L1–L2) in adults and at about L3 in newborns – the vertebral column grows faster than the cord

2. Size and shape

  • About 45 cm long in men (a little shorter in women), about as thick as a little finger
  • Cylindrical, slightly flattened from front to back
  • Cervical enlargement (C5–T1) – nerves for the upper limbs
  • Lumbar enlargement (L1–S3) – nerves for the lower limbs

3. Lower end

  • Tapers into the cone-shaped conus medullaris
  • A thread of pia mater, the filum terminale, continues down to the coccyx
  • The lower nerve roots hang down in a bundle like a horse's tail – the cauda equina

4. Coverings

  • Dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater
  • The dural sac and subarachnoid space (with CSF) continue down to S2, below the end of the cord

5. Spinal nerves

  • 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
  • Each is formed by a dorsal (posterior) root – sensory, with a dorsal root ganglion – and a ventral (anterior) root – motor
  • So every spinal nerve is mixed

6. Internal structure (cross-section) A. Grey matter – H-shaped (butterfly-shaped) in the centre

  • Anterior (ventral) horns – motor neurons to skeletal muscles
  • Posterior (dorsal) horns – sensory neurons
  • Lateral horns (T1–L2) – sympathetic neurons
  • Central canal – contains CSF

B. White matter – surrounds the grey matter; divided into anterior, lateral and posterior columns (funiculi) containing tracts:

  • Ascending (sensory) tracts
    • Dorsal (posterior) columns – fine touch, vibration, position sense
    • Spinothalamic tracts – pain, temperature, crude touch
    • Spinocerebellar tracts – unconscious position sense to the cerebellum
  • Descending (motor) tracts
    • Corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts – voluntary movements
    • Extrapyramidal tracts – posture and muscle tone

7. Functions

  • Conduction – carries sensory messages up to the brain and motor commands down
  • Reflex centre – for spinal reflexes such as the knee jerk and withdrawal reflex
  • Centres for micturition and defecation (sacral segments)

8. Applied / nursing importance

  • Lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5 – below the end of the cord; the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests passes through L4
  • Spinal cord injury – paraplegia (lower limbs) or quadriplegia (all four limbs); care includes log-rolling, pressure-area care, bladder and bowel care
  • Poliomyelitis destroys anterior horn cells → flaccid paralysis

Conclusion The spinal cord runs from the foramen magnum to L1, gives off 31 pairs of spinal nerves, has central H-shaped grey matter and surrounding white matter tracts, and serves as both a conducting pathway and a reflex centre.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the formation, circulation and drainage of cerebrospinal fluid.
answer_html:
Introduction Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a clear, colourless fluid that fills the ventricles of the brain, the central canal of the spinal cord and the subarachnoid space. It protects and nourishes the brain and spinal cord.

1. Formation

  • Formed mainly by the choroid plexuses – tufts of capillaries covered by ependymal cells that project into the ventricles, especially the lateral ventricles (also the third and fourth)
  • Formed by filtration and active secretion from blood plasma
  • About 500 ml is formed every day, but only about 150 ml is present at any time – so CSF is renewed three to four times a day

2. Circulation

  1. Lateral ventricles
  2. → through the interventricular foramina (of Monro)
  3. → third ventricle
  4. → through the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) – the narrowest part of the pathway
  5. → fourth ventricle
  6. → through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and the two lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka)
  7. → subarachnoid space – CSF flows around the brain (collecting in cisterns) and down around the spinal cord - A small amount enters the central canal of the spinal cord - Circulation is helped by continuous formation, arterial pulsations and movements of the body

3. Drainage (absorption)

  • CSF is absorbed through the arachnoid villi and arachnoid granulations – small projections of arachnoid into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus
  • From there it returns to the venous blood
  • Absorption depends on CSF pressure being slightly higher than venous pressure; the villi act like one-way valves

4. Normal characteristics (briefly)

  • Clear and colourless
  • Pressure about 60–150 mm of water when lying down
  • Glucose about two-thirds of blood glucose; very little protein; very few cells (lymphocytes)

5. Functions (briefly)

  • Cushions the brain and spinal cord against injury
  • Keeps the pressure inside the skull steady
  • Brings nutrients and removes waste products

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Hydrocephalus – blockage of the CSF pathway (commonly at the narrow aqueduct) or poor absorption; in infants the head enlarges and the fontanelle bulges; treated with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt
  • Lumbar puncture – CSF is taken from the subarachnoid space at L3–L4 to diagnose meningitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage, or to give spinal anaesthesia
  • CSF leak from the nose or ear after a skull-base fracture – do not plug the nose or ear; report it
  • Raised intracranial pressure – headache, vomiting, papilloedema

Conclusion CSF is formed by the choroid plexuses, flows from the lateral ventricles through the third and fourth ventricles into the subarachnoid space, and is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid villi.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the neuromuscular junction with a labelled diagram.
answer_html:
Introduction The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the meeting point of a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre. Here the nerve impulse is transmitted chemically to the muscle and makes it contract. It is a special type of synapse.

1. Motor unit

  • One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies form a motor unit
  • Each muscle fibre has one neuromuscular junction, usually near its middle

2. Structure A. Presynaptic part (nerve terminal)

  • As the motor axon reaches the muscle, it loses its myelin sheath and divides into terminal branches
  • Each terminal is swollen and contains:
    • Thousands of synaptic vesicles filled with the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh)
    • Many mitochondria (energy for making ACh)
    • Calcium channels in its membrane

B. Synaptic cleft

  • A narrow gap between the nerve terminal and the muscle membrane
  • Contains a basement membrane rich in the enzyme acetylcholinesterase

C. Postsynaptic part (motor end plate)

  • A specialised, thickened part of the muscle membrane (sarcolemma)
  • Thrown into junctional folds that increase its surface
  • Carries nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

3. Steps of neuromuscular transmission

  1. A nerve impulse (action potential) reaches the axon terminal
  2. Calcium channels open and calcium ions enter the terminal
  3. Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release ACh into the cleft
  4. ACh diffuses across and binds to the receptors on the motor end plate
  5. Sodium ions enter the muscle fibre → end-plate potential
  6. This starts a muscle action potential that spreads over the fibre → the muscle contracts
  7. Acetylcholinesterase rapidly breaks down ACh into choline and acetate, so each nerve impulse produces only one contraction; choline is taken back to make new ACh

4. Properties

  • Transmission is one-way (nerve to muscle)
  • There is a short delay (about 0.5 ms)
  • Can be blocked by drugs and toxins

5. Applied / nursing importance

  • Myasthenia gravis – an autoimmune disease in which antibodies destroy the ACh receptors; drooping eyelids, double vision and weakness that worsens with activity; treated with anticholinesterases (neostigmine, pyridostigmine)
  • Organophosphorus poisoning – very common with pesticides in rural India; the poison inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so ACh accumulates → excess secretions, small pupils, slow pulse, muscle twitching and paralysis; treated with atropine and pralidoxime
  • Neuromuscular blocking drugs (succinylcholine, vecuronium) are used in anaesthesia – the patient needs ventilator support until their effect wears off
  • Snake bite (cobra, krait) venom blocks the NMJ → ptosis and respiratory paralysis; anti-snake venom and ventilation
  • Botulinum toxin prevents ACh release

Conclusion At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine released from the motor nerve terminal crosses the synaptic cleft and acts on receptors of the motor end plate to make the muscle contract; many diseases, poisons and drugs act at this junction.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the parts of the brain. Describe the functional areas of the cerebral cortex. (3 + 7)

diagram.caption: Functional areas of the cerebral cortex

answer_html:
