Introduction The brain is the control centre of the body. It lies in the cranial cavity, protected by the skull, meninges and CSF. It weighs about 1.4 kg in adults (about 2% of body weight) but receives about 15% of the cardiac output and uses about 20% of the body's oxygen.

(a) Parts of the brain (3 marks)

1. Forebrain (prosencephalon)

  • Cerebrum – two cerebral hemispheres; the largest part; thinking, memory, voluntary movement, sensation, speech
  • Diencephalon – the central core
    • Thalamus – the relay station for almost all sensations going to the cortex
    • Hypothalamus – controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, emotions, the autonomic nervous system and the pituitary gland
    • Epithalamus – contains the pineal gland (melatonin)

2. Midbrain (mesencephalon)

  • Connects the forebrain with the hindbrain
  • Contains centres for visual and auditory reflexes (turning the head towards a sound or light)
  • Contains the cerebral aqueduct and the nuclei of the 3rd and 4th cranial nerves

3. Hindbrain (rhombencephalon)

  • Pons – a "bridge" of fibres connecting the cerebellum with the rest of the brain; contains respiratory centres and nuclei of cranial nerves 5–8
  • Medulla oblongata – continuous with the spinal cord; contains the vital centres – cardiac, vasomotor (blood pressure) and respiratory centres; reflex centres for vomiting, coughing, sneezing and swallowing; nuclei of cranial nerves 9–12; the motor tracts cross here (decussation of pyramids)
  • Cerebellum – behind the pons and medulla; maintains balance, posture and muscle tone, and coordinates voluntary movements

The midbrain, pons and medulla together form the brainstem. Damage to the brainstem is life-threatening because of the vital centres.

(b) Functional areas of the cerebral cortex (7 marks) The cortex has different areas for different functions. They are often numbered according to Brodmann's map. Each area may be a primary area (receives or sends signals directly) or an association area (interprets them).

1. Frontal lobe

  • Primary motor area (area 4)
    • In the precentral gyrus
    • Starts voluntary movements of skeletal muscles of the opposite side of the body
    • The body is represented upside down (motor homunculus); the hands, lips and tongue have the largest areas because they make fine movements
  • Premotor area (area 6)
    • In front of the motor area
    • Plans and organises skilled, learned movements (writing, typing)
  • Frontal eye field (area 8) – voluntary movements of the eyes
  • Broca's motor speech area (areas 44, 45)
    • In the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (the left side in most right-handed and many left-handed people)
    • Controls the muscles of speech to form words
  • Prefrontal cortex
    • The front part of the frontal lobe
    • Personality, judgement, planning, concentration, social behaviour, intelligence

2. Parietal lobe

  • Primary somatosensory area (areas 3, 1, 2)
    • In the postcentral gyrus
    • Receives touch, pain, temperature, pressure and position sense from the opposite side of the body
    • Body represented as a sensory homunculus
  • Somatosensory association area (areas 5, 7)
    • Interprets sensations; recognises objects by touch without seeing them (stereognosis)
    • Awareness of one's own body

3. Temporal lobe

  • Primary auditory area (areas 41, 42) – in the superior temporal gyrus; perceives sound
  • Auditory association area (area 22) – interprets sounds
  • Wernicke's sensory speech area – the back part of area 22 in the dominant hemisphere; needed to understand spoken and written language
  • Hippocampus – on the medial side; forms new memories
  • Olfactory area – near the uncus; smell

4. Occipital lobe

  • Primary visual area (area 17) – around the calcarine sulcus; receives impulses from the eyes; seeing
  • Visual association areas (areas 18, 19) – recognise and interpret what is seen (faces, objects, words)

5. Other areas

  • Gustatory (taste) area – in the insula and the lower part of the postcentral gyrus
  • Limbic system (cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, amygdala) – emotions, behaviour, motivation and memory

Summary table

Lobe Main areas Function
Frontal 4, 6, 8, Broca's (44, 45), prefrontal movement, speech production, personality
Parietal 3, 1, 2; 5, 7 body sensation and its interpretation
Temporal 41, 42; Wernicke's (22); hippocampus hearing, understanding language, memory
Occipital 17; 18, 19 vision and its interpretation

(c) Applied aspects

  • Stroke of the left middle cerebral artery → right-sided hemiplegia with aphasia
  • Broca's (expressive) aphasia – the patient understands but speaks slowly, with great effort and few words
  • Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia – speech is fluent but makes little sense, and the patient cannot understand what is said
  • Damage to the prefrontal cortex (head injury, tumour) changes personality and judgement
  • Damage to the occipital cortex causes cortical blindness
  • Epilepsy – the type of seizure depends on the area of cortex involved
  • Nursing: use a picture or communication board, speak slowly in simple sentences, check understanding, position paralysed limbs correctly, prevent falls and pressure injuries, involve the speech therapist and physiotherapist

Conclusion The brain consists of the forebrain (cerebrum and diencephalon), midbrain and hindbrain (pons, medulla, cerebellum). Its cortex has definite areas for movement, sensation, speech, hearing, vision and memory, so the symptoms of brain damage depend on which area is affected.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Define synapse. Name its types.
answer_html:
Definition A synapse is the junction between two neurons (or between a neuron and a muscle or gland cell) where the nerve impulse is passed from one cell to the next.

Parts

  • Presynaptic terminal (with vesicles containing neurotransmitter), synaptic cleft (a narrow gap of about 20 nanometres) and postsynaptic membrane (with receptors)

Types

  1. According to transmission:
    • Chemical synapse – the commonest; uses neurotransmitters (acetylcholine, noradrenaline, dopamine); conducts one way, with a slight delay
    • Electrical synapse – direct passage of current through gap junctions; very fast; two-way
  2. According to the parts that meet:
    • axodendritic, axosomatic and axoaxonic

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Define dermatome. Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition A dermatome is the area of skin supplied by the sensory fibres of a single spinal nerve (one spinal segment).

Examples of dermatome landmarks

  1. C6 – thumb
  2. C7 – middle finger
  3. C8 – little finger
  4. T4 – level of the nipple
  5. T10 – level of the umbilicus
  6. L1 – inguinal region (groin)
  7. L4 – medial side of the leg
  8. L5 – dorsum of the foot and great toe
  9. S1 – lateral border of the foot and little toe

Uses: finding the level of spinal cord injury, checking the level of spinal anaesthesia, and understanding herpes zoster (shingles), whose rash follows a dermatome, and referred pain.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What are the basal ganglia?
answer_html:
Definition The basal ganglia (basal nuclei) are masses of grey matter deep within the cerebral hemispheres, near the thalamus.

Components

  1. Caudate nucleus
  2. Putamen
  3. Globus pallidus (putamen + globus pallidus = lentiform nucleus; caudate + lentiform = corpus striatum)
  4. Functionally related: subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra (in the midbrain)

Functions: planning and smooth control of voluntary movements, maintaining muscle tone and posture.

Applied: Parkinson's disease – loss of dopamine-producing cells of the substantia nigra, causing tremor at rest, rigidity and slow movements; Huntington's chorea – jerky involuntary movements.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: What is the internal capsule? State its importance.
answer_html:
Definition The internal capsule is a compact band of white matter (nerve fibres) in each cerebral hemisphere, lying between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.

Parts: anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular and sublenticular parts.

Fibres carried: motor fibres (corticospinal in the posterior limb, corticobulbar in the genu), sensory fibres (thalamus to cortex) and the optic and auditory radiations.

Importance: because so many fibres are packed into a small area, a small haemorrhage or infarct here (from the thin lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery) causes contralateral hemiplegia, loss of sensation and sometimes loss of half the visual field – the commonest cause of stroke-related paralysis.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the neuroglial cells and state their functions.
answer_html:
Definition Neuroglia (glial cells) are the supporting cells of the nervous system. They do not conduct impulses but support and protect neurons. They are more numerous than neurons and can divide.

A. In the central nervous system

  1. Astrocytes – star-shaped; support neurons, form part of the blood–brain barrier, regulate the chemical environment, form scars after injury
  2. Oligodendrocytes – form the myelin sheath in the brain and spinal cord
  3. Microglia – act as phagocytes (defence)
  4. Ependymal cells – line the ventricles and central canal; help form and circulate CSF

B. In the peripheral nervous system

  1. Schwann cells – form the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves; help nerve regeneration
  2. Satellite cells – surround nerve cells in ganglia

Applied: most primary brain tumours arise from glial cells (gliomas); multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Explain the anatomical basis of lumbar puncture.
answer_html:
Introduction Lumbar puncture is the insertion of a needle into the subarachnoid space in the lower back to collect CSF, measure pressure or give drugs (spinal anaesthesia).

Anatomical basis

  1. In adults the spinal cord ends at the lower border of L1 (about L1–L2), but the subarachnoid space with CSF continues down to S2
  2. Below L2 the space contains only the floating nerve roots (cauda equina), which move away from the needle – so the puncture is done at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 space, below the end of the cord
  3. A line joining the highest points of the iliac crests passes through the L4 spine – used to find the level
  4. Bending the back forward (lateral fetal position or sitting bent forward) opens the spaces between the spinous processes
  5. Layers pierced: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid

After care: lie flat as advised, watch for headache and CSF leak.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the brainstem.

diagram.caption: Parts of the brainstem (anterior view)
labels: cranial nerve roots III to XII

answer_html:
Introduction The brainstem is the stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum and diencephalon above with the spinal cord below. It contains vital centres and the nuclei of most cranial nerves. It consists of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.

1. Midbrain (mesencephalon)

  • The uppermost and shortest part, passing through the opening in the tentorium
  • Cerebral peduncles in front – carry descending motor fibres
  • Tectum behind with four small swellings – superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (auditory reflexes)
  • Contains the cerebral aqueduct (connecting the third and fourth ventricles), the substantia nigra and the red nucleus
  • Nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV (eye movements, pupil constriction)

2. Pons

  • A broad bridge-like part in front of the cerebellum, connected to it by the middle cerebellar peduncles
  • Carries ascending and descending fibres and connects the two halves of the cerebellum
  • Contains the pneumotaxic and apneustic centres that help regulate breathing
  • Nuclei of cranial nerves V, VI, VII and VIII

3. Medulla oblongata

  • The lowest part, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum
  • Pyramids in front – here most motor fibres cross to the opposite side (decussation of the pyramids) – this is why one side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body
  • Olives at the sides
  • Contains the vital centres: cardiac, vasomotor (BP) and respiratory centres
  • Reflex centres for vomiting, coughing, sneezing, swallowing and hiccups
  • Nuclei of cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII

4. Reticular formation

  • A network of neurons throughout the brainstem; the reticular activating system keeps us awake and alert (consciousness)

5. Functions (summary)

  • Pathway for all fibres between the brain and spinal cord
  • Vital functions – heartbeat, BP, breathing
  • Reflexes – pupillary, swallowing, coughing, vomiting
  • Consciousness and sleep–wake regulation
  • Origin of cranial nerves III–XII

6. Applied anatomy

  • Brainstem injury or stroke – may cause coma, breathing problems and cranial nerve palsies with crossed paralysis
  • Raised intracranial pressure may push the cerebellum down through the foramen magnum (coning), compressing the medulla – sudden respiratory arrest; nurses watch for Cushing's triad (rising BP, slowing pulse, irregular breathing), pupil changes and falling GCS
  • Brain death is confirmed by the absence of brainstem reflexes
  • Opioid overdose depresses the respiratory centre

Conclusion The brainstem – midbrain, pons and medulla – connects the brain with the spinal cord, contains the vital cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres and the nuclei of cranial nerves III–XII, and its reticular formation maintains consciousness.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the cerebellum.

diagram.caption: Cerebellum – posterior view and sagittal section

answer_html:
Introduction The cerebellum ("little brain") is the second largest part of the brain. It is concerned with coordination of movement, balance and muscle tone. It works below the level of consciousness.

1. Location

  • In the posterior cranial fossa, behind the pons and medulla, separated from them by the fourth ventricle
  • Separated from the occipital lobes of the cerebrum above by a fold of dura – the tentorium cerebelli

2. External features

  • Two cerebellar hemispheres joined in the midline by a narrow vermis
  • The surface has many narrow, parallel folds called folia
  • Lobes: anterior lobe, posterior (middle) lobe and flocculonodular lobe

3. Internal structure

  • Cortex – outer grey matter with three layers (molecular, Purkinje cell and granular layers)
  • White matter – inside; its branching pattern on section is called the arbor vitae ("tree of life")
  • Deep nuclei in the white matter – dentate (the largest), emboliform, globose and fastigial

4. Connections – the cerebellar peduncles

  • Superior peduncle – to the midbrain (mainly outgoing fibres)
  • Middle peduncle – to the pons (the largest; incoming fibres from the cerebral cortex)
  • Inferior peduncle – to the medulla (incoming fibres from the spinal cord and vestibular system)

5. Functions

  • Coordination of voluntary movements – smooth, accurate, well-timed movements
  • Maintenance of balance and posture (with the vestibular system)
  • Regulation of muscle tone
  • Motor learning – learning skills such as cycling, writing, giving injections

6. Blood supply

  • Superior cerebellar, anterior inferior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (from the vertebral and basilar arteries)

7. Applied anatomy – cerebellar lesions (signs appear on the same side as the lesion)

  • Ataxia – unsteady, drunken gait; broad-based walk
  • Intention tremor – tremor when reaching for an object
  • Dysdiadochokinesia – inability to do rapid alternating movements
  • Nystagmus, slurred (scanning) speech and hypotonia
  • Alcohol intoxication temporarily affects cerebellar function
  • Nursing – fall prevention, assistance with walking and eating, safety in the bathroom

Conclusion The cerebellum lies in the posterior cranial fossa with two hemispheres and a vermis, a folded cortex, deep nuclei and three peduncles; it coordinates movements, maintains balance and muscle tone, and its damage causes ataxia and intention tremor.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the brachial plexus.
answer_html:
Introduction The brachial plexus is a network of nerves that supplies the upper limb. It is formed in the neck and passes through the axilla into the arm.

1. Formation – "Read That Darn Cadaver Book"

  • Roots – the ventral rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1
  • Trunks (in the neck):
    • upper – C5 and C6
    • middle – C7
    • lower – C8 and T1
  • Divisions – each trunk divides into an anterior and a posterior division (behind the clavicle)
  • Cords (in the axilla, named by their relation to the axillary artery):
    • lateral cord – anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks
    • medial cord – anterior division of the lower trunk
    • posterior cord – all three posterior divisions
  • Branches (terminal nerves)

2. Main terminal branches

  • Musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cord) – flexors of the arm (biceps, brachialis); skin of the lateral forearm
  • Median nerve (lateral and medial cords) – most flexors of the forearm and muscles of the thumb; skin of the lateral palm
  • Ulnar nerve (medial cord) – small muscles of the hand; skin of the medial hand (little finger)
  • Axillary nerve (posterior cord) – deltoid and teres minor; skin over the deltoid
  • Radial nerve (posterior cord) – all extensors of the arm and forearm (triceps, wrist and finger extensors); skin of the back of the arm and hand

3. Other branches

  • Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior), suprascapular nerve, pectoral nerves, thoracodorsal nerve, medial cutaneous nerves

4. Applied anatomy

  • Erb's palsy (upper trunk, C5–C6) – from excessive stretching of the neck and shoulder (difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia, fall on the shoulder); the arm hangs by the side, medially rotated, with the forearm pronated – "waiter's tip" position
  • Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1) – from upward pulling of the arm (breech delivery, grabbing a branch while falling); claw hand, sometimes with Horner's syndrome
  • Crutch palsy – pressure in the axilla from badly fitted crutches injures the radial nerve (wrist drop); crutches should leave 2–3 finger-breadths below the axilla, with weight on the hands
  • Positioning during surgery – avoid abducting the arm beyond 90° to prevent stretch injury
  • Axillary nerve injury with shoulder dislocation and fracture of the neck of the humerus
  • Brachial plexus block – regional anaesthesia for arm surgery

Conclusion The brachial plexus, formed by C5–T1, is organised into roots, trunks, divisions and cords and gives the musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, axillary and radial nerves to the upper limb; its injuries cause Erb's and Klumpke's palsies and crutch palsy.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the sciatic nerve.
answer_html:
Introduction The sciatic nerve is the largest and longest nerve of the body. It supplies the back of the thigh and almost all of the leg and foot. It is important to nurses because it can be injured by wrongly placed gluteal injections.

1. Origin

  • From the sacral plexus; roots L4, L5, S1, S2, S3

2. Course

  • Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below the piriformis muscle
  • Enters the gluteal region, lying deep to the gluteus maximus, midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter
  • Descends in the back of the thigh, deep to the hamstring muscles
  • Divides usually at the upper angle of the popliteal fossa into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal (fibular) nerve

3. Branches and supply

  • In the thigh – the hamstring muscles (flexors of the knee) and part of the adductor magnus
  • Tibial nerve – muscles of the back of the leg (calf muscles) and the sole; skin of the sole
  • Common peroneal nerve – winds around the neck of the fibula; supplies muscles of the front and side of the leg (dorsiflexors and evertors of the foot) and skin of the front of the leg and dorsum of the foot
  • Sensory – most of the skin of the leg and foot (except the medial side, supplied by the saphenous nerve)

4. Surface marking in the gluteal region

  • A curved line from a point midway between the posterior superior iliac spine and the ischial tuberosity, to a point midway between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter, and then vertically down the back of the thigh
  • It lies in the lower and inner parts of the buttock – hence dorsogluteal injections must be given only in the upper outer quadrant

5. Applied anatomy

  • Injection injury – an injection given too low or too medially in the buttock may damage the nerve, causing pain, numbness and foot drop; the ventrogluteal site avoids this risk
  • Sciatica – pain radiating down the back of the leg due to pressure on the roots, usually from a prolapsed intervertebral disc (L4–L5 or L5–S1); the straight leg raising test is positive
  • Posterior dislocation of the hip may injure the nerve
  • Common peroneal nerve injury at the neck of the fibula (tight plaster, prolonged leg-crossing, pressure from bed rails or lithotomy stirrups) causes foot drop – pad the area and check foot movements
  • Piriformis syndrome – compression by the piriformis muscle

Conclusion The sciatic nerve (L4–S3), the largest nerve of the body, passes from the pelvis below the piriformis through the lower inner buttock to the back of the thigh, dividing into the tibial and common peroneal nerves; safe gluteal injections and prevention of foot drop depend on knowing its course.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe the thalamus.
answer_html:
Introduction The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon. It is often called the "gateway to the cerebral cortex" because almost all sensory information passes through it before reaching the cortex.

1. Location and shape

  • A pair of large, egg-shaped masses of grey matter, one on each side of the third ventricle
  • The two thalami are usually joined across the ventricle by a small bridge (interthalamic adhesion)
  • Lie above the hypothalamus and medial to the internal capsule

2. Structure

  • Divided into groups of nuclei by a thin Y-shaped sheet of white matter:
    • Anterior nuclei – part of the limbic system; memory and emotion
    • Medial nuclei – emotional behaviour, connections with the frontal lobe
    • Lateral and ventral nuclei – ventral posterior nuclei relay body and face sensations; other ventral nuclei relay signals from the cerebellum and basal ganglia to the motor cortex
    • Lateral geniculate body – relay station for vision
    • Medial geniculate body – relay station for hearing

3. Functions

  • Sensory relay – relays touch, pain, temperature, pressure, taste, vision and hearing to the appropriate areas of the cortex (smell is the only sense that does not pass through it)
  • Crude awareness of pain and temperature
  • Motor control – links the cerebellum and basal ganglia with the motor cortex
  • Consciousness and alertness – with the reticular activating system
  • Emotion and memory – through limbic connections

4. Blood supply

  • Branches of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery

5. Applied anatomy

  • Thalamic stroke – loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body
  • Thalamic pain syndrome – severe burning pain on the opposite side after a thalamic stroke
  • Thalamic involvement in coma and disturbances of consciousness
  • Close relation with the internal capsule – haemorrhage often affects both, causing paralysis with sensory loss

Conclusion The thalamus, a paired egg-shaped mass beside the third ventricle, is the main relay station for sensory impulses to the cortex and also takes part in motor control, consciousness, emotion and memory.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Describe a typical spinal nerve and the plexuses formed by spinal nerves.

diagram.caption: Formation of a typical spinal nerve

answer_html:
Introduction Spinal nerves connect the spinal cord with the body. There are 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. All are mixed nerves – they carry both sensory and motor fibres.

A. Formation of a typical spinal nerve

  1. Dorsal (posterior) root – carries sensory fibres into the spinal cord; has a swelling, the dorsal root ganglion, containing the cell bodies of sensory neurons
  2. Ventral (anterior) root – carries motor fibres from the anterior horn cells
  3. The two roots join in the intervertebral foramen to form the spinal nerve (only about 1 cm long)
  4. The spinal nerve soon divides into:
    • Dorsal ramus – supplies the deep muscles and skin of the back
    • Ventral ramus – larger; supplies the front and sides of the trunk and the limbs; forms the plexuses
    • Meningeal branch – supplies the meninges
    • Rami communicantes (white and grey) – connect with the sympathetic ganglia

B. Plexuses Except in the thoracic region, the ventral rami join and branch to form networks called plexuses.

1. Cervical plexus (C1–C4)

  • In the neck; supplies the skin and muscles of the neck
  • Gives the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) to the diaphragm

2. Brachial plexus (C5–T1)

  • Supplies the upper limb – musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves

3. Lumbar plexus (L1–L4)

  • Supplies the lower abdominal wall and the front and medial side of the thigh
  • Femoral nerve (quadriceps, knee jerk) and obturator nerve (adductors of the thigh)

4. Sacral plexus (L4–S4)

  • Supplies the buttock, back of the thigh, leg, foot and perineum
  • Sciatic nerve, gluteal nerves and pudendal nerve (perineum, external anal and urethral sphincters)

5. Thoracic nerves

  • The ventral rami of T1–T12 do not form a plexus; they run as intercostal nerves (and the subcostal nerve) supplying the chest and abdominal wall in segments (dermatomes)

C. Applied anatomy

  • Prolapsed disc compresses a spinal nerve root, causing pain and numbness in its dermatome (sciatica in L5 and S1)
  • Herpes zoster – the virus lies dormant in a dorsal root ganglion and causes a painful rash along one dermatome
  • Spinal anaesthesia and nerve blocks – the level of block is checked by dermatomes
  • Phrenic nerve injury paralyses the diaphragm
  • Peripheral neuropathy in diabetes affects the longest nerves first (feet) – foot care is important

Conclusion A typical spinal nerve is formed by the union of dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots and divides into dorsal and ventral rami; the ventral rami form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses, while the thoracic nerves run as intercostal nerves.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Name the cranial nerves and state their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, arising from the brain and brainstem. They are numbered in Roman numerals from front to back. Some are sensory, some motor and some mixed (both).

Memory aids

  • Names: "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, Such Heaven!"
  • Type (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both): "Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most"
No. Nerve Type Main functions
I Olfactory sensory smell
II Optic sensory vision
III Oculomotor motor most eye movements, raising the eyelid, pupil constriction, accommodation
IV Trochlear motor eye movement (superior oblique – looking down and in)
V Trigeminal mixed sensation of the face, scalp, cornea, teeth; muscles of chewing
VI Abducent motor eye movement outwards (lateral rectus)
VII Facial mixed muscles of facial expression, taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, tears and saliva
VIII Vestibulocochlear sensory hearing and balance
IX Glossopharyngeal mixed taste from the back one-third of the tongue, swallowing, gag reflex, parotid secretion, carotid sinus reflex
X Vagus mixed swallowing and speech (pharynx, larynx); parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs and gut
XI Accessory motor sternocleidomastoid and trapezius – turning the head, shrugging the shoulders
XII Hypoglossal motor movements of the tongue

Testing in nursing assessment (examples)

  • I – identify familiar smells (coffee, soap) with eyes closed
  • II – visual acuity and fields
  • III, IV, VI – follow a finger with the eyes; pupil reaction to light (important in head injury)
  • V – touch the face; corneal reflex; clench the teeth
  • VII – smile, raise the eyebrows, close the eyes tightly (facial palsy – Bell's palsy)
  • VIII – whisper test, balance
  • IX, X – say "aah", gag reflex, swallowing (check before feeding stroke patients)
  • XI – shrug the shoulders against resistance
  • XII – put out the tongue (deviates to the weak side)

Applied

  • Fixed dilated pupil in head injury – pressure on the oculomotor nerve (an emergency sign)
  • Bell's palsy – facial nerve paralysis; protect the eye on the affected side
  • Trigeminal neuralgia – severe facial pain
  • Loss of gag and swallowing reflexes – risk of aspiration

Conclusion The twelve cranial nerves – sensory, motor or mixed – control smell, vision, eye movements, facial sensation and expression, hearing, swallowing, speech, visceral functions and tongue movements; testing them is part of neurological assessment.

subject: Applied Anatomy
question: Classify the nervous system. Describe the anatomy of the autonomic nervous system – sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions – with their differences. (2 + 6 + 2)

diagram.caption: Sympathetic (thoracolumbar) and parasympathetic (craniosacral) outflow
labels: cranial nerves III VII IX X

answer_html:
(a) Classification of the nervous system (2 marks)

1. Anatomical classification

  • Central nervous system (CNS) – brain and spinal cord
  • Peripheral nervous system (PNS) – 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and ganglia

2. Functional classification

  • Somatic nervous system – controls voluntary skeletal muscles and conveys conscious sensations
  • Autonomic nervous system (ANS) – controls involuntary functions of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands; divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions (and the enteric nervous system of the gut)

(b) Anatomy of the autonomic nervous system (6 marks)

General plan

  • Unlike the somatic system (one neuron from the CNS to the muscle), the ANS uses two neurons in series:
    • a preganglionic neuron with its cell body in the brainstem or spinal cord
    • a postganglionic neuron with its cell body in an autonomic ganglion outside the CNS
  • It is controlled by the hypothalamus, brainstem and limbic system

A. Sympathetic division – thoracolumbar outflow

  1. Origin – preganglionic cell bodies lie in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from T1 to L2
  2. Preganglionic fibres leave through the ventral roots and pass via white rami communicantes to the sympathetic chain
  3. Ganglia:
    • Paravertebral ganglia (sympathetic chain or trunk) – a chain of ganglia on each side of the vertebral column from the base of the skull to the coccyx (3 cervical, about 11–12 thoracic, 4 lumbar, 4–5 sacral ganglia)
    • Prevertebral ganglia – in front of the aorta: coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric ganglia
  4. Fibres – short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibres; one preganglionic fibre connects with many postganglionic neurons, so effects are widespread
  5. Postganglionic fibres reach spinal nerves through grey rami communicantes (to sweat glands, blood vessels and hair muscles of the skin) or form plexuses around arteries to the organs (cardiac, pulmonary, coeliac plexuses)
  6. Adrenal medulla – receives preganglionic fibres directly; it acts like a modified sympathetic ganglion and releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood
  7. Neurotransmitters – acetylcholine at the ganglia; noradrenaline at most target organs (acetylcholine at sweat glands)

B. Parasympathetic division – craniosacral outflow

  1. Origin – preganglionic cell bodies lie in:
    • brainstem nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X
    • the sacral spinal cord, S2–S4
  2. Cranial part:
    • III (oculomotor) → ciliary ganglion → pupil constriction, accommodation
    • VII (facial) → pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia → tears, nasal secretion, saliva (submandibular and sublingual)
    • IX (glossopharyngeal) → otic ganglion → parotid saliva
    • X (vagus) – about 75% of all parasympathetic fibres; supplies the heart, lungs and gut up to the left colic flexure; ganglia lie in the walls of the organs
  3. Sacral part – pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) to the descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, bladder and reproductive organs (micturition, defecation, erection)
  4. Fibres – long preganglionic and short postganglionic; ganglia lie near or within the walls of the organs, so effects are more localised
  5. Neurotransmitter – acetylcholine at both the ganglia and the target organs

(c) Differences between sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions (2 marks)

Point Sympathetic Parasympathetic
Outflow thoracolumbar (T1–L2) craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4)
Ganglia near the spinal cord (chain, prevertebral) near or in the organ walls
Preganglionic fibre short long
Postganglionic fibre long short
Distribution widespread, all over the body limited to the head, viscera and pelvis
Transmitter at organ mostly noradrenaline acetylcholine
Overall effect "fight or flight" – prepares for emergencies "rest and digest" – conserves energy
Heart rate increased decreased
Pupils dilated constricted
Bronchi dilated constricted
Gut movement and secretion decreased increased
Bladder relaxes the wall (retention) contracts the wall (voiding)

Applied anatomy

  • Horner's syndrome – damage to the cervical sympathetic chain: drooping eyelid (ptosis), constricted pupil (miosis) and absence of sweating on the same side of the face
  • Autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury above T6 – a sudden rise in BP triggered by a full bladder or constipation; nurses must check the catheter and bowels at once
  • Drugs – atropine blocks parasympathetic action (dry mouth, fast pulse); beta blockers block sympathetic effects on the heart
  • Sympathectomy – for excessive sweating or poor circulation
  • Vagal stimulation – during suctioning or rectal procedures may slow the heart

Conclusion The nervous system is classified into the CNS and PNS, and functionally into somatic and autonomic systems. The autonomic system uses two-neuron pathways: the sympathetic division (thoracolumbar, short preganglionic fibres, ganglia near the cord, mainly noradrenaline) prepares for fight or flight, while the parasympathetic division (craniosacral, long preganglionic fibres, ganglia in the organs, acetylcholine) supports rest and digestion.
